text:
Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) recently joked (?) about creating his own floating city:

https://t.co/A2ituMlVNF

While Luckey may have been joking, all the parts to build a floating city already exist--someone just needs to put the kit together.

Check out these ten examples of real floating tech, from floating hospitals to floating nuclear plants.

1. Floating nuclear power plants: Russia's Akademik Lomonosov is a barge-mounted nuclear station moored in the Arctic port of Pevek to supply power and heat to remote northern communities [1].

2. Floating hospitals: Military and humanitarian hospital ships such as the U.S. Navy's USNS Mercy and USNS Comfort house 1,000 hospital beds and 12 operating rooms, deploying to coastal regions for disaster relief and emergency medical surges [2].

3. Offshore wind and solar farms: Oceans of Energy's Nymphaea Aurora floats roughly 1,400 solar panels inside the operating Hollandse Kust Noord wind farm, 18.5 km off IJmuiden [3].

4. Floating data centers: Barge-mounted facilities like Nautilus Data Technologies' 6.5 MW Stockton 1 site in California use surrounding river or ocean water for closed-loop cooling without evaporative cooling towers, easing land and freshwater constraints in port cities [4][5]. China's Shanghai Lingang project went further in May 2026, submerging a 24 MW datacentre 10 metres below the surface 10 km off Shanghai and powering it from a nearby offshore wind farm, which its operators report cuts power consumption by more than a fifth against a land-based equivalent [6].

5. Floating space ports: SpaceX's Autonomous Spaceport Drone Ships are modified ocean barges with station-keeping thrusters that hold position hundreds of kilometers offshore to catch returning Falcon 9 rocket boosters [7][8].

6. Floating manufacturing plants: Floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) vessels like Shell's Prelude off Western Australia extract, process, and liquefy natural gas directly over offshore fields, bypassing the need for long subsea pipelines to shore [9][10].

7. Floating cities (cruise ships): Mega-cruise ships like Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas--20 decks high with capacity for roughly 7,600 passengers and 2,400 crew--operate as self-contained floating towns [11][12].

8. Floating airports: USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN-78) puts an entire airfield on a hull and is capable of supporting up to 75 aircraft [13]. In 2026, Electra's two-seat EL2 prototype landed and took off from a 300-foot floating barge used for helicopter parking in Lower Manhattan, a test of a hybrid-electric design that needs under 150 feet of flat surface to launch and land [14].

9. Floating docks: Submersible floating dry docks allow navies and shipyards to flood pontoons, float a vessel inside, and pump the ballast out to lift the ship clear of the water for hull repairs and maintenance [15][16]. China's Shuiqiao barges can jack themselves above the swell and lower bridges to link ship to shore, creating a temporary dock nearly a kilometre out from shore [17].

10. Floating fish farms: Coastal net pens and massive moored offshore rigs like Norway's Ocean Farm 1 raise farmed fish such as salmon in open water to scale seafood production [18].

text:
I was boarding a plane late yesterday morning after a weekend ministry trip to London and received a text from my friend Jonathan Arnold, telling me that Pastor Malcolm Watts had collapsed in the early morning hours. By the time I arrived home, I had received messages from Jonathan and several other friends telling me that Malcolm Watts had died.

I imagine that Pastor Watts’s family, his church, and his many, many friends, especially those in the ministry, are deeply grieving his passing today, yet not as those who have no hope.
Pastor Watts served as the minister of the Emmanuel Evangelical Church in Salisbury, England for fifty years, from 1971-2021, and remained an active member of that church in his retirement, serving the last few years alongside his longtime and close friend John Thackway. Though retired from pastoral ministry, he had continued as editor of the church’s newsletter, The Messenger, as Chairman of the Salisbury Seminary, and as Vice President at the Trinitarian Bible Society, among other ministry and leadership duties.

I first ran across Pastor Watts by listening to his sermons on sermonaudio(dot)com. He was a powerful preacher, whose style often began slowly and then boiled over with controlled passion and pathos. When I eventually met and heard him in person, I had the sense that I was meeting one of the Puritans of old. He was pious and sober, but also warm, friendly and open, sometimes erupting in hearty laughter at things which amused him. He held deep convictions arrived at after much careful and prayerful study. When he reached a conviction which he believed to be Biblical, he was not to be moved.

Pastor Watts and his wife visited us in Virginia back in 2011. He spoke at the Keach Conference that year alongside his friend Joel Beeke (what a conference we had that year!), and he also preached in the morning and afternoon services the Sunday following at CRBC. The messages that stood out to me that weekend: He gave a memorable address on the providential preservation of Scripture at Keach, based on chapter 5 of the 1689 Confession, and a powerful Lord’s Day morning sermon at CRBC on the transfiguration titled “Jesus Only” from Matthew 17:1-9. I also recorded two interviews with him during his visit which I posted as early episodes of Word Magazine (WM 6 on Worship and WM 7 on Church Government).

Pastor Watts not only influenced me by his preaching but also by his writing. Among his most read works is a booklet still kept in print and available online by the Trinitarian Bible Society titled The Lord Gave the Word: A Study in the History of the Biblical Text. Reading this work fueled my own commitment to the traditional Protestant text. He also wrote the booklet, co-authored with David Silversides, The Worship of God. The Importance of Purity of Worship, the Westminster Directory of Public Worship and How Should Our Churches Worship Today, drawn from messages presented at the 1997 Salisbury Conference. Among his many essays published in the Messenger, an article from January 2011 offers a compelling argument for Christian burial rather than cremation and made a deep impression upon me, shaping my own pastoral views on this topic. Also in 2011, he published the book What is a Reformed Church? with Reformation Heritage. I have passed along this book to more than one inquirer or new member prospect at CRBC. More recently he contributed the article on the canon of Scripture in the 2026 Bible League Trust anthology It is Written: A Believer’s Guide to the Doctrine of Scripture.

In 2024 I had the privilege of visiting the Emmanuel Evangelical Church and speaking at the Salisbury Conference on the topic “Experiencing the Word of God.” By this time, Pastor Watts was fully in retirement and was bearing the burden of his wife’s decline, but he attended the conference meetings, listened intently, and was gracious in feedback and hospitality. On that visit, my wife and I were also struck by the number of faithful and mature members in the church who had come to know the Lord and be baptized under Pastor Watts’s ministry and also how many Christian couples had also been married under his ministration. He spent the Lord’s Day afternoon, between morning and evening services, with us at Pastor Thackway’s home and regaled us with many stories from his life and ministry. What a blessed memory.

Last weekend I was in London speaking at a conference marking the 500th anniversary of Tyndale’s NT at Westminster Baptist Church. I heard from others on Sunday that Pastor Watts had also been preaching in London that weekend. He gave what I think was his last message on Saturday, November 14, 2026 at the 135thAnniversary Service of the Uxbridge Road Tabernacle (Reformed Baptist Church). I listened to the sermon today. It is a typically moving and sober sermon from Pastor Watts, focusing on the Lord Jesus Christ as our Prophet, Priest, and King.

Imagine. He preached on Saturday to a gathering of those in the church militant, encouraging and edifying the saints, proclaiming the gospel. Then, on Tuesday morning, he entered into the fellowship of the glory of the church at rest and with her risen and exalted Lord, Jesus Christ.

Now absent from the body his servant is present with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8).

SDG!

Note: I have posted Pastor Watts's sermon from last Saturday at the Uxbridge Road Tabernacle in the comments.

text:
Before the feed is all GTA VI! 

In some of my call testing to boost, I was able to get Lucent at both ends of the call. A call left my house over my copper line. The call left a Lucent 5ESS over a MCI trunk in New York, then landed on a Lucent-heritage P-CSCF in AWS Ohio. Bell Labs, end to end, 40 years apart.

Fun Facts about this call:
1. The normal local route to the Boost number gets “all circuits are busy.” The call only went through because I forced it onto MCI with the 10-10-220 dial-around code.

2. STIR/SHAKEN came back as Attestation C (gateway only) while still showing TN-Validation-Passed. That’s what you get when a call starts on copper: the signature verifies, but it can only vouch for the gateway.

3. The cake I mean codec is a lie. G.711 narrowband audio over copper from the 5ESS at my wire center was transcoded into AMR-WB, a wideband codec, so it’s 8 kHz voice in a 16 kHz container. EVS was offered too, dead last as usual.

4. The radio leg was AT&T LTE (PLMN 310-410), the core was Boost’s, the border was a Nokia SBC in us-east-2, and the origin was a 5ESS in New York. That's a whole lotta Bell Labs; Holmdel would be proud! 

5. My Cisco 9861 logged 52 seconds. The real breakdown was about 21s to set up, 8.3s ringing, and 22.3s talking. The FXO port can’t see answer supervision, so the phone started counting at loop seizure.

6. The copper to my house is about 3,000 ft at roughly 28 mA. That’s probably the healthiest link in the whole chain.

(I'm inferring us-east-2 from the hostname in the SIP headers, which contained use2az2, an AWS Availability Zone in us-east-2)

text:
The “You” in the Machine: Manipulation, Social Media, and the Limits of Free Speech.

Let’s start with something you’ve probably noticed without having a name for it. You put on a video about Carl Jung, and within a minute the narrator is talking straight to you. You’ve always felt different. You see through people. You hide your real self to keep the peace. It feels personal, almost like being recognized. But that video was made once and shown to millions of people.

Today’s lecture asks four questions. What is going on in that moment? How do modern platforms change it? When a society protects free speech, where does persuasion become dangerous enough for the law to step in? And what can you do about the large territory the law leaves alone?

Before we start, a warning. This lecture is going to say “you” to you the whole way through, and by the end you’ll know how to check whether it earned the right to.

Part one is the techniques.

The first technique is synthetic personalization. The linguist Norman Fairclough named it in his nineteen eighty-nine book, Language and Power. It means addressing a mass audience as though each person were being spoken to alone. Advertisers have done this for a century: you deserve a break, you’ve earned this. It turns a broadcast into something that feels like a conversation. And a speaker who seems to be talking with you seems to know you, which quietly gives them authority over you.

The second technique is the Forer effect, also called the Barnum effect. In nineteen forty-eight the psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students what he said were personal personality profiles, based on a test they had taken. Every student actually got the same paragraph, put together largely from an astrology book he’d bought at a newsstand. Asked how well it described them on a scale topping out at five, the class averaged about four and a quarter. The paragraph used statements that fit almost anyone. You have a great need for other people to like and admire you. You can be critical of yourself. You have a great deal of unused potential. Statements like these feel specific, but they aren’t.

Here is something the usual telling of the Forer story leaves out, and I think it explains why the trick works so well. In English, the word “you” does two jobs. Sometimes it means you, the specific person I’m talking to. Sometimes it means anyone at all, as in “you can’t win them all.” Linguists call the second one the generic you. In twenty seventeen, the psychologists Ariana Orvell, Ethan Kross, and Susan Gelman reported in the journal Science that people use the generic you to state norms, things true of people in general. They also found that people reach for it when they’re trying to make sense of something painful. Saying “you” instead of “I” lets a person treat a bad experience as part of the human condition rather than a private failure. In a later paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the same three researchers found that readers feel more connection to passages written in the generic you. On Kindle, readers highlighted those passages more often.

Now put that next to Forer. A Barnum statement is a generic-you sentence dressed as a specific-you sentence. “You have a great need for others to like you” is true as a statement about people. Delivered to you personally, it lands as an insight about you. The listener hears the warmth of being understood that comes with the generic you, and the flattery of being singled out that comes with the specific you, at the same time. That double meaning is the engine of a large share of self-help, astrology, and pop psychology content.

The third mechanism is the self-reference effect. Memory researchers have studied it since Rogers, Kuiper, and Kirker named it in nineteen seventy-seven. People remember information better when they process it in relation to themselves. So the word “you” does more than set a tone. It makes the message stick.

Sticking isn’t the same as believing, though, and the step between them matters. The best-documented route from hearing something to believing it is repetition. In nineteen seventy-seven, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues showed that repeating a plausible statement raises how true people judge it to be. It’s now called the illusory truth effect. Most researchers think it works through fluency: a statement you’ve met before is easier to process, and ease feels like truth. In twenty fifteen, Lisa Fazio and her colleagues found the effect even for statements that people’s own knowledge should have contradicted. People leaned on the feeling of ease and set aside what they knew. So keep two mechanisms apart. Self-reference makes a message memorable. Repetition makes it feel true. And as we’ll see in part two, the feed supplies the repetition.

One more finding marks the edge of all this, and it’s useful. “You” isn’t always persuasive. The marketing researchers Mohamed Hussein and Zakary Tormala, in a paper called You Versus We, studied messages in conflict: workplace disputes, political arguments, online forums. In those settings, messages using “you” came across as aggressive. They were less persuasive, less likely to be shared, and more likely to be censored than the same messages written with “we.” In an analysis of more than a quarter of a million online comments, “you” raised the odds that a moderator removed a comment. So “you” persuades when it’s warm and repels when it accuses. That’s why the manipulative “you” you meet in your feed is almost always flattering. The accusing version gets ignored or deleted.

A fair-minded listener should notice that none of these techniques is dishonest in itself. A good teacher says “you” constantly. So does a drill sergeant, and so does a coach. Second-person address can be the clearest way to teach, and the generic you, as we just saw, is one of the ways people make sense of hard things. The difference between teaching and manipulation is what the “you” is attached to. Ask three questions. Would the statement be true of almost anyone? Does it flatter you by saying you’re rare, gifted, or one of the few who understand? Does it lead somewhere, like a course, a subscription, or a reason to keep watching? When all three answers are yes, the technique is working for the creator, not for you.

Part two is how the platforms amplify it.

These techniques are old. What’s new is the delivery system, and on one point we now have measurements instead of guesses. In twenty seventeen, the marketing researchers Ryan Cruz, James Leonhardt, and Todd Pezzuti studied real brand posts on Facebook and then ran two experiments. Posts that addressed the reader with “you” drew more involvement and better attitudes toward the brand. Their explanation was the self-reference effect from part one: “you” makes readers process the message in relation to themselves. So the chain from the second person, to self-reference, to engagement has been observed on a real platform, not just in a lab.

Now add the feed. A modern feed doesn’t show you what’s true or what’s important. It mostly shows you what people like you kept watching and reacting to. Relatable, flattering, second-person content holds attention. Attention earns reach, and reach earns money. A creator doesn’t have to set out to manipulate anyone. They only have to notice which videos do well and make more of them, and their imitators do the same. Over time the system selects for the technique, the way a river cuts a channel without meaning to. That account is reasoning built from the pieces I’ve described. Nobody has measured the whole chain from start to finish, so hold it as a well-supported model, not a finding.

The feed also supplies the repetition. The same message comes back again and again, from the same creator and from a hundred imitators using the same phrases. That’s the condition the illusory truth research says turns familiar claims into believed ones.

How common is misleading personalized content? I looked for a study that counts the word “you” across whole platforms and didn’t find one. The counts that exist are narrower, like the Facebook brand posts. The best evidence on the content itself comes from mental health advice, which is where Jung-style videos usually sit. In twenty twenty-five, the Guardian asked psychologists and psychiatrists to review the hundred most popular videos under a mental health tips hashtag on TikTok. They judged fifty-two of them to contain misinformation. Some of those videos took ordinary emotions and labeled them as symptoms of illness. That’s the Barnum effect with clinical vocabulary added. In twenty twenty-two, a telehealth company called PlushCare reviewed five hundred such videos and put the misleading share above four in five. But PlushCare sells appointments with doctors and therapists, so its number deserves more caution. The fair summary: misleading, personalized persuasion is common in popular advice content, but we don’t have a clean measure of how common.

Part three is the legal line.

Now the harder question. If manipulation is everywhere, why not ban it? In the United States, the First Amendment answers that, and the line it draws is narrower than most people expect.

First, clear away a myth. People often say you can’t shout fire in a crowded theater. The line comes from Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes in a nineteen nineteen case, Schenck versus United States. The government had jailed Charles Schenck for mailing about fifteen thousand leaflets urging men to resist the military draft. The “clear and present danger” test from that era was used to imprison critics of the war. The theater line was an aside, and it has been stretched far beyond its context ever since. The test behind it was overruled half a century later.

The case that overruled it is Brandenburg versus Ohio, from nineteen sixty-nine. A Ku Klux Klan leader gave a filmed speech at a rally that included talk of “revengeance,” the word he actually used. The Supreme Court overturned his conviction and set the test still used today. The government can punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking only when it’s directed at inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. Abstract advocacy, however ugly, is protected. A crowd being aimed at a target right now is not. Notice who the speaker was in that case. The protection that covers your speech also covered his, and that was deliberate.

The second major line is true threats. In Counterman versus Colorado, in twenty twenty-three, a man had sent hundreds of unwanted Facebook messages to a local singer over about two years. The Court held that to convict someone for a threat, the state must show the speaker at least consciously disregarded a substantial risk that the words would be taken as a threat of violence. That’s a recklessness standard. It asks about the speaker’s state of mind, not just how the words landed.

Beyond those two, the Court has listed only a few historic categories of speech the government may restrict for their content. In United States versus Stevens, in twenty ten, it named obscenity, defamation, fraud, incitement, and speech integral to criminal conduct. It also refused to add new categories just because a kind of speech seems to do more harm than good. Two years later, in United States versus Alvarez, the Court made a point that matters directly for our Jung video: there is no general exception for false statements. Flattery, vague psychology, misleading advice, and one-sided persuasion generally fall outside every category. Under American law, the video that keeps telling you who you are is protected speech. The line moves only when the “you” is selling something with a knowingly false claim, because then fraud comes into view.

There’s a second layer people often miss: the platforms themselves. YouTube and TikTok are private companies. In Moody versus NetChoice, in twenty twenty-four, a majority of the Court wrote that when a platform curates its main feed, it is engaging in its own expression. That suggests the government can’t simply order a platform to carry content it doesn’t want to carry. Be careful with that ruling, though. Its binding part only sent the cases back to the lower courts, and legal scholars still argue over how much of the reasoning will hold.

The pressure can run the other way too, with officials leaning on platforms to take content down. In the same year, in National Rifle Association versus Vullo, a unanimous Court held that officials may not coerce private companies into suppressing speech the officials dislike. But in Murthy versus Missouri, the case about federal officials pressing social media companies, the Court dismissed the suit because the challengers lacked standing. It never decided where persuading a platform ends and coercing it begins. So in practice, the everyday moderation of manipulative content happens through each company’s own rules, which they write, enforce, and change as they see fit.

Part four is the debate.

So where should the dangerous borderline be? Reasonable people split three ways, not two, and I’ll give each side its best case in its own voice. Each will also say what would change its mind.

The first side wants to keep the line narrow. It says: whoever gets the power to decide what counts as manipulation will eventually be someone you disagree with. Speech laws written against one group have a way of being used against another, and the Schenck era is the proof. The Court in Alvarez warned against handing government a list of topics on which false statements can be punished, because such a list has no natural stopping point. Ordinary speech is full of persuasion. Outlaw manipulative technique and you hand prosecutors a tool that fits almost anything, this lecture included. The better answer is more speech, sharper audiences, and skills like the ones in part five. What would change this side’s mind is a narrow rule about platform design, one that never touches the content of speech, that measurably reduces harm and isn’t turned against unpopular speakers.

The second side wants to regulate the machinery. It says: the law was built for soapboxes and pamphlets. A feed that pushes one creator to millions of people, tuned by software to each viewer’s habits, is a different kind of thing. Its supporters mostly don’t want to ban speech. They want rules for the system that distributes it: disclose how content is ranked, offer a feed that isn’t personalized, audit for systemic risks. The European Union’s Digital Services Act leans that way. Every online platform must explain in plain language the main factors its recommendations use. The very largest platforms must also offer at least one feed option not based on profiling, assess their systemic risks, and submit to independent audits. This side’s strongest evidence is new. In twenty twenty-six, the economists Germain Gauthier, Roland Hodler, Philine Widmer, and Ekaterina Zhuravskaya published a field experiment in Nature. About five thousand American users of X were randomly assigned to the algorithmic feed or the chronological one for seven weeks in twenty twenty-three. Switching the algorithm on increased engagement and shifted users’ political opinions in a more conservative direction, especially on which issues they ranked as priorities. What would change this side’s mind is evidence that ranking changes how long people stay and what they see, but not what they believe.

The third side rejects something the first two share: the assumption that the feed is what pushes bad persuasion onto passive viewers. Its clearest statement is a twenty twenty-four review in Nature by Ceren Budak, Brendan Nyhan, David Rothschild, Emily Thorson, and Duncan Watts. They say three popular beliefs outrun the evidence: that the average person sees a lot of false or inflammatory content, that algorithms are mostly responsible for that exposure, and that social media is a primary cause of problems like polarization. Their review found exposure to such content low for most people and concentrated among a narrow fringe strongly motivated to seek it out. This side points to an earlier field experiment. In twenty twenty-three, Andrew Guess and a large team, working with Meta during the twenty twenty election, switched thousands of Facebook and Instagram users to a chronological feed for three months. What people saw changed a great deal, and they spent much less time on the platforms. But their polarization, political knowledge, and other key attitudes did not change significantly. On this view, the problem is demand: people who go looking for this content will find it, whatever the feed does. What would change this side’s mind is a large, well-designed field experiment showing that the algorithm moves the beliefs of ordinary users, not just a motivated fringe.

That brings us to the claim all three sides would switch on: does a feed’s ranking change what people believe, or only what they see and how long they stay? Both big experiments bear on it, and together they show something neither shows alone. Gauthier and colleagues tested the switch in both directions. Turning the algorithm on shifted opinions. Turning it off had no comparable effect. Their explanation: the algorithm led users to follow conservative political activist accounts, and users kept following them after the algorithm was gone. So the Meta experiment and the X experiment may not contradict each other. The Meta study only switched the algorithm off, for people who had already lived with it for years. If the X result holds, switching off was the wrong test. The algorithm’s effect lives in who you end up following, and that outlasts the algorithm itself.

Each side has to concede something to that. The narrow-line side has to concede that “more speech” doesn’t answer an effect that persists through a person’s follow list. The machinery side has to concede that its signature remedy, a feed not based on profiling, is exactly the switch-off condition that showed little effect. If regulation is going to work, the lever is probably earlier: what an algorithm does when it’s first switched on, and whom it leads people to follow. And the third side has to concede that the X result is the kind of evidence it said would change its mind, though one experiment on one platform over seven weeks doesn’t settle the question. One caution covers all of this. These studies measured political attitudes, not belief in pop psychology. Applying them to the Jung video is a reasonable inference, not a finding.

All three sides generally agree that incitement and true threats belong on the dangerous side of the line. The open question is everything below it. So far, that’s being settled more by platform policy and individual judgment than by law.

Part five is the defense you can carry.

The most common reply to everything I’ve said is: sure, but it doesn’t work on me. Researchers have a name for that reply. In nineteen eighty-three, the sociologist W. Phillips Davison described the third-person effect: people expect persuasive messages to influence others more than themselves. It has held up in more than eighty published studies and a meta-analysis. Remember Forer’s students. Every one of them rated the same horoscope paragraph as a close fit for themselves. Feeling immune is part of how the technique works. So the defense has to be a habit, not a feeling.

Here’s the drill. When a video tells you who you are, swap “you” for “everyone” and see if the sentence still works. You’re turning a disguised generic you back into an honest one. If the sentence still works, it was a statement about people in general dressed up as an insight about you. That doesn’t make it worthless. It just isn’t about you.

When a video flatters you, ask what it wants from you next. When it turns hostile and says you’re the problem, notice that this is the same tool aimed the other way. It usually wants you angry enough to share it.

When it makes a specific claim, like a diagnosis, a statistic, or a quote from Jung, treat that as the checkable part and check it.

And one habit the research in part four suggests: if a feed’s lasting effect runs through who you follow, then who you follow is the part you control. Every so often, go through that list and ask how each account got there.

Run that drill on this lecture too. It has said “you” from the first sentence. Some of those were the honest generic kind. A few were me trying to keep your attention. A lecture that holds up under those questions has earned your attention. One that doesn’t hasn’t.

That’s the lecture. The techniques are old, and they work best when they flatter. The platforms reward them at scale, and the newest evidence suggests a feed’s influence can outlast the feed itself. American law draws its hard line only at imminent incitement, true threats, and a few narrow categories. Everything above that line is left to the platforms, to an open scientific question about what feeds actually do to belief, and to each viewer.

text:
No, not for a rebuild. Keep Stroud.

In superflex dynasty, a young QB who can start is the most valuable thing you can own, and Stroud is exactly the kind of player you build around. Penix is the bigger risk. He's had an injury history and has struggled this year. Swapping Stroud for Penix moves you backward at your most important position.

Charbonnet is the right player to sell. Running backs lose value fast, and he's coming off an ACL injury, so moving him now while he's producing is smart rebuilding.

Washington is an interesting piece. He's broken out this year and is still young enough to grow with your roster. The 2027 2nd is a nice add, but it doesn't make up for the QB downgrade.

Counter by taking Stroud out of it. Offer Charbonnet for Washington plus the 2027 2nd. If they want a QB, ask what they'd give for Charbonnet plus a lesser QB, but don't move Stroud unless you're getting a first-round pick or a younger QB with real upside back.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | NOVEMBER 18 — CLOSING BELL

#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

A brutal day for metals. Higher rate expectations, a stronger dollar and growing doubts about demand hit the sector hard.

📉 US FUTURES SETTLEMENTS
🥇 Gold: $3,736.80 | −3.2%
🥈 Silver: $45.00 | −4.8%
🔶 Copper: $5.66/lb | −5.3%

Gold and silver reached their lowest settlements since September 2025. Copper recorded its biggest daily percentage decline since July 2025.

🌎 THE MACRO SQUEEZE
The dollar touched a fresh 19-month high. Waller called for either a half-point December hike or a faster pace of tightening in 2027.

Tonight’s Fed minutes offered little comfort: almost all participants expected further hikes would be appropriate under their economic outlook. Some were willing to consider a larger move if inflation disappointed.

🔶 COPPER’S CONTRADICTION
Prices plunged while China’s copper import premium reached a record $360/tonne. Local physical tightness is colliding with concerns about Chinese demand and the pace of AI investment.

That tension deserves watching closely.

☢️ URANIUM
Uranium shares also struggled. My concern is what weaker equity prices and expensive capital do to project financing. Delayed mines can deepen future supply constraints, even while investors sell the sector today.

🛢️ ONE POTENTIAL RELIEF VALVE
Brent settled at $91.95 and WTI at $83.26 after larger-than-expected US inventory builds. Sustained weakness in energy could help cool inflation, although today it provided little comfort to metals.

I remain bullish on the long-term supply picture. But these sessions underline why cash, funding visibility and position sizing matter.

The companies that can finance their way through the downturn deserve particular attention.

text:
Washington State 

Puget Sound Partnership 

Part 2

Nov. 18, 2026

The Puget Sound Partnership funded the analysis to better understand the broader benefits of investments being made in Puget Sound recovery. Industrial Economics, Incorporated (IEc) conducted the study using detailed spending information from more than 200 restoration projects, with data from the Washington Recreation and Conservation Office, Washington Department of Ecology and Washington State Conservation Commission.

The Partnership coordinates the regional effort to recover Puget Sound, working with Sovereign Indian Tribes, federal, state and local governments, and other partners to identify recovery priorities, track investments and assess progress. The new analysis adds an economic perspective to that work by examining where restoration dollars go and the jobs, businesses, and economic activity they support.

Applying the study’s economic multipliers to restoration-related capital programs represented in Washington’s enacted 2025–2027 budget, researchers estimate that current annual spending supports nearly 7,500 jobs and approximately $1.8 billion in regional business revenues. The calculation includes more than 60 programs and represents spending across a broad range of Puget Sound restoration activities.

The study also notes that the economic activity generated while restoration work is underway is only one category of benefit. Restored ecosystems can provide longer-term benefits through improved water quality, salmon recovery, recreation, tourism, flood protection, fisheries, and other resource-based industries.

Beyond their economic and environmental benefits, restoration projects can strengthen local communities. Restoration sites offer opportunities for students to learn about local ecosystems through hands-on science and environmental education. Volunteer planting and stewardship events bring community members together, while partnerships among local businesses, schools, and non-profit organizations can help build lasting connections and support for restoration efforts.

The Partnership tracks the statis and trends of ecosystem conditions through Vital Sign Indicators. These Vital Signs represent the components of the ecosystem that are important to the Puget Sound recovery community, such as streams, birds, and cultural wellbeing.

About the Leadership Council

The Leadership Council is the governing body of the Puget Sound Partnership. Its seven members are leading citizens chosen from around the Sound and appointed by the Governor to serve four-year terms.

About the Puget Sound Partnership

The Puget Sound Partnership is the state agency formed to lead the region’s collective effort to restore and protect Puget Sound. Working with hundreds of government agencies, Sovereign Indian Tribes, scientists, businesses, and non-profits, the Partnership mobilizes partner action around a common agenda, advances Sound investments, and tracks progress to optimize recovery.

text:
DEKRYPT THE WORLD // AI INTELLIGENCE BRIEF
NOVEMBER 18, 2026
NVIDIA DELIVERS — BUT THE AI POWER STRUGGLE IS GETTING BIGGER

Nvidia just delivered another massive quarter.

Anthropic priced one of the largest technology IPOs in history.

Washington is tightening scrutiny of Chinese AI.

And lawmakers are warning that AI-enabled cyber threats may already be moving faster than U.S. defenses.

The AI race is no longer only about building better models.

It is increasingly about compute, access, security and control.

NVIDIA POSTS ANOTHER RECORD QUARTER

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of:

$115.84 BILLION

Revenue more than doubled year over year, marking Nvidia’s 17th consecutive quarterly estimate beat.

Demand for AI infrastructure remains extremely strong.

But investors remain cautious.

Nvidia shares closed down roughly 2.9% Wednesday and remain about 36% below their October record high.

A major reason:

Leadership uncertainty.

Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has now explicitly ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang despite Huang’s offer to return.

Colette Kress remains interim CEO while executive-search firm Heidrick & Struggles leads the search for a permanent replacement.

Why it matters: Nvidia’s business continues to perform at extraordinary levels, but investors now have to separate the strength of the company from the uncertainty surrounding its leadership.

NVIDIA STOPS SHIPPING ADVANCED AI CHIPS TO CHINA

Nvidia also confirmed that it is no longer shipping its licensed Hopper-generation data-center chips to China.

The company sold roughly:

$2.4 BILLION

of licensed Hopper products to China last quarter.

But Nvidia included no further China shipments in its current outlook.

The company has not said whether the halt is permanent.

Meanwhile, roughly 600,000 H200 chips have reportedly been sitting in Hong Kong awaiting approval for shipment into mainland China.

Why it matters: China is rapidly disappearing from Nvidia’s near-term growth assumptions just as Chinese demand for AI compute continues to rise.

The U.S.–China AI competition is increasingly becoming a battle over access to computing power.

ANTHROPIC PRICES IPO ABOVE EXPECTATIONS

Claude maker Anthropic priced its IPO Wednesday at:

$83 PER SHARE

That is above its marketed range of:

$70–$78

Shares are expected to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under:

ANT

The offering could value Anthropic at roughly:

$1.4 TRILLION

Demand has reportedly been several times greater than the number of shares available.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate reached roughly:

$81 BILLION

as of October 31.

Why it matters: This is the first major public-market test of a frontier AI model company.

If ANT trades strongly Thursday, it could reinforce investor confidence in the entire AI sector.

If it struggles, the market may begin questioning whether AI valuations have moved too far ahead of earnings.

WASHINGTON CONSIDERS DISCLOSURE OF CHINESE AI USE

The Trump administration is considering requiring U.S. companies to publicly disclose when they use Chinese AI models.

The proposal has reportedly been discussed by the Treasury Department and White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.

The goal would not necessarily be to ban Chinese models.

Instead, companies could be required to disclose their use publicly.

Models such as Alibaba’s Qwen are increasingly being used by American businesses for specialized applications.

Why it matters: Washington’s focus is expanding beyond Chinese chips.

Now Chinese AI models themselves are becoming part of the national-security debate.

CHINA IS USING U.S. AI TO TRAIN ITS OWN MODELS

A Reuters review of more than 300 Chinese academic papers, patents, corporate disclosures and government documents found growing use of American AI-model outputs to train domestic Chinese systems.

The technique is known as:

DISTILLATION

Developers use powerful models to generate answers, code and reasoning examples that can then help train smaller systems.

Distillation is widely used internationally and is not inherently illegal.

But at industrial scale, it could help Chinese developers improve models while reducing some dependence on restricted U.S. computing hardware.

Why it matters: Chip restrictions may slow Chinese AI development—but they do not prevent Chinese developers from learning from American models.

The AI competition is becoming a battle over both:

COMPUTE + KNOWLEDGE

LAWMAKERS WARN AI CYBER THREATS ARE OUTPACING DEFENSES

A bipartisan pair of U.S. senators warned the White House today that AI-enabled cyber threats are developing faster than current defensive systems.

Their concerns include AI systems capable of:

• Discovering vulnerabilities
• Exploiting software weaknesses
• Operating autonomously
• Targeting critical infrastructure
• Attacking financial systems

The senators called for faster deployment of AI-powered defensive tools and stronger security standards for autonomous agents.
Why it matters: AI may dramatically increase the speed at which vulnerabilities are discovered.
That benefits defenders.
But attackers get access to the same acceleration.
Cybersecurity may become one of the first fields where we regularly see:

AI VS AI.

DEKRYPT WATCH

Thursday: Anthropic begins trading as ANT
Watch: Nvidia CEO search
Watch: Nvidia China-chip restrictions
Watch: U.S. disclosure rules for Chinese AI
Watch: AI-powered cyber defense
Watch: Chinese model distillation
Watch: AI infrastructure valuations
Watch: OpenAI’s potential future IPO

BOTTOM LINE

Nvidia proved that AI demand remains enormous.

Anthropic is about to test whether public markets believe the valuations.

Washington is tightening control over who gets access to AI technology.

China is finding new ways to develop around those restrictions.

And cybersecurity leaders are warning that autonomous AI capabilities may be advancing faster than defenses.
The next stage of the AI race isn't simply:
WHO BUILDS THE BEST MODEL?
It is becoming:
WHO CONTROLS THE COMPUTE?
WHO CONTROLS ACCESS?
WHO CONTROLS THE MODELS?
AND WHO CAN SECURE THEM?
That is a much bigger contest.
DEKRYPT THE WORLD

𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐂𝐄 𝐒𝐔𝐒𝐏𝐄𝐍𝐃𝐄𝐃 𝐌𝐈𝐂𝐑𝐎𝐒𝐎𝐅𝐓'𝐒 𝐆𝐑𝐄𝐄𝐍 𝐂𝐀𝐑𝐃𝐒 𝐎𝐕𝐄𝐑 𝐇-𝟏𝐁 𝐋𝐀𝐘𝐎𝐅𝐅𝐒 — 𝐍𝐎𝐖 𝐈𝐓'𝐒 𝐁𝐄𝐂𝐎𝐌𝐈𝐍𝐆 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐋𝐀𝐖

Vice President JD Vance didn't mince words when he announced the Trump administration was suspending Microsoft from the federal green card program last month: “𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘭𝘢𝘺 𝘰𝘧𝘧 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘮 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦𝘪𝘨𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦𝘥 𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘢𝘯𝘵𝘴.”

Vance laid out exactly what he meant by that phrase. An H-1B worker is “𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘺 𝘴𝘶𝘣𝘰𝘳𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘢𝘯𝘺” — lose the job, lose the right to stay in the country. “𝘐𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘵𝘰𝘰 𝘶𝘱𝘱𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺'𝘳𝘦 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘫𝘰𝘣, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺'𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘥𝘦𝘱𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦,” he said. 𝐓𝐡𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐧𝐬, and that's exactly why, Vance argued, they're paid below the American market rate while U.S. workers get shown the door.

The administration's October 8 action suspended Microsoft, Adobe, and six IT outsourcing firms — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini — from filing new green card labor certifications, citing active federal investigations into Microsoft's reported layoffs of 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝟔,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬 alongside thousands of H-1B filings. The eight companies combined have sought nearly 3 million foreign workers since 2009, pulling in over 230,000 H-1B approvals and more than 100,000 permanent labor certifications (Department of Labor).

That wasn't a one-off. On November 16, the Labor Department sent a sweeping new PERM rule to the Federal Register that turns Vance's warning into permanent policy: any employer that laid off American workers in a similar job and area within the 𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 — not just six months, the current standard — could be barred from filing for their foreign replacements. Employers would have to actually offer the job back to the Americans they cut, advertise openings for 90 straight days, and lose the Schedule A shortcut that's let companies fast-track certain hires around American applicants altogether.

𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐣𝐨𝐛 𝐢𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐬. 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐨𝐧 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐢𝐝: 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐲𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞.

text:
Sir Edward Marsh (b. 18 November 1872) was a British civil servant, literary patron, art collector, and one of the great social connectors of Edwardian and Georgian England. Known affectionately as “Eddie,” he moved effortlessly between the corridors of political power and the drawing rooms, studios, and bedrooms of Britain's artistic elite. Born in London into a distinguished family, educated at Westminster School and Cambridge, Marsh entered the civil service in 1896 and eventually became private secretary to several prominent ministers, most notably Winston Churchill, whom he served in various capacities for more than two decades. Their friendship endured long after their professional association ended.

Eddie's extraordinary circle of acquaintances included writers, artists, politicians, and aristocrats. His influential Georgian Poetry anthologies (published between 1912 and 1922) helped establish the reputations of Rupert Brooke, Siegfried Sassoon, Walter de la Mare, and other poets. Brooke, whom he adored and whose literary estate he helped administer after his death in 1915, was among his closest friends.

As a collector and patron, he supported artists including Duncan Grant (also an intimate friend of Brooke), Mark Gertler, Stanley Spencer, and Paul Nash, often purchasing their work when encouragement was more plentiful than money. Through Grant, his connections also extended to members of the Bloomsbury Group—Virginia Woolf, Vanessa Bell, Lytton Strachey, and E. M. Forster. Other associates included Bertrand Russell, G. E. Moore, Maurice Baring, Katherine Mansfield, Robert Graves, and the composer and actor Ivor Novello. Additionally, he served as a de facto editor for both Somerset Maugham and the best-selling author Hugh Walpole.

Marsh became one of Maugham's most trusted literary advisers, particularly from the mid-1930s onward. A meticulous editor with an almost fanatical devotion to good English, Eddie reviewed hundreds of pages of Maugham's manuscripts and proofs, correcting grammar, improving phrasing, and questioning stylistic choices. Their correspondence reveals considerable mutual affection. Maugham once joked that Marsh's corrections had improved not only his prose but also his character by thoroughly humiliating his literary vanity. He offered to pay Eddie for his services, but Eddie refused. In gratitude, Maugham dedicated the British edition of Strictly Personal (1941) to him. Their friendship—one of genuine warmth and teasing humor—continued until Marsh's death.

Eddie also maintained a friendship and literary collaboration with Walpole, the enormously successful novelist whose popularity during the 1920s and 30s far exceeded his subsequent literary reputation. He served as a textual editor of Walpole's writing, bringing the same exacting standards to his work that he applied to Maugham's.  Both Maugham and Walpole benefitted greatly from his collaboration.

Eddie’s gift was not merely knowing celebrated people but introducing them to one another, finding them publishers, patrons, commissions, and occasionally rescuing them from financial embarrassment. He was, in effect, an unofficial employment agency, literary salon, and discreet matchmaking service for Britain's talented and unconventional. His memoir, A Number of People (1939), offered a glimpse into this astonishing social universe, and it should come as no surprise that many of Eddie’s closest friends and associates were gay.

Eddie, himself, was homosexual in an era when being so was illegal and discretion was essential, and his emotional and romantic attachments to men were woven into his extensive friendships. He never married, and his private life remained carefully guarded, although his attraction to men was well understood within his intimate circle. His devotion to Rupert Brooke was particularly intense, and Brooke's early death at age 27 left him devastated. Yet Marsh remained a remarkably sociable, generous, and well-connected figure, equally at home entertaining literary rebels and serving the political establishment. Knighted in 1937, he continued to cultivate friendships and support younger artists until his death in 1953, at age 80. Few men of his generation knew so many remarkable people—or did so much, so quietly, to advance their careers.

Edward Marsh’s enduring legacy was less a body of original work than the remarkable collection of careers, friendships, and artistic achievements he helped nurture. In a society obsessed with knowing the right people, Eddie had the considerable advantage of knowing practically everyone. 🏳️‍🌈

text:
Online, people are blaming the FAA's AI system, SMART, for the ground stop. The FAA's Q&A says: "No. The two systems are not related. SMART is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system." Duffy says SMART "had zero impact." The vendor, Air Space Intelligence, says the same. So does MIT's R. John Hansman, via PolitiFact, who says it has no direct connection to the comm system.

Now the contract, read directly on https://t.co/feByU70yJP. Award 693KA726C00064, FAA to Air Space Intelligence, signed June 23, 2026, running to 2038. The ceiling is $875,950,000. That is potential value, not money paid. Obligated so far: $23,340,500. Twelve offers. The record describes "flow management data and services." The word SMART is not in the part we read, and PolitiFact says the contract covers SMART and another system.

The donation: Air Space Intelligence's PAC gave $2,500 in March to Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, Republican of Wisconsin and Duffy's son-in-law, per Snopes, PolitiFact and the Washington Examiner. We have not opened the FEC record. Posts saying $12,500 are wrong, per Snopes. We found no evidence that SMART caused the stop, or that the donation influenced the award. Neither Duffy nor the FAA has said whether Duffy was personally involved in the award. So was he?
OFFICIAL, the contract figures (USAspending record, read directly; one source)
CLAIM, "not related" (FAA and the vendor are interested parties, plus one expert)
CLAIM, the donation figure (three outlets, FEC record not opened)
VERDICT (our opinion): the AI-caused-the-shutdown claim fails; the donation is a fair procurement question with no evidence of influence found.

#OvertPsyops Readout: Ron Johnson, Social Security, and the "Ponzi Scheme" Confession

This is a headline worth slowing down for! A sitting U.S. Senator, chair of the Senate Budget Committee, has publicly called a program that tens of millions of Americans were told to trust a "Legal Ponzi Scheme," a "scam," and "grotesque." Let's run this through γραφή (scripture), λόγος (logic), and the #OvertPsyops framework and see what surfaces.

1. The Admission Itself: ἀλήθεια (truth) Leaking Through the Cracks

For decades the public was taught to think of FICA as "my money" sitting in a "lock box." Now the chair of the Budget Committee says plainly: "Actually, it's not. Your money was spent… as soon as it was collected from your paycheck."

Notice what this means logically. If the people who manage the system admit the public's understanding was false, then someone allowed that false understanding to persist for generations. That is a textbook psyop: a comforting story told to the masses while the real mechanics run quietly underneath. The κόσμος (world) system thrives on that gap between what people believe and what is actually happening.

Ἰησοῦς Χριστός (Jesus THE Christ) warned exactly where misplaced trust leads:

Do not θησαυρίζετε (store up treasures) for yourselves upon the γῆ (earth), where moth and rust ἀφανίζει (destroy) and where κλέπται (thieves) break through and steal; but store up for yourselves θησαυροί (treasures) in οὐρανός (heaven), where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break through nor steal. (Ματθαῖος (Matthew) 6:19-20)

Full Greek text: Μὴ θησαυρίζετε ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὅπου σὴς καὶ βρῶσις ἀφανίζει, καὶ ὅπου κλέπται διορύσσουσιν καὶ κλέπτουσιν· θησαυρίζετε δὲ ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐν οὐρανῷ, ὅπου οὔτε σὴς οὔτε βρῶσις ἀφανίζει, καὶ ὅπου κλέπται οὐ διορύσσουσιν οὐδὲ κλέπτουσιν.

A government "trust fund" spent the moment it is collected is the very definition of a treasure that thieves break into. The public was trained to place its ἐλπίς (hope) in Caesar's ledger instead of in Θεός (God).

2. The Logic Break: Two Different Messages on the Same Day

Here is where the λόγος (logic) flow snaps. Compare the two reports, both published Wednesday morning:

In the Fox News report, Johnson's written "solution" is to repeal the benefit-reduction provision and "quit scaring seniors."

On Fox Business, Johnson says the government should "just shut it down" and "hope" Americans recover some of their money.

Those two positions cannot both stand. One says protect seniors from reductions; the other says end the program and let them hope for pennies on the dollar. When a leader calls something a scam and then offers contradictory exits, the result in the public mind is fear, confusion, and paralysis. That is ἄλογος (illogical) messaging, and confusion is the signature of the διάβολος (devil, the illogical one), who works mainly by disrupting the flow of logic in the human mind.

3. Who Pays for the Collapse? The Elderly and the Vulnerable

Scripture is crystal clear that caring for the elderly and the widow is a mark of genuine πίστις (faith). The early ἐκκλησία (assembly) in Πράξεις (Acts) 6:1 organized a daily διακονία (service/distribution) so widows would not be neglected. Παῦλος (Paul) writes:

But if anyone does not προνοεῖ (provide for, think ahead for) his own, and especially those of his household, he has denied the πίστις (faith) and is worse than an ἄπιστος (unbeliever). (1 Τιμόθεος (1 Timothy) 5:8)

Full Greek text: εἰ δέ τις τῶν ἰδίων καὶ μάλιστα οἰκείων οὐ προνοεῖ, τὴν πίστιν ἤρνηται καὶ ἔστιν ἀπίστου χείρων.

Notice the Greek: προνοέω (provide) literally means to think ahead, to plan beforehand. It is not a Latin concept of merely handing out money. A system that spends today's contributions, borrows against children and grandchildren, and then tells the elderly to "hope" is the exact opposite of προνοέω (think ahead).  https://t.co/OqG5G8378x

4. The Root Issue: φιλαργυρία (love of money)

Johnson blames Congress for spending surpluses on "other government programs" and promising benefits it could not fund. Strip away the policy jargon, and the root is ancient:

For the ῥίζα (root) of all the κακά (evils) is φιλαργυρία (love of money), which some reaching for were led astray from the πίστις (faith) and pierced themselves through with many ὀδύναι (sorrows). (1 Τιμόθεος (1 Timothy) 6:10)

Debt-based systems that spend tomorrow's labor today are built on φιλαργυρία (love of money) and on placing the weight of the present onto the backs of children. That is a heavy φορτίον (burden), the opposite of the ἐλαφρός (light) burden of Χριστός (The Christ).

5. Context From Tommy's Archive

Tommy's blog has long documented Ron Johnson. A 2010 Talking Points Memo report archived on Tommy's blog covers Johnson testifying before the Wisconsin State Senate against legislation that would have eliminated the statute of limitations on child sexual abuse claims, which would have made it easier for victims to seek damages from the Catholic Church and other institutions, while he served on the finance council of the Diocese of Green Bay. See: https://t.co/BnYSX60rQx

6. The #OvertPsyops Bottom Line

The admission that Americans were "misled" is partly ἀλήθεια (truth). But truth from the κόσμος (world) system often arrives packaged with fear to steer the public toward a pre-chosen outcome. Do not let fear drive you. The fear that belongs to a believer is the fear of Θεός (God), real dread of judgment that causes us to depart from κακός (evil), not fear of politicians and headlines.

Practical, γραφή (scripture) based response: seek Θεός (God) with all your καρδία (heart), προνοέω (think ahead) for your household, care for the elderly and widows in your own family and community directly, and refuse to place your ἐλπίς (hope) in Caesar's promises. Do your own research and test everything by λόγος (logic).

For more, see the work by Tommy Richards (https://t.co/d8rLNntk9M, @tlthe5th)

text:
Emily had prepared a list of relatives, childhood friends, former classmates, and people she had worked with over the years.

Jason's mother reviewed the list and immediately started removing names.

She said certain guests weren't important enough to attend such an expensive wedding.

She also added 17 people from their own family and social circle.

Emily disagreed, particularly because several of the people being removed were relatives she had known her entire life.

Jason told her that his parents were contributing significantly to the wedding, so their preferences deserved consideration.

I stayed out of the disagreement initially.

Then Jason called me privately.

He explained that his parents wanted final approval over the guest list because they were paying for the venue.

I told him that contributing money didn't automatically give someone ownership of the wedding.

He said I was misunderstanding the situation.

According to him, his parents were making a substantial financial commitment and shouldn't be expected to pay for an event where they had no control.

I reminded him that I was also contributing $28,000.

He replied that my contribution was different because I was Emily's father.

That statement irritated me.

I asked him to explain why my money came with no decision-making authority while his parents' money apparently purchased it.

He said his family had certain standards and that I needed to respect their traditions.

I ended the conversation.

The following weekend, both families met at a restaurant to finalize the arrangements.

Jason's mother arrived with a printed guest list.

She had removed 34 people from Emily's original list and added 22 names of her own.

When Emily objected, Jason told her not to embarrass his mother in front of everyone.

I finally intervened.

I told them that if the wedding was becoming a financial competition between families, I was withdrawing my contribution.

Jason immediately accused me of threatening the wedding because I wasn't getting my way.

His mother called my decision childish.

I told them I wasn't going to spend $28,000 helping organize an event where my daughter couldn't even decide who was allowed to attend.

Emily started crying.

Jason stood up and said he wasn't going to marry into a family that treated his parents like strangers.

The meeting ended badly.

Two days later, Emily called me and said Jason was furious because the venue deposit had already been paid and his parents were demanding that I reconsider.

I told her my offer had been withdrawn.

She accused me of making her wedding more difficult and said she didn't want to choose between her father and her future husband.

I haven't changed my decision.

The wedding is now postponed while they try to reorganize the finances.

Jason has told several relatives that I ruined his wedding because I couldn't tolerate his parents having a say.

His mother has also stopped speaking to me.

Last Friday, Emily sent me the updated wedding budget.

They had removed several luxury arrangements and reduced the guest list to 120 people.

At the bottom of the message, she wrote that she wished I had simply paid the money and allowed everyone to enjoy the day.

I haven't responded.

Apparently, contributing $28,000 makes me family, but having an opinion about how my money is used makes me the problem.

text:
I'm 56, divorced, and I've spent most of my adult life building a construction supply business. I started with one delivery truck and eventually grew it into a company with 23 employees.

My daughter, Emily, is 29 and works as a marketing director. She's my only child, and I've always tried to give her opportunities I never had growing up.

When she got engaged to a man named Jason, I was genuinely happy for her.

Jason seemed polite, had a decent job in commercial real estate, and came from a financially comfortable family.

Six months before the wedding, Emily and Jason came to my house to discuss their plans.

They wanted a wedding with approximately 180 guests at a luxury hotel. The estimated budget was $68,000.

I offered to contribute $28,000 toward the wedding, provided they handled the remaining expenses with their savings and contributions from Jason's family.

Emily was thrilled.

Jason thanked me and said he appreciated my generosity.

His parents offered to pay for the reception venue, which was estimated to cost $19,000.

Everything seemed settled until the guest list discussion started.

text:
Starbucks has offered a major college benefit for years, and it also gives employees stock ownership.**

The main program is the **Starbucks College Achievement Plan (SCAP)**, launched in 2014 with Arizona State University (ASU) Online. Eligible U.S. partners (employees) can earn a first-time bachelor’s degree with **100% upfront tuition coverage**—Starbucks pays ASU directly for the remaining costs after any grants/scholarships, so employees generally don’t pay out of pocket or wait for reimbursement. It covers more than 150 (sometimes listed as 180+) online degree programs, includes academic support/coaching, and has a “Pathway to Admission” for those who don’t initially qualify. There’s no requirement to stay with the company after graduating. Nearly 20,000 partners have graduated through it, with tens of thousands more participating; it’s available to benefits-eligible full- and part-time workers (often marketed as accessible from early in employment, with average hours requirements in the 20+/week range for eligibility in practice).

They also offer **student loan management tools** (via https://t.co/prEd36Uleu) for eligible partners and families—resources, coaching, repayment strategy help, and refinancing options. This is support/management for existing debt, not a direct large-scale loan payoff or reimbursement of past college costs already paid.

On the ownership side relevant to the Kevin O’Leary clip in that post: Starbucks has long run **Bean Stock**, annual restricted stock unit grants to eligible full- and part-time partners (including hourly store workers). As of mid-November 2026, nearly 200,000 received new grants; the program has delivered over $2.75 billion in pre-tax gains to more than 2 million partners since 1991. They also have performance-based rewards and other financial benefits.

In short, Starbucks funds substantial education benefits and equity for workers as part of compensation—these come from the company’s resources (including profits)—alongside ordinary wages, tips, etc. Residual profits after costs and investments go to shareholders (who provide capital). The SCAP is one of the more generous retail education benefits precisely because it’s upfront coverage with few post-graduation strings.

text:
Imagine you finished a summer internship and received an offer to return full time next year. Amazing. You sign it and breathe a huge sigh of relief. The next 365 days are going to be unreal. All of your anxieties wash away and you start moving like a completely different person

You're getting out of the house more. Striking up conversations with people. Working on that passion project again. You stopped overanalyzing everything. You're much more willing to put yourself out now there without worrying about the consequences. Your brain knows you've already secured the bag

Then one day you wake up to an email. Unexpected budget cuts. Your offer is rescinded. Three months before you were supposed to start. It punches you in the gut and completely transforms your energy. Now you're less light on your feet, more serious, you go back to being a nervous wreck and start living in your head again

But think about who you were in the nine months before it happened. You were an absolute luck magnet. How did you justify behaving with such abundance? It was because you got the job right? Wait no, not true. You didn't even start yet. The money never hit your account, your LinkedIn never got to change titles

Also with your offer being rescinded, that means the past nine months were totally a waste, right? Just because a specific outcome didn't end up transpiring within this specific period of time, you're supposed to regret having felt that secure in yourself? 

So basically what you're saying is that all it took was the belief that you already had what you wanted? And that you never actually needed to have it today in order for you to embody the same level of confidence as if you did have it? Did you ever need a letter to give you a reason to embrace the aura of a winner, or could you have simply given that permission to yourself? Interesting

text:
There are pieces of your life scattered all over the internet, and some of them are for sale. Data brokers amass web searches, financial records, and location data from millions of individuals and sell them to various clients, including the US government. Information on your recent online purchases or the route that you take to work could be sitting on hard drives around the world, waiting to be used.

While reassembling those pieces isn’t trivial, there is early evidence that LLMs might make it far easier. LLM agents could potentially do the work of intelligence analysts in a fraction of the time and for a fraction of the cost, which would enable the state to aim its all-seeing eye toward anyone, not just its highest-priority targets.

“A lot of what we think of as privacy protection isn’t so much like something that’s written in the law,” says Karen Levy, a professor of information science at Cornell University. “It just has to do with how hard or how expensive it is to learn stuff about people.” When mobile phones became widespread, gathering data about people got much cheaper, but making use of that data remained difficult. Powerful LLMs could change that.

Worries over how LLMs could facilitate mass surveillance recently made headlines around the world. According to reporting from the New York Times and the Atlantic, contract negotiations between Anthropic and the US Department of Defense fell apart in late February because Anthropic balked when the DOD demanded leeway to use the company’s models to analyze commercially available data on US citizens. When Anthropic’s rival OpenAI agreed to a DOD deal mere hours later, OpenAI faced an immediate wave of public backlash for apparently swanning past Anthropic’s red lines. Under pressure, OpenAI and the DOD later revised the contract terms.

For avid followers of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the company’s firm stance probably didn’t come as a surprise. In a lengthy essay published to his personal website in January, Amodei had argued that AI-enabled mass surveillance could constitute a crime against humanity. The core concern underlying his dispute with the DOD was that the government might use LLM-based systems such as Claude to analyze reams of data obtained from brokers and build detailed profiles of individual Americans at scale.

There’s plenty of precedent for AI being used for mass surveillance: Most notably, governments worldwide use facial recognition to track citizens and noncitizens alike, and recent reporting indicates that US Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have leaned heavily on facial recognition apps in order to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. While there’s not yet any smoking-gun evidence that the US government (or anyone else) is using LLMs to conduct surveillance in the way that Amodei warns about, there’s a clear appetite for such capabilities.

Artificial analysts

The sort of surveillance against which Amodei cautions is only possible in the United States because of a legal loophole. If the police suspect you of a crime and want to peruse the location data stored on your phone to see if you were present at the scene, they need a signed warrant from a judge. That’s because the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution protects anyone in the United States from “unreasonable searches” by the government.

But when the government buys bulk data from brokers, it isn’t itself searching—it’s taking advantage of searches conducted by the people who collected and compiled the data. That creates a paradox: The government can’t look at the location information on your phone without a warrant, but if a dataset that the government has purchased contains your phone’s location data, and the government is able to link it to you, then it can effectively perform an end run around the Fourth Amendment.

The good news is that finding your information in these databases probably isn’t as easy as just searching for your name. The data that brokers sell is often stripped of obvious identifiers—it might contain, for example, location traces from millions of cell phones but not the corresponding phone numbers. But that’s not an insurmountable obstacle. A 2019 New York Times investigation of bulk cell phone location data found that it was often possible to identify the owners of individual phones by making note of their apparent work and home locations.

Even though deanonymizing data does take some effort, it’s safely within the skill set of intelligence analysts, or indeed any competent internet user, and law enforcement has used ostensibly anonymized location data to tie people to specific crimes. But those are focused searches. While the government, or other organizations, might be able to access data that describes the locations of tens or hundreds of millions of Americans, it would take an utterly impractical number of human analysts to tie all of that data to specific individuals. AI agents could potentially do it faster and more cheaply.

“One way to look at the kerfuffle with Anthropic is that the DOD wants to be able to exploit this [commercial data] loophole to the max,” says Greg Nojeim, director of the security and surveillance project at the Center for Democracy & Technology.

There’s evidence indicating that LLM agents are up to the job. At the start of this year, Northeastern University professor Tianshi Li shared a particularly ironic example. Using an LLM agent, Li analyzed a publicly available Anthropic dataset that consisted of interviews with several scientists about how they use AI. Anthropic had redacted some personally identifying information in the scientists’ responses, but the agent that Li used was able to connect descriptions of some of the subjects’ research with specific studies that they had authored. Though the agent only managed to identify a fraction of the interviewed scientists, when it did succeed it was fast and cheap: Each attempt took about four minutes and cost less than fifty cents. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

Other studies have shown that LLMs can match pseudonymous forum accounts to LinkedIn profiles; identify writers’ native languages; isolate potentially identifying information from a user’s online post history; and infer social media users’ psychological traits, locations, incomes, sexes, and ages, among other attributes. While some of these tasks could be completed by the average person if given adequate time, others, such as native-language identification, would be challenging for anyone but an expert. “In practice, they’re doing what a competent investigator would do,” wrote Nico Dekens, senior vice president of engineering at the intelligence software company ShadowDragon, in an email to MIT Technology Review.

All of these results suggest that agents could give an unskilled worker the capabilities of a team of highly trained intelligence analysts. “[An agent] can gather information on its own and it can make plans, so it’s not like a static search query,” Li says. “It both lowers the barrier to entry and maybe pushes the limits of surveillance even farther.”

If political leaders wanted to quash dissent or punish opponents at scale, the combination of bulk data and countless virtual analysts could enable them to do so. A team of LLM agents might be able to identify the real people behind social media accounts that express negative views about the government or leverage a location dataset to compile a list of people present at a protest. Those in power could then make their lives difficult. “If government agents want to harass people, there are many opportunities to do so,” says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

In the United States, such harassment might take subtle forms—being pulled aside for excessive screenings at the airport, for example. Elsewhere, the consequences could be more drastic. Members of China’s Uighur ethnic minority, for example, have been extensively surveilled by their government for years, and police may choose to investigate individuals based on surveillance data. For Uighurs, such investigations can result in internment and forced labor. And China appears to be interested in integrating LLMs into its surveillance system: An unsecured dataset discovered last year on a Baidu server indicates that Chinese companies are using LLMs to flag online posts for the purpose of “public opinion monitoring,” which is a priority for the Chinese government.

All of this is made worse by the fact that LLMs make mistakes. The advantage of using LLMs for mass surveillance is that they can do far more work than human analysts far more quickly, but that also makes thoroughly checking their work impossible. And because mass surveillance is, by its very nature, secretive, some who fall victim to such errors may not have any recourse.

Privacy on a precipice

For now, these threats are theoretical. It’s almost impossible to determine how the US intelligence community is using LLMs in any detail: While most government agencies are required to report how they use AI, intelligence agencies are exempt. And the companies that provide tools that the government might use to conduct surveillance are cagey about the details of their tech, at least in public materials.

“There are legitimate reasons for secrecy about how informational assets are being obtained and used for intelligence or defense purposes,” Nojeim says. “But the amount of secrecy that surrounds this use is particularly troubling because the tech is so powerful and so new and so difficult for Congress to oversee.”

That said, there are some suggestive signs about how the government might be using LLMs. For example, government agencies, including ICE and the Drug Enforcement Administration hold subscriptions to ShadowDragon’s software, and, according to Dekens, the company is currently working on incorporating LLMs into the tools it offers. “LLM agents are already very good at the mechanical side of analysis,” he wrote. “Right now, the most effective way to use them is as a copilot and workflow layer.”

And the government could certainly take advantage of those capabilities, as it has access not only to commercially available bulk data but also to proprietary datasets compiled by individual agencies. Historically, those datasets had been siloed in different agencies—the Internal Revenue Service had your tax data and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services had your health records, and they didn’t share. Last year, however, the Elon Musk–led Department of Government Efficiency reportedly mounted a crusade to centralize all that data. With the data in one place and powerful AI tools at their fingertips, members of government agencies can, in principle, construct detailed profiles of anyone.

DOGE’s data-centralization efforts and the LLM-enabled acceleration of analyst work are two sides of the same coin. In principle, both changes could help the government operate more effectively and economically. But there’s a cost. “I think there’s sometimes an assumption that inefficiency is always bad,” says Levy. “But in privacy, you actually really want things to be hard.”

Few organizations would choose inefficient procedures of their own volition, but Congress could force the government down that path. Shortly after the Anthropic debacle, a bipartisan group of senators and representatives introduced a bill that would require the government to obtain a warrant before purchasing data from data brokers. Public outcry, too, seems to have had an effect: After OpenAI was overwhelmed by opprobrium for accepting DOD contract terms that Anthropic had rejected, the company and the Pentagon modified the contract to include additional surveillance protections.

But government surveillance is not the only concern. Private companies could just as easily purchase bulk data and analyze it with LLM agents, and they are less subject to legal constraints and public opposition, especially if they aren’t household names. If it is indeed possible for LLM agents to build detailed profiles of large numbers of individuals using bulk data, companies could use those capabilities to investigate job applicants or determine whether someone is insurable. “It is very, very hard to hold to account companies that are doing whatever they want to with our data,” Levy says. “It’s hard to even know what’s happening.”

In the absence of legislation preventing such uses, we might need to rethink how we understand our own privacy. It has always been possible that someone online might unearth your address or connect you with your pseudonymous accounts, but given the effort that would take, it was easy to feel safe. Even in the wake of Edward Snowden’s 2013 revelations about the National Security Agency’s extensive surveillance of US citizens, many people reassured themselves that their privacy was still intact because the government had no reason to look into their lives.

That kind of privacy depends entirely on friction: the time and effort required to link a secret social media account with its real-life owner, or the skill and resources needed to analyze bulk datasets. Stay under the radar, and no one will care enough to overcome that friction. But LLM agents could lessen that effort, or remove it entirely. If the government and other organizations can construct detailed profiles of millions of people at the drop of a hat, no one is beneath their notice.
