California Congressman Robert Garcia didn’t wait for the gavel. The incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee told New York Magazine exactly who’s on his list before he even has subpoena power: “𝘍𝘰𝘳 𝘌𝘱𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘪𝘯, 𝘐 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘉𝘭𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘩𝘦, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘉𝘶𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘶 𝘰𝘧 𝘗𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘐 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘨𝘰 𝘑𝘋 𝘝𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘚𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘦 𝘞𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘴.”

On Wednesday he made it official. Garcia sent a dozen letters ordering recipients to preserve every record tied to his planned investigations — Vice President Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and the Bureau of Prisons director and warden now holding Ghislaine Maxwell. 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐩𝐨𝐞𝐧𝐚 𝐡𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞𝐝 — these are just the opening sh∗ts.

Garcia isn’t hiding his intentions. On election night, as Democrats’ midterm wins rolled in, he had a two-word warning for Trump’s allies: “𝘓𝘢𝘸𝘺𝘦𝘳 𝘶𝘱.” Weeks later he told New York Magazine his committee’s reach has no limits at all: “𝘖𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵’𝘴 𝘫𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘴 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨. 𝘞𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘰𝘯𝘦.”

The White House isn’t playing along. Spokeswoman Lauren Bis pointed to Trump’s own post-midterm offer to work with Democrats, then drew the line: “𝘐𝘧 𝘋𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘴 𝘤𝘩𝘰𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘱𝘶𝘳𝘴𝘶𝘦 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘮 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘭𝘦𝘧𝘵 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘦𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘤𝘩𝘰𝘰𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘈𝘮𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘱𝘦𝘰𝘱𝘭𝘦.” A separate White House official pushed back just as hard, warning that “𝘪𝘧 𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘻𝘦𝘥 𝘋𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘢𝘣𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘻𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴, 𝘴𝘶𝘣𝘱𝘰𝘦𝘯𝘢𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘭 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘦𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘰𝘧 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘴.”

Here’s the fact Garcia doesn’t advertise: 𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐧’𝐭 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐩𝐨𝐞𝐧𝐚 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐥 𝐉𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐲, when Democrats are actually sworn into the majority. Until then, every one of these letters is a voluntary request with zero legal teeth — a political enemies list dressed up as oversight, published months before he has any power to enforce it.

𝐑𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐭 𝐆𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐢𝐚 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐡𝐢𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐢𝐭 — 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞.

While there is big news about Oregon's housing board agreeing to spend nearly $1 million per unit for a stalled affordable housing project in North Portland adjacent to I-5, on the other side of this debate is a transaction that has been barely covered in the local news:

Catholic Charities, which like other local NGO's such as the Latino Network and Hacienda CDC, has found itself invested in the local affordable housing business, just dumped 19 of their affordable housing properties in a fire sale to a California company, EAH Housing, which is also a non-profit.

The amount of the transaction, which represents over 1000 units thoughout the Portland Metro area?

$30 million...or less than $30,000 per unit, which is roughly 3% of the cost to build the previously mentioned property in North Portland (now named Monarca).

Even more interesting is that the current property management firm, Guardian Real Estate Services - which has at outstanding complaints and/or lawsuits on at least four other affordable housing properties it manages, will remain the property manager at these 19 properties.

Catholic Charities, which claimed they got into the affordable housing game to "help people," and not make big bucks on development fees and other revenue streams offered in the affordable housing grift, says that the sale would allow the non-profit to focus on its social services mission and pay off debt, which it probably should have done anyway considering that affordable housing owners often deal with past-due rent bills, rising operating and insurance costs, and increasing demands on property managers to deal with complex behavioral health needs.

Of course "complex behavioral health needs" is affordable housing speak for wide-spread vandalism, drug use and trafficking, and other dangerous criminal behavior.

text:
November 18 Saint Odo (Odon or Eudes) of Cluny: Benedictine, abbot of Cluny.
(† 942)
Patronage: for rain
.
On Christmas Eve of the year 877, a pious but childless Christian nobleman of Aquitaine implored Our Lord, by the fecundity of His Holy Mother and His Incarnation, to grant him a son. His prayer was heard; Odon was born, and his grateful father, in a prayer offered him — still an infant in his arms — to Saint Martin of Tours (†400) to be his spiritual son. Odon was later taught by a wise priest, then was placed in the court of the Count of Anjou and that of the Duke of Aquitaine. There he was influenced by the passions which reign in courts, and neglected his prayers to think only of games, hunting, and military pursuits. But God did not abandon him, and he was haunted in his dreams by the dangers of a disordered life. He prayed to the Blessed Virgin and begged Her one Christmas Eve to lead him on the narrow path of sanctity.
.
He was then sixteen years old, and the next day he fell ill with a sickness which increased and for three years kept him on the verge of death. When his father told him he had consecrated him to Saint Martin, Odon renewed this consecration and promised to enter into his service; suddenly then his headaches left him and he recovered from his illness.
.
He went to Tours to serve in the church of Saint Martin for a time. But when a hermitage was built nearby he retired there to devote himself to prayer and study, while continuing to visit the tomb of Saint Martin every night. He began to study the Scriptures and abandoned all pagan readings. Later he was inspired to enter the monastery of Baume in the diocese of Besançon, and there he received the habit from Saint Bernon, the abbot, in the year 909. He was charged with the instruction of novices and boarding students. When later he returned home on a visit to his parents, they were so touched by his words that despite their age they renounced the world and entered a monastery. When Odon returned to Baume he was ordained a priest.
.
When Saint Bernon, who had governed six monasteries, died, three of those were entrusted to Saint Odon; these were Cluny, newly founded in 910, Massay, and Deols. He resided in Cluny, of which he is often titled the Founder, because he organized and enlarged this new house. His reputation attracted a large number of vocations. His special care was for children; at that period the schools had taken refuge in the cathedrals and monasteries. He watched with gentleness over the habits, studies, and repose of these dear children. He personally taught them as well as the monks. The Rule of Saint Benedict, providing for the education of children as well as the formation of monks, was followed zealously. Many alms were given to the poor, without concern for the morrow. The charity of Cluny was so abundant that in one year food was distributed to more than seven thousand indigent persons.
.
Saint Odon visited Rome three times; there he reformed a monastery, and later in France he submitted several abbeys to the discipline of Cluny. These were organized into a federation under the sole abbot of Cluny, with great unity of statutes and regime. It was said that from Benevent to the Atlantic Ocean, the most important monasteries of Italy and Gaul rejoiced in being under his commandment. After celebrating the feast of Saint Martin at Tours in 942, Saint Odon fell ill; and having exhorted all the religious who had come there to see him and learn how to be regular in their observance, he blessed them and gave up his soul to God. He was buried at Tours in the church of Saint Julian.
.
Reflection: It needs only for a Catholic to show devotion to any Saint, says Father Newman, in order to receive special benefits from his intercession.
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor St. Odo, and I give Thee thanks for all the graces Thou hast bestowed upon him. I ask Thee to please increase grace in my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to him by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, St. Odo might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

text:
Cancer Research Fraud: How Fabricated Results Fooled Elite Journals and Duke University

Anil Potti offered the perfect miracle for medical grant committees: read gene activity in a tumor and predict which chemotherapy would work. That promise attracted prestige, major publications, and a route toward commercial tests. Federal investigators exposed the deception beneath the sales pitch. Results advertised as evidence for personalized cancer treatment were supported by false data. Potti made his scientific claims look stronger than the evidence allowed, while cancer patients faced the consequences.

The deception was precise enough to audit. Potti claimed six of 33 patients responded to dasatinib, although only four were enrolled and none responded. Investigators found he reversed treatment outcomes for 24 of 133 subjects, switched recurrence labels for 46 of 89 samples, and altered drug sensitivity and R-code values. Those changes could falsely inflate the apparent accuracy of cancer treatment predictors. It takes an extraordinary talent for creative accounting to make zero responses become six.

Duke’s oversight deserves its own retraction. Researchers Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes exposed serious data problems years before the trials ended. Medical student Bradford Perez warned insiders. Joseph Nevins, Potti’s senior collaborator, failed to thoroughly examine the underlying data until years later. Three Duke trials were ultimately halted. Potti settled with federal officials without admitting liability. Apparently, Duke’s scientific safeguards needed a peer-reviewed study to determine whether the house was on fire.

text:
WHY ROGLIČ MOVING TO NSN MAKES SENSE TO ME?

It came as a shock: Primož Roglič moves to NSN Cycling Team. Lotto, Rockets, Tudor and Pinarello were all mentioned as possible destinations, but in the end, this was a total surprise. However, this option might actually be the best one to me. Why?

1. Freedom and a different role

At Red Bull Bora, Roglič was part of an extremely ambitious project with several top GC leaders and a lot of expectations. Same for Visma in the end. 

Despite NSN signing some very good riders, he should still get the much-needed freedom and, more importantly, more room to shape his own racing calendar and ambitions. It could be a great opportunity to enjoy racing in his last year in a slightly different environment.

2. Still a strong group of climbers

Unlike some of the other smaller teams he was linked with, at NSN he will still have some very strong riders around him. The team previously had very almost zero top climbers, but suddenly, alongside Roglič, they will have Carapaz, Buitrago and Van Eetvelt. So he won’t be alone when the peloton gets smaller.

3. Different goals

Although Roglič’s programme hasn’t been announced yet, chasing a Tour de France stage win, the Tour de Suisse GC and potentially another Vuelta could be among his ambitions. Carapaz, meanwhile, wants to focus on the Giro d’Italia GC, which could make their programmes fit together very well.

4. A team that can offer him a good contract

Primož deserves one more good payday towards the end of his career. And among the teams interested in signing him, NSN is certainly in a position to offer that. After all, Carapaz also made the move there, reportedly because NSN could offer better financial conditions than EF.

5. The “Never Say Never” message

“Never Say Never” simply fits the narrative of a rider who has repeatedly come back from setbacks. I know many people still don’t like this team because of its past, but they are trying to build something new, and bringing in Primož is another step in that direction.

What do you wish from Primož in his last year of the career? Me Tour stage win.

text:
Mississippi had no religious exemption for school vaccines for 44 years.

Then in 2023, a federal judge put it back.

His reasoning is the argument every parent needs to know:
If the state gives out MEDICAL exemptions case by case, it has to offer a RELIGIOUS one too.

That comes straight from a 2021 Supreme Court case, Fulton v. City of Philadelphia.
When the government lets itself make exceptions for some reasons, it can't refuse to consider religious ones.

Judge Sul Ozerden declared the law unconstitutional as applied to the parents who sued.
The state didn't even file an opposition to the final ruling.

Mississippi started accepting religious exemptions on July 15, 2023.

text:
It’s Just Not Cricket: The Courage to Speak, the Conspiracy of Silence
By Dr Salman Ahmad 

Before asking what is “just not cricket,” let us remember what is.

When Greg Chappell rallied more than twenty former international captains to seek humane treatment for Imran Khan in Pakistan’s Adiala jail, cricket recovered its moral voice. Former rivals were demanding medical care, family access and dignity. Australia’s current captain, Pat Cummins, added his support.

As the producer of Leading from the Front, my film about Imran, https://t.co/8vEzipOYdx  I found that solidarity moving. Nobody had to endorse his politics to defend his humanity. These cricketers understood something their political counterparts too often forget: an opponent is not an enemy, and compassion requires no permission slip.

That is cricket at its best.
Now consider Sandpapergate.
Following Usman Khawaja’s revelations, Cameron Bancroft’s account in The West Australian alleges that knowledge of the sandpaper extended throughout Australia’s team. He describes bowlers’ feedback, collective awareness and information withheld from investigators.

Cummins denies prior knowledge. These are contested accounts, not verdicts. But Cricket Australia’s refusal to reopen its investigation, while offering a forum for recollections, raises an unavoidable question: is the institution seeking the truth, or managing its volume?

Recognising Cummins’s humanitarian stance does not require accepting his account without scrutiny. Scrutinising that account should not erase his humanitarian stance.

Integrity is not a fan club.

Back in 2018, I watched the events in South Africa unfold, then saw Steve Smith crying on television, his father beside him. Disappointing those who taught us right from wrong can wound more deeply than losing a trophy.

But tears cannot do the work of institutions.
My perspective also carries Pakistan’s experience. In Leading from the Front, I explored how innuendo against our cricketers bordered on racism. This was not merely scrutiny of leather and seam. It was suspicion cast over a people, their talent and their integrity.

At The Oval in 2006, Darrell Hair and fellow umpire Billy Doctrove penalised Inzamam-ul-Haq’s Pakistan for alleged ball-tampering. Inzamam was subsequently cleared of that charge. Who could return the dignity lost in the headlines?

Now a Pakistani-Australian, Khawaja, is demanding accountability within Australian cricket. The answer must not be national revenge. It must be equal standards.

Sport’s other scandals offer lessons, provided we distinguish their crimes.

The 1919 Black Sox conspiracy involved deliberately losing baseball’s World Series for gamblers. Sandpapergate involved cheating to win. FIFA’s corruption crisis concerned bribery and football’s administration. Different offences; a familiar surrender of public trust to private advantage.

After Black Sox, commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis banned eight implicated players despite criminal acquittals. His declaration condemned knowing silence as well as participation in fixing.

Baseball did not become holy. A century later, the Houston Astros’ illegal sign-stealing operation exposed organised cheating again. But sanctions reached the club, manager and general manager. Responsibility did not stop with the hands operating the machinery.

American football’s Deflategate likewise brought individual and organisational sanctions over disputed football-pressure manipulation—not a finding of gambling-related match-fixing.

The recurring weakness is human.
A youngster wants acceptance. A captain wants victory. A coach wants results. An administrator wants the scandal gone. Everybody borrows an excuse until nobody owns the truth.

A dressing room becomes an echo chamber. Loyalty becomes obedience. Silence becomes selection insurance.

Change means making honesty safer than concealment.

1/2

text:
Cornelius Harnett was called the Samuel Adams of North Carolina. He helped lead the colony into revolution, served in Congress, and then died as a British prisoner in his own hometown. Almost nobody outside North Carolina knows his name.

Harnett was a successful merchant in Wilmington. When Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765, he became one of the leaders of resistance in North Carolina. In late 1765, Harnett and the local Sons of Liberty confronted the colony's stamp distributor and pressured him into resigning. In 1766 hundreds of armed men from the Cape Fear region surrounded the house of the royal governor, William Tryon, in protest. Harnett was one of the leaders.

When the war came, he became one of the most powerful men in the state. He served as president of North Carolina's Council of Safety, which essentially ran the government in the early days of the revolution. In April 1776, the North Carolina Provincial Congress passed the Halifax Resolves, making North Carolina the first colony to officially authorize its delegates to vote for independence. Harnett chaired the committee that wrote them.

That August, when news of the Declaration of Independence arrived, Harnett was the one who stood up and read it aloud to a crowd at the courthouse in Halifax. The crowd reportedly lifted him onto their shoulders afterward.

The British singled him out. When Gen. Henry Clinton offered pardons to North Carolinians who returned to their loyalty, Harnett was one of the few men specifically excluded.

He served in the Continental Congress from 1777 to 1780 and signed the Articles of Confederation.

In January 1781, British troops under Maj. James Craig captured Wilmington. Harnett, sick with gout, tried to escape but was caught. According to the story, British soldiers threw him across a horse like a sack of grain and brought him back to town. He was held for a time in a crude, open-air blockhouse, exposed to the winter weather.

His health collapsed. The British eventually released him on parole, but it was too late. He died in April 1781, seven months before the British left Wilmington.

He was buried in Wilmington. His gravestone carries a line from the poet Alexander Pope describing a man who belonged to no sect and found God through nature.

He helped start the Revolution in North Carolina. He just didn't live to see it end.

text:
Videocon ruling: dissenting lenders must be paid in money, and an approved plan can go back to the CoC

A resolution plan that pays dissenting financial creditors in debentures does not pay them at all. That is the core of the Supreme Court's 16 November 2026 judgment in the Videocon group insolvency, Twin Star Technologies Ltd v. Bank of Maharashtra. The Court also confirmed that NCLAT can send an approved plan back to the Committee of Creditors when a statutory defect needs a commercial fix.

For anyone structuring, approving or auditing a resolution plan, both holdings matter.

Background

Videocon Industries Ltd and 12 group companies went through a consolidated corporate insolvency resolution process. Twin Star Technologies, a Vedanta group company, offered ₹2,962.02 crore against admitted claims of about ₹64,838 crore, a haircut of roughly 95.85%.

The plan gave financial creditors ₹200 crore upfront. The balance came as non-convertible debentures of ₹2,700 crore face value carrying a 6.65% coupon, redeemable in instalments starting 25 months after closing and running to the sixth year.

The CoC approved the plan with 95.09% of the voting share. CCI approval came on 8 December 2020, before voting closed on 11 December 2020.

NCLT Mumbai approved the plan on 8 June 2021, but directed that dissenting creditors receive their liquidation value in cash upfront. NCLAT stayed that approval in July 2021 and, on 5 January 2022, set it aside and remitted the plan to the CoC. Dissenting lenders included Bank of Maharashtra, IFCI, SIDBI and ABG Shipyard. Twin Star appealed.

What the Court held

A bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe upheld the remand. As reported, the holdings are these.

First, section 30(2)(b) of the IBC was not met. Following Jaypee Kensington v. NBCC, payment to a dissenting financial creditor means payment in money. Discharge through debentures redeemable over six years is not payment. A general clause in the plan stating compliance with section 30(2)(b) and regulation 38(1)(b) of the CIRP Regulations cannot replace a specific provision for payment, and the plan did not secure the priority that regulation 38(1)(b) gives dissenters.

Second, NCLT could not repair the defect by ordering cash upfront. That direction changed the structure of the plan and the order of distribution. Only the CoC can alter a plan, and only with the voting share required by section 30(4). Tribunals cannot substitute their own commercial judgment.

Third, NCLAT has power to remit a plan to the CoC where a statutory defect requires commercial modification. Rejecting the plan outright would push the debtor towards liquidation, which defeats the purpose of the Code. The Court referred to the 2026 amendment adding a proviso to section 31(2), which allows the Adjudicating Authority to ask the CoC to rectify defects before rejecting a plan. It decided the case on the law as it stood at the time, but treated the amendment as confirming the policy.

Fourth, the CoC is not functus officio once it approves a plan. It continues until the plan is implemented or the debtor goes into liquidation. Here approval had not become final, because it was under appeal under section 61(3) and stayed.

Fifth, the Court laid down guardrails for remand. It must advance the objectives of the Code, rest on a finding of non-compliance with section 30(2) or another section 61(3) ground, be used sparingly, and carry strict timelines.

Sixth, the foreign oil and gas assets of subsidiaries fall outside the CIRP and the liquidation estate, under the Explanation to section 18 and section 36(4)(d). A holding company does not own its subsidiaries' assets through its shareholding.

The objection on CCI approval failed, because approval came before voting concluded.

Directions

The matter goes back to the CoC. Operational creditors through the VIL Vendors Association have liberty to pursue other remedies. GAIL's claim is to be dealt with by the resolution professional, and the Union of India may place its contentions on the oil and gas block interests before the RP and the Adjudicating Authority.

Separately, NCLT Mumbai has declared former promoter V.N. Dhoot bankrupt on SBI's personal guarantee petition, with dues reported at ₹12,668.06 crore.

Who is affected

Resolution applicants who use deferred consideration, debentures or other instruments to stretch cash outflow.

CoC members, particularly lenders who vote against a plan and want their statutory minimum in cash.

Resolution professionals, who certify that a plan meets section 30(2) before it goes to vote.

Auditors of banks, NBFCs and acquirers, who must judge when a recovery under an approved but appealed plan can be recognised.

My analysis

The judgment does not stop a resolution applicant from paying assenting creditors in instruments. It stops the plan from forcing instruments on those who dissent. That distinction should now appear in every plan in plain terms: a separate clause, a fixed cash amount for dissenters at least equal to their liquidation value entitlement, and a payment timeline that gives them priority over assenting creditors.

For resolution professionals, a compliance certificate that recites section 30(2)(b) is not enough. The RP should be able to point to the clause that pays dissenters and show the arithmetic.

For lenders, the ruling strengthens a dissenting vote. A minority creditor who votes against a plan can insist on cash. That changes the negotiation inside the CoC, because applicants will price the dissenters' cash into the bid.

For auditors, the lesson is about timing. An approved plan under appeal is not final. Here the approval came in 2021 and the plan is back with the CoC in late 2026. Recognising recoveries or reversing provisions on approval alone, without considering pending appeals, carries real risk.

The guardrails on remand are useful. They tell NCLAT that remand is an exception, not a routine second chance. Applicants should still expect a remand where the defect is curable, instead of outright rejection.

Questions remain. Will the CoC reconsider Twin Star's plan with a revised payout to dissenters, or invite fresh bids after six years? How will the cash for dissenters be funded within a bid of ₹2,962 crore? And how will the new section 31(2) proviso operate in other pending cases?

Action points

1. Resolution applicants: review any pending plan that pays dissenters in NCDs, deferred instalments or equity, and restructure it to pay them in cash.

2. Resolution professionals: before putting a plan to vote, record which clause pays dissenting financial creditors, how much and when, and how the regulation 38(1)(b) priority is met.

3. Lenders: when deciding whether to dissent, compute your liquidation value entitlement and insist that the plan pays it in money.

4. CoC advisers: build a remand scenario into timelines where an approved plan is under appeal under section 61(3).

5. Auditors of lenders: do not treat approval by the Adjudicating Authority as final while an appeal is pending; assess the recovery and its timing on that basis.

6. Group structures: where the debtor's value sits in foreign subsidiaries, test early whether those assets fall inside the estate at all.

A dissenter's vote now carries a clear right: cash, on time, ahead of the assenting creditors.

This article is general information, not professional advice. The analysis relies on reported accounts of the judgment; read the full text before acting.

text:
163 years ago today Abraham Lincoln boarded a train for the little town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, where the next afternoon he would deliver 272 words that would redefine the meaning of the nation. On the eve of the most famous speech in American history, it is worth clearing away the myth and remembering what actually happened.

Four and a half months earlier, Gettysburg had been the scene of the largest and bloodiest battle ever fought on the continent. The dead had been so numerous that the town could not cope, and a new national cemetery was created to properly bury the Union soldiers who had fallen there. On November 19, 1863, that cemetery was to be formally dedicated, and the main event was to be a grand two-hour oration by Edward Everett, the most celebrated speaker in America. Almost as an afterthought, Lincoln was invited to offer a few appropriate remarks.

On November 18, Lincoln left Washington by train for Gettysburg. And here is where the legend needs correcting. The beloved myth is that Lincoln, careless and unprepared, scribbled the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope during the train ride, dashing off his immortal words almost by accident. It is a charming story, and it is not true. Lincoln took the speech seriously and had been working on it beforehand. He understood that the dedication was an opportunity to say something important about why the war was being fought and what the deaths of so many men had to mean.

He arrived in Gettysburg that evening and stayed at the home of David Wills, the man who had organized the cemetery, on the town square. That night, in his room, he continued to work on and refine his remarks, polishing the short, carefully constructed speech he would give the next day. Outside, the town was crowded with visitors come for the ceremony, and a crowd gathered to serenade the president, who gave a few brief, modest words and begged off saying more.

What he had prepared was astonishingly short, only about two minutes long, a handful of sentences that he must have known would be overshadowed in length by Everett's two-hour oration. But in those few lines, Lincoln would reach past the specific battle and the specific cemetery to recast the entire war as a test of whether a nation conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal could endure, and to call the living to a new birth of freedom. He would transform a dedication of graves into a statement of national purpose that still defines America to itself.

But that was tomorrow. On this day, Lincoln was simply a careworn president on a train and then in a borrowed bedroom, working over a speech, on his way to a grieving town to honor its dead.

MARKET REGIME
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
RISK-OFF.
Bitcoin and Ethereum are down roughly 14–16% over seven days. Sentiment remains in extreme fear, stablecoin supply is contracting, and the dollar has strengthened as markets price in a more hawkish Federal Reserve.

The weakness is not limited to crypto. Gold and oil also fell sharply in the Nov 18 session.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
TOP NEWS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Fed minutes reinforce the risk of higher rates.

Minutes from the October meeting, released on Nov 18, showed that almost all participants judged further rate increases would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two participants had preferred a 25-basis-point increase at that meeting. Separately, Governor Christopher Waller called for a possible 50-basis-point increase in December or a faster pace of tightening in 2027.
→ The Fed has not announced a new rate decision. But the policy direction described in the minutes leaves less room for markets to assume an early pivot.

Bitcoin struggles to follow the stock-market rebound.
After Nvidia beat earnings expectations, Nasdaq-100 futures rose about 1%. Bitcoin, however, remained under pressure. CoinDesk reported that the traditional BTC basis trade now offers only around 3–5% annualized returns, compared with 20–40% in early 2024. Talos found that major equity perpetuals offered higher average funding than major crypto perpetuals in 2026.
→ The old incentive for institutions to hold hedged Bitcoin exposure has weakened. Capital is finding alternative places to earn carry.

Binance secures a major court order in its recovery effort.
An Abu Dhabi Global Market Court order requires 18 companies, including Circle and World Liberty Financial, to maintain freezes on assets linked to the Oct 29 theft from Binance-operated wallets. Binance has previously said about $2.85B had been frozen or intercepted. The original hack is outside this research window; the new court action is not.
→ A legal order can help preserve frozen assets, but frozen funds are not the same as recovered funds. A further hearing is scheduled for Dec 1.

Visa Direct extends stablecoin prefunding into Asia-Pacific.

Visa plans to let eligible businesses use stablecoins to prefund cross-border payouts through Visa Direct. Singapore-based dtcpay is the pilot partner. Recipients receive local fiat, while a licensed partner handles conversion, compliance screening and settlement.
→ Stablecoins are moving deeper into payment infrastructure, beyond exchange trading.

DBS and Circle expand institutional USDC access.
Eligible institutional clients in Asia can now mint and redeem USDC directly through DBS, with dollar-to-USDC settlement available around the clock.
→ Direct bank access can reduce reliance on secondary-market liquidity and traditional banking cutoffs.

Backpack completes its U.S. regulatory licensing stack.
Backpack received National Futures Association approval to operate as a Futures Commission Merchant, following its earlier CFTC Designated Contract Market and Derivatives Clearing Organization approvals.
→ Crypto-native derivatives platforms are pursuing a more formal route into the U.S. market. The approval does not, by itself, confirm a launch date.

Variational raises $110M at a $1.5B valuation.
The on-chain derivatives protocol’s Series B was led by Bain Capital Crypto. The funding is intended to expand markets and raise open-interest limits. Its Omni platform has processed more than $475B in cumulative volume since early 2025, according to company figures reported by The Block.
→ Investors are still funding on-chain derivatives and traditional-asset exposure, even as crypto spot markets remain weak.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
THE MORNING TAKE
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Today’s market shows two different stories.

The infrastructure around crypto continues to develop: banks are opening stablecoin access, payment networks are testing new settlement routes, and derivatives firms are raising capital or completing regulatory steps. These are meaningful developments for the industry.

But they have not translated into stronger demand for BTC and ETH. Stablecoin supply is lower over the past week, sentiment remains deeply fearful, and the latest complete U.S. ETF session showed a significant Bitcoin outflow. Institutional infrastructure growth and spot-market strength are not the same thing.

The important question is where capital is actually going. Is it returning to crypto assets, or is it choosing payment rails, tokenized markets and derivatives instead?

Are you watching the price, or the direction of capital behind it?

text:
✝️ EVERYBODY'S LOOKING FOR FREEDOM
The World Offers a Thousand Escapes, but Jesus Offers a New Life

Everybody's looking for freedom.

The wealthy seek freedom from worry. The poor seek freedom from hardship. The lonely seek freedom from isolation. The wounded seek freedom from painful memories. The guilty seek freedom from yesterday.

Some search for freedom in money, pleasure, relationships, success, independence, or the approval of others.

Yet humanity faces a remarkable contradiction:

We have more opportunities to pursue freedom than perhaps any generation before us, yet countless people remain prisoners of their own hearts.

We can travel across continents while carrying the same fears. We can change our surroundings without changing our thinking. We can escape difficult circumstances and discover that our deepest captivity has followed us.

Because not every prison has walls.

Some prisons are built from resentment. Others from shame, jealousy, pride, addiction, bitterness, or the relentless need to be accepted.

And sometimes the strongest chains are those we have mistaken for freedom.

📖 John 8:36 (WEB)

"If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed."

🌿 THE FREEDOM THAT CANNOT SATISFY

The world often defines freedom as the ability to do whatever we desire.

But consider this carefully:

If you cannot say no to your desires, are you truly free?

A person controlled by anger is not free simply because nobody prevents him from expressing it.

A person enslaved to possessions is not free simply because he can afford more.

And someone who constantly needs admiration has surrendered the keys to his happiness to everyone around him.

Freedom without self-control can become another form of captivity.

Jesus did not come merely to improve our circumstances. He came to transform the person living within them.

🕊️ WHEN CHRIST BREAKS THE INVISIBLE CHAINS

📖 2 Corinthians 3:17 (WEB)

"Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty."

Notice what Scripture does not say.

It does not promise that wherever the Spirit is, there will be no suffering, opposition, disappointment, or difficulty.

Instead, it reveals something far more extraordinary.

The presence of God can establish freedom within a person even before their circumstances change.

Paul and Silas sang praises while imprisoned.

Their bodies were confined, but their worship was not.

Their circumstances restricted their movement, but they could not imprison their communion with God.

The prison doors eventually opened, but their spiritual freedom existed before the earthquake.

That is the astonishing difference between earthly freedom and freedom in Christ.

The world says, "Change everything around you, and perhaps you will find peace."

Jesus says, "Come to Me, and I will begin changing what is happening within you."

❤️ FREEDOM IS NOT THE ABSENCE OF LOVE

There is another beautiful mystery.

The more deeply we belong to Christ, the less we need to be controlled by the opinions of the world.

We become free to forgive without demanding revenge.

Free to give without expecting repayment.

Free to love without constantly calculating what we might receive.

Free to admit our weaknesses because our identity no longer depends upon pretending to be perfect.

The highest expression of freedom is not living without responsibility. It is becoming free enough to love without fear.

📖 Galatians 5:13 (WEB)

"For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don't use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another."

What an extraordinary paradox!

Christ frees us from slavery to sin so that we may willingly serve one another in love.

🙏 A PRAYER FOR TRUE FREEDOM

Heavenly Father,

You see every invisible chain that burdens the human heart.

You know the fears we conceal, the wounds we carry, the temptations we battle, and the memories we cannot seem to release.

Lord Jesus, deliver us from everything that competes with Your truth.

Where bitterness has imprisoned us, teach us forgiveness.

Where fear has restricted us, establish courage.

Where shame has silenced us, restore our confidence in Your mercy.

Holy Spirit, lead us into the beautiful liberty of belonging completely to God.

May we never confuse independence from You with freedom.

And may the freedom we receive become compassion, healing, and hope for others.

In the mighty name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

Everybody is looking for freedom. But the greatest freedom is not discovering a life where nothing can restrain us. It is discovering a Savior whose love can no longer be taken from us.

The world offers freedom to follow every desire. Jesus offers freedom from being ruled by them.

And that changes everything.

📖 John 8:32 (WEB)

"You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free."

Why Is the Federal Reserve Still Talking?

When Chairman Kevin Warsh ascended to the throne of the world's most powerful institution, he promised one thing: no more forward guidance. 

Under his watch, the Federal Reserve would no longer lay down the policy path and offer a peek into the central bank's crystal ball. Some of the top officials must have missed Warsh's memo.

The US central bank must have a new dual mandate: talk and talk some more.

Any time Kevin Warsh has made a public appearance, he has offered no hint of forward guidance. Jokes, self-deprecation, and allusions to reforms have allowed him to avoid predicting the Fed's moves.

The likes of Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan have not emulated this discretion. Instead, they have uttered remarks that spooked Wall Street.

In an overseas speech this week, Waller warned that persistent higher-than-expected inflation could force him and his colleagues to pull the trigger on a jumbo-sized rate hike next month. Here is what he said in his prepared comments:

"If the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings — with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher — then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."

His oration came just before the October Consumer Price Index, which, in the words of Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, was "borderline disturbing."

text:
Thursday, November 19, 2026

Free Indeed: From the Tyranny of “I Can’t” to the Liberty of Christ in Me

Scripture Reading: John 8:31-36  (“King James Version”)

31. Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
32. And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
33. They answered him, We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free?
34. Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.
35. And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever.
36. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.

Key Verse: John 8:36 (“King James Version”)

36. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.

Note to reader: All verses quoted are from "King James Version."

The Two Freedoms—Savior and Son

Oswald Chambers’ classic from “My Utmost for His Highest,” titled “Winning into Freedom,” keyed to John 8:36. Chambers draws a sharp, practical distinction that runs throughout his teaching: the difference between “individuality” and “personality.”

Individuality is the natural, self-assertive “I” that remains after the new birth. It is the husk of the personal life—protective in childhood but, if untransfigured, becomes egotistical, isolating, and prone to the complaint “I can’t.” It is the remnant of selfish independence that still says no when God calls. Chambers insists this is not primarily the problem of sin (which Jehovahs already dealt with in redemption) but of the natural life that must still be offered and sacrificed.

Personality, by contrast, is the full meaning of a being created by Jehovah who has lived on earth and formed godly character. It never says “I can’t.” When it contacts Jehovah it absorbs and always wants more, because we are designed with a great capacity for Him. The majority of believers, Chambers observes, are only beginning to be personalities; they have not yet rid themselves of individuality.

The process is clear and active: Jehovah delivers from sin; “we” must deliver ourselves from individuality by presenting our natural life and sacrificing it through obedience until it is transformed into spiritual life. Jehovah’s order is already present in every facet of our natural existence; we are to cooperate with it rather than resist with “I can’t.” Jehovah will not discipline us or bring every thought into captivity—we must do it. The famous practical instruction follows: do not go to Jehovah saying “I suffer from wandering thoughts.” Stop listening to the tyranny of individuality and get emancipated into personality.

Chambers then makes a precise Christological point: do not substitute “Savior” for “Son.” The Savior sets free from sin; the Son sets free from individuality. This is the freedom of Galatians 2:20—“I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.” Paul’s natural individuality is broken; his personality is united (not merely merged) with the Lord. The result is freedom “indeed”—free from the inside out, free in the very essence of being.

Theologically, the passage is rooted in the identification of the believer with Christ in death and life. Practically, it refuses both quietism (“God must do everything”) and legalistic self-effort. Freedom is not license; it is the liberty of a personality fully yielded and therefore fully alive to Jehovah. This is the consistent witness of the three teachers the user names: Chambers on the emancipation of the personal spirit, Spurgeon on self-denial becoming joy under the law of Christ, and Branham on the necessity of dying to self so that the Word (Christ) may live and produce fruit.

 Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. They answered him, We be Abraham’s seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free? Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever. If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.

Individuality Versus Personality

Individuality is the natural covering that isolates and asserts itself. Personality is the godly character formed by living before Jehovah and absorbing His life. Most of us are only beginning to be personalities; the husk of individuality still governs our reactions, our thoughts, and our refusals. Charles Spurgeon spoke of the proper recognition of the self (“I, yet not I”)—humble, responsible egoism under Christ rather than proud egotism. William Branham repeatedly taught that one must die to self and to one’s own thoughts before the living Word can be seen and can bear fruit. Chambers simply says: stop listening to the tyranny of individuality and get emancipated into personality.

The Active Sacrifice of the Natural Life

Jehovah pays no attention to our natural individuality in the development of our spiritual life, but He expects us to pay attention to it. His order is already written into the ordinary circumstances of daily existence. We help that order along by offering the natural life and sacrificing it through obedience until it is transformed. Spurgeon noted that true consecration does not restrict the faculties; it liberates them into the element for which they were designed—obedience to Christ. Self-denial itself becomes joy when the heart is perfectly loyal. Branham’s language is stronger: to serve Christ one must become a bond-slave by daily crucifying the flesh so that Jehovah may take hold and motivate.

Capturing Thoughts and Daily Emancipation

Jehovah will not bring our thoughts into captivity; we must. Do not pray, “Lord, I suffer from wandering thoughts.” Stop suffering. Refuse to listen to the voice that says “I can’t.” Every time that voice is answered with obedient action, individuality is weakened and personality is strengthened. The life hidden in Christ (Colossians 3:3) becomes the practical atmosphere in which the believer moves.

Additional Scriptures for Meditation  
 
Galatians 2:20   

20.  I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.

Romans 6:6–11 

6. Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.  
7. For he that is dead is freed from sin.  
8. Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him:  
9. Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.  
10. For in that he died, he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God.  
11. Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Luke 9:23 

23. And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.

Philippians 2:5–8 
  
5. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:  
6. Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:  
7. But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:  
8. And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

Romans 8:13   

13. For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.

Philippians 2:5–8 

5. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:  
6. Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:  
7. But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:  
8. And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

Romans 8:13 
 
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.

Questions and Answers

1. What is the difference between individuality and personality in this teaching?  

A.  Individuality is the natural, self-assertive “I” that says “I can’t” and isolates. Personality is the being created by Jehovah that has formed godly character by living before Him and absorbing His life. Freedom means the breaking of the first so the second may be united with Christ.

2. Why does Chambers refuse to let us pray about wandering thoughts?

A.  Because Jehovah will not do for us what He has given us the responsibility to do. Continuing to “suffer” is still listening to individuality. Emancipation begins when we stop the tyranny by active refusal and obedience.

3. How does Galatians 2:20 illustrate true freedom? 

A. Paul’s individuality is crucified; he no longer lives as an independent “I.” Christ lives in him. The life he now lives in the flesh is by the faith of the Son of Jehovah. This is freedom “indeed”—from the inside out.

4. What practical role do Spurgeon and Branham play in this theme?
  
A. Spurgeon shows that self-denial under Christ is not loss but the highest liberty and joy; the true “I” is preserved and fulfilled only in the “not I.” Branham insists that one must die to self, to feelings, and to one’s own thinking before the living Word can be seen and can reproduce itself through the believer.

How to Apply This in Daily Life

- When the familiar “I can’t” arises, treat it as the voice of individuality and answer it with one concrete act of obedience in the next five minutes.  
- Each morning offer the natural life of that day: “Here is my schedule, my desires, my thoughts—transform them by obedience.”  
- Capture thoughts at the moment they wander; do not negotiate or pray about them first—refuse and redirect.  
- In relationships and work, practice the mind of Christ (Philippians 2): choose the lower place, the unnoticed service, the denial of self-assertion.  
- Daily confess with Paul: “I am crucified with Christ; nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.” Let the confession become the atmosphere.  
- Expect the capacity for God to enlarge. Personality always wants more of Him; feed that hunger with the Word and with obedience.

When the Son has set you free from the tyranny of individuality, you are free indeed—free in the very essence of your being, free to absorb Jehovah, free to let Christ live His life through you. This is the freedom Chambers, Spurgeon, and Branham all point toward: not the absence of a cross, but the presence of the risen Son.

Prayer 🙏  : The Surrender of the Husk

I come before You today with a quiet and trembling heart, my merciful, omnipotent, and sovereign Heavenly Father.  I ask Jesus Christ to forgive us of our transgressions.   Lord Jesus, You have already redeemed my soul and conquered the power of sin within me, yet I bring before You today the stubborn shell of my natural life. text:
🥊 Lauren Price to fight for undisputed world title in Cardiff after WBO belt added

Lauren Price is one win away from making Welsh boxing history, with a shot at undisputed world champion status now on the line when she meets Michaela Kotaskova in Cardiff on Friday.

According to BBC Wales, the vacant WBO welterweight title has been added to the bout at the Utilita Arena. The Olympic champion was already putting her IBF, WBA and WBC belts on the line, so victory would bring all four major titles together.

The WBO strap had belonged to American Mikaela Mayer, who has given it up ahead of a December rematch with Chantelle Cameron. That bout will see Mayer challenge for Cameron's unified WBO, WBA and WBC super-welterweight titles.

Explaining her decision on social media, Mayer wrote: "As much as I looked forward to unifying for undisputed, it's dragged out too long and the Cameron rematch is now my priority.

"No need to be holding up the welterweight division in the meantime."

Price, 32, learned of the development late on Tuesday and says it has given her even more to fight for this week.

"It will mean a little bit more history," said Price. "And it just hits home a little bit because it would mean I'd achieved everything I set out to do in boxing.

"As an amateur, it was to go and win an Olympic gold. As a pro it's to become undisputed world champion. If get that win on Friday night I will have ticked every accolade there is.

"I've got the chance to grab that with both hands and I'm adamant I'm not only keeping the belts in Wales, I'm adding one."

She goes into the contest unbeaten in 10 professional fights. Her most recent outing was in April, when she outpointed mandatory challenger Stephanie Pineiro to retain her titles.

Price also holds the IBO and Ring Magazine belts. A win would see her become the first boxer from Wales to hold the four major world titles at the same time.

Joe Calzaghe came close in 2007, when he defeated Mikkel Kessler to collect the WBO, WBA and WBC super-middleweight belts. By then, however, he had already given up the IBF title.

Price would also join an exclusive group of British women to have reached undisputed status, becoming the fourth after Savannah Marshall, Chantelle Cameron and Ellie Scotney.

Kotaskova, 34, from the Czech Republic, is the reigning WBF champion and has never lost at welterweight. Across 15 professional fights, her only defeat came in the division above, when Chantelle Cameron beat her on points in a bout fought over three-minute rounds.

She described the chance to fight for undisputed status as "a huge surprise" and said it offered an opportunity to create history in her homeland.

She also had a message for Price: "It won't be easy for her. I have followed her career for many years and I saw in her last fight the first time there wasn't a big difference between fighters.

"Nobody's perfect; every fighter has some weaknesses and there's always a way to win. I see a chance."

A strong Welsh presence fills out the rest of the card. Rhys Edwards takes on Scotland's Lee McGregor, a former British and European champion, for the WBA continental featherweight title.

Promoter Ben Shalom said: "Friday night is about Welsh boxing. Lauren is creating opportunities for Welsh boxers.

"There are many more nights to come and they will get bigger and bigger."

Shalom also suggested Edwards could soon be topping bills himself. However, 29-year-old McGregor insisted he is far from finished: "A lot of people think I'm past it and are writing me off, but I'm determined to prove a lot of people wrong."

Elsewhere on the bill, Willy Gilheaney meets Argentina's Alberto Ignacio Palmetta with the WBA continental gold welterweight belt at stake.

The fight will be broadcast live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer.

text:
The US had a lot of piecemeal laws like that, which was a big part of the reason the 14th amendment was passed.  Even worse, when black people did own businesses, sometimes they were targeted with violence if seen as too successful.  One historical example brought up frequently is "Black Wall Street," the nickname for a very successful business area in the Greenwood neighborhood of Tulsa, Oklahoma.  Whites burned it to the ground and killed hundreds of people in 1921 -- you can google it for details, also can search for info on the "Black Codes" and "Jim Crow" laws.  It was...  the south being the south again. 🙄  I've met people up north who are ready to fight the Civil War again, if necessary.  The south really hurt its own reputation with all of that hate going on.

With South Africa, a constitutional amendment against racial discrimination would be nice, or at least something like our 14th, but there's the sad reality of assets/land distribution being skewed heavily toward white South Africans during apartheid.  That problem is real, and it needs a realistic and humane solution.  I know that the government has tried different things, like land reform, and a lot of other things according to a google search, but it's an experimental situation.  There is no perfect model for coming out of this pain-free.  And so they'll have to adjust things as they go, and maybe they'll change business ownership rules if enough people complain, or they realize that they're not attracting many investors that way.

Of course, if someone owns a percentage of a business, that means they do a good part of the work, right?  That SHOULD make their partner's life easier, at least if it's a good partnership.  

Anyway, I'm from a country with a very imperfect history on race relations.  I can't offer much of an opinion because I don't know the country that well.  When I was in college in the 80s, the big cause was ending apartheid.  We'd see 3 or 4 black kids beaten to death by police in South Africa every night on the evening news.  It was a lot like our own Vietnam War coverage of the previous decades.  SA police even beat Steve Biko to death, who was known to Americans as a part of the "black is beautiful" movement.

And of course we'd see that the white South Africans had their areas with nice houses, and the black people had been pushed into these little areas where they lived in squalor in "shantytowns."  Some had jobs in the white areas.  We'd seen all of that before -- in America's SOUTH. 🤨 If you ever want to trigger a northerner, especially back then...  And then there were the mining jobs, which were terrible, but gave South Africa a good part of its wealth in comparison to poorer African countries.

I specialized in African for my history degree, minored in American, partly because I liked the way the field was opened by anthropologists, and also because I didn't want to spend most of my time reading about European monarchs by majoring in European history.  There are over 50 countries in Africa, and although South Africa was among those with a large population, it was a mess in the 80s with its civil war going on.  If I'd continued for my PhD instead of being lured into the computer field, I wouldn't have even visited because it was too dangerous.  Nigeria was more populous, Egypt more famous, and so on.  Yet when Apartheid fell, I expected South Africa to eventually become a nice country, much more stable, and I think it has. 

But it still has poverty, and inequality in assets and opportunities that remain from the apartheid era.  Nobody expects folks from SA to solve everything instantaneously.  It's good to be honest with yourself, though, and admit that the system was stacked against certain groups, and that they need and deserve some respect, and help reversing injustices of the past.   Maybe some of the attempts to fix things will make everyone's situation worse, but others will work.  Keep in touch with your representatives to let them know how you feel about these changes, and share what you think would do better.

Elon...  He has influence, but only to a point, and he doesn't live there anymore.  There's also the problem of being seen as anti-indigenous when he's on the side of whites on a certain issue.  That's bad for his businesses everywhere.  About the most he can do is complain about discrimination against white people, which seems ridiculous in our country but does seem to apply to South Africa in certain ways.  I think your own representatives would have more influence, and maybe that law will be a flop, driving investors away, and it'll be changed anyway.  It's all trailblazing from here!  I hope you can help make your country better for everyone. 🌞

😃 Good luck!

text:
AI Field Notes #138

Codex found Java4Shell, a critical Java flaw, in one hour for under $200 in tokens. Your patch window is now measured against that.

- Two poisoned releases of Microsoft's agent-framework stole Azure and GitHub keys from Nov 17 installs
- OpenAI's own system card rates GPT-6.2 at its Critical cyber threshold
- Gemini 4 Neon ships at $3 per million tokens, no benchmarks yet
- 64.5% of coding-agent spend in a 27,280-run test went to failed runs
- Citi: if your AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours

TODAY'S STORIES:

1. Java4Shell: Codex found a critical Java flaw in an hour for under $200 in tokens
If you run Java 17 or later on x86 servers, patch this week: Oracle and Amazon Corretto builds are out, and Red Hat's are coming. An ops engineer should remember the price tag. When $200 and an afternoon finds a flaw like this, the time between a patch release and an attack shrinks with it.

2. Microsoft agent-framework: two poisoned PyPI releases stole Azure and GitHub credentials
Any engineer whose build pulled agent-framework 1.26 or later on November 17 should treat every secret on that machine as stolen. Pin version 1.26.0 and rebuild, then rotate the keys. Uninstalling the package stops the stealer and does nothing about the tokens already sent.

3. Gemini 4 Neon: Google's fourth new model in a month lands at $3 per million tokens
A backend engineer choosing a Gemini tier now has four names and a price list that reshuffles in two weeks. Hold your routing decisions until scores arrive, and budget on the December prices, since the introductory ones expire.

4. FrontierHarness v1.1: 64.5% of coding-agent spend went to runs that failed
Choosing a coding agent by leaderboard rank settles half the question. If your team runs open models, try two or three harnesses on your own tasks before standardizing, and measure cost per passed task. The per-token price hides the failures you pay for.

5. Claude Code team says Claude writes about 90% of its code, then explains how it checks it
A senior engineer's job is being rewritten in public here: less time reading every diff, more time deciding what "done" means and auditing the evidence. If your team is adding agents, write the verify step first, and switch enforcement on only after watching what it would block.

6. MAI Cyber 2 Flash: Microsoft says its security model costs $0.45 a task against $34.38
A security analyst on Microsoft's stack will see the default model change under them next month. Benchmarks run by the vendor deserve a second look, so try your own tasks first. Still, a 76-fold price gap survives a lot of skepticism.

7. Microsoft buyouts: Nadella says 60,000 staff needed 'agency' as jobs shift to managing AI
A mid-career engineer at any large software company just heard the plan stated plainly. The work that stays is directing agents and checking them, and fewer people do it. Ask what your team would look like at 11, and which of those seats you could hold.

8. Citi joins JPMorgan and Bank of America: if your AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours
Before you connect a budgeting assistant to your checking account, read your bank's updated terms. Read-only tools carry less risk than ones that hold your password. A freelancer who lets an agent pay invoices is now self-insuring against that agent's security.

9. Anthropic IPO prices at $83, above its range, raising over $94 billion with a private sale
More than $200 billion on the balance sheet buys a lot of chips and data centers. For a developer building on Claude, that points to more capacity and looser rate limits, eventually. Anyone holding an index fund will likely end up owning a slice of a company whose board answers to a trust.

10. OpenAI says its models squeezed 14% more out of AMD's flagship GPU design in five months
Chip design runs on multi-year cycles and scarce specialists. If the claim holds, those cycles shorten and AI labs start improving their own suppliers' chips. A junior hardware engineer should learn the AI design tools now, while knowing them is still unusual.

11. Cerebras splits inference with AMD GPUs and claims 5x the tokens per megawatt
Developers who pay for fast inference could see more of it on offer without a new power plant being built. Nothing changes in your code today. If you buy capacity, start asking providers for throughput per megawatt, because it will reach your bill before it reaches their marketing.

12. Mistral Vibe Desktop: Europe's AI lab ships a Mac and Windows agent app, minus computer use
For a developer at a European bank or ministry that cannot send code to a US lab, this is the option on the approved list, and it now resembles the tools colleagues elsewhere use. It is a generation behind on capability. Compliance may decide that is an acceptable price.

13. Snapchat Easy Lens CLI lets Claude Code, Cursor and Codex build and publish AR Lenses
Platforms have started shipping their developer tools as commands for agents first. A freelance AR developer who charged for build time should expect clients to try the one-day version before calling. Taste and an audience are what remain billable.

14. Genie 4: Google opens its playable world model to AI Ultra subscribers, now with sound
A game designer can sketch a level by describing it and hand a playable mock-up to the team the same afternoon. It will not ship as a game. As a way to test an idea before anyone models a single asset, it costs a subscription.

15. Harvard study: 54% of power for America's biggest data centers came from gas and coal
If you live in Virginia, Ohio, Oregon or Iowa, more than half of this load sits on your grid. A parent reading a utility notice about a rate increase or a new gas plant now has a peer-reviewed number to bring to the public hearing.

16. Mullin blames 'the SI' for a week of outages; Microsoft, the FAA and Chase blame bugs
When a cabinet official blames a machine mind on cable news, the boring explanation gets harder to hear. An engineer who has shipped a bad release knows which one is likelier. Ask for the dull thing: published incident reports with root causes.

17. Pangram flags 99% of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as AI-written; its publisher holds firm
An editor or a prize juror now faces the same bind: the detector is confident, the writer denies it, and there is no third witness. Keep drafts and version history for anything you submit. Proof of process is becoming part of the manuscript.

ONE STORY THAT MOVES THE FLOOR:

A Microsoft engineer weighing one of October's 60,000 buyout offers got the explanation on November 18. Satya Nadella said it was about staff feeling they had agency, then described the Cowork team: 11 developers who build a software factory that builds the product. If your team shrank to 11, would your seat be one of them?

Full issue with sources, plus the daily email: link in my profile.

Me: The Secret Team: The CIA and Its Allies in Control of the United States and the World 

Ai: The Secret Team: The CIA and Its Allies in Control of the United States and the World by L. Fletcher Prouty, originally published in 1973, is a controversial and provocative examination of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the American intelligence establishment, and the hidden networks of military, political, and corporate power that the author argues influence U.S. foreign policy and international affairs.
Written by L. Fletcher Prouty, a retired U.S. Air Force colonel who served as the Pentagon's principal liaison with the CIA on military support for clandestine operations, the book draws upon his professional experience to describe how intelligence agencies and military organizations operate behind the scenes.
Prouty examines the development of covert operations during the Cold War, focusing on the relationship between the CIA, the Pentagon, the White House, and powerful political figures. He explores the administration of President Dwight Eisenhower, the influence of CIA Director Allen Dulles, and the conflicts between intelligence agencies and elected political leadership.

Among the major subjects discussed are:
The CIA and covert operations: How intelligence agencies conduct secret political and military activities beyond ordinary public scrutiny.
The Cold War: How anti-communism, military strategy, and national security became instruments of American foreign policy.
The U-2 incident: The controversial 1960 spy-plane crisis and its implications for American-Soviet relations.
The Bay of Pigs invasion: The CIA-sponsored attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro's government in Cuba.
President John F. Kennedy: Prouty's interpretation of Kennedy's relationship with the intelligence establishment and the events surrounding his presidency and assassination.
The military-industrial establishment: The connections between intelligence agencies, military institutions, defense contractors, and political influence.
One of the book's central arguments is that an unofficial network of intelligence officers, military personnel, government officials, and influential private interests operates with considerable independence from elected government. Prouty calls this network the Secret Team.
The book is particularly controversial because Prouty advances allegations about intelligence operations, political manipulation, and the Kennedy assassination that are not established historical facts. His interpretations should therefore be read critically and compared with independent historical research.

Why the book is significant
The Secret Team is an important work within the literature of intelligence criticism and alternative interpretations of American political history. It offers readers an insider's perspective on the relationship between intelligence agencies and military power while raising fundamental questions about government accountability, secrecy, democracy, and the limits of presidential authority.

In essence: This is a book about the possibility that some of the most consequential decisions affecting American foreign policy and international affairs are made not entirely in public government institutions, but through secretive networks of influence operating behind them.
