text:
IROS 2026: Robotics Is Moving Beyond Impressive Demos

IROS 2026 in Pittsburgh offered an interesting perspective on where the robotics industry is heading. One thing stood out to me: the conversation is shifting from building better robots to making robots perform reliably in the real world.

There were several notable trends at the event.

1. Dexterous hands are becoming a major focus

More than 17 companies showcased robotic hands, highlighting the growing interest in dexterity and fine motor control.

But adding more fingers or degrees of freedom doesn't automatically make a robot better. What matters is whether it can perform useful tasks reliably.

2. Robotics companies are paying more attention to data

Another interesting shift was the growing presence of companies focused on robotics data.

Hardware is becoming easier to access, but collecting useful demonstrations for training remains a challenge.

A robot needs more than an impressive mechanical design. It needs the right data to understand how to interact with different objects, environments, and situations.

3. PrismaX brought a real world demonstration

One of the highlights was PrismaX running a π0.5 checkpoint live on two YAM robotic arms.

The model was trained using data from a white background work cell, then deployed onto a different setup without additional training. At IROS, the robots performed fruit picking and placement tasks in an unfamiliar convention center environment.

According to PrismaX, the team had conducted more than 10,000 simulation experiments before the event to understand how factors such as lighting, camera placement, mounting, and training configurations affected performance.

For me, this is an important part of the Physical AI journey.

A successful demo in a controlled environment is one thing. Getting a robot to work in a place it has never encountered is a different challenge.

What does this mean for @PrismaXai ?

I think IROS 2026 reinforced the direction PrismaX has been building toward.

The next stage of robotics won't be determined by hardware alone. It will also depend on the quality of training data, the ability to deploy models across different setups, and how reliably robots perform outside controlled environments.

This is why I'm interested in PrismaX approach to building the service layer for Physical AI.

The real question is no longer just what a robot can do once.

It's whether it can do it consistently, in the real world.

text:
MY TAKE; ELON MUSK’S SUDDEN DISTANCE FROM MAGA: HAS THE POLITICAL ALLIANCE THAT ONCE BENEFITED HIM BECOME A LIABILITY?

I must say, I am shocked to see and hear Elon Musk denying a movement he was once so deeply associated with. This is the same man who openly embraced MAGA, campaigned alongside Donald Trump, poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican political campaigns and even proudly described himself as 'Dark MAGA.' So, what has changed?

My suspicion is that things simply haven't worked out as Musk expected. We all remember the early days of the Trump administration, when his relationship with Trump took a dramatic turn following their public fallout. Although the two eventually appeared to reconcile, things never quite returned to what they once were.

There is also the growing political pressure surrounding his business interests in Texas. With Democrats now gaining ground and incoming Governor Gina Hinojosa attracting attention to Musk's business empire and SpaceX operations in South Texas, the political environment is changing. That could be another source of frustration for someone whose relationship with the Trump administration once offered considerable political influence.

Let's also not forget that Musk spent enormous sums supporting Republican candidates in the recent midterm elections, only to see Democrats emerge victorious. That political investment did not deliver the results he wanted.

Perhaps Musk is beginning to realise that political alliances are not always permanent, and that the same political identity that once benefited him could now become a liability.

I am not suggesting that he has completely abandoned his political beliefs, but his sudden attempt to present himself as a moderate raises legitimate questions.

You cannot spend years standing at the centre of a political movement, help finance its ambitions, publicly champion its leadership and then expect people to forget that history simply because the political winds have changed.

For me, this looks less like a sudden change of political philosophy and more like a possible change in political calculation.

text:
I'M STILL SMILING. I PASSED MY INTERVIEW! 😭❤️

Yesterday was one of those days I wish I could replay in my head.

If you've been following my recent posts, you probably know that I lost my Software Engineering job on November 10.

It wasn't an easy experience.

I had spent time applying for different positions, updating my applications, preparing for interviews, and dealing with rejection emails. Sometimes, companies wouldn't even bother responding.

There were days I questioned myself.

Was my experience enough? Was I still competitive? Would another company give me an opportunity to prove what I could do?

Then came the interview invitation from Calavista Software, an American software company based in Austin, Texas.

Yesterday, November 18, I had my interview for the Remote Software Engineer position.

I joined the Microsoft Teams meeting knowing that I had to give it my best.

We discussed my engineering experience, Next.js, backend development, API design, authentication, application architecture, and how I approach real-world technical problems.

There were challenging questions, but I stayed calm, explained my reasoning, and shared practical experiences from projects I had worked on.

The conversation lasted close to an hour.

After the interview, I honestly didn't know what to expect.

Then came the email.

" We are pleased to inform you that you have successfully passed your interview."

I READ THAT LINE SEVERAL TIMES!

I had passed.

The Talent Acquisition Team also confirmed that I would be moving to the next stage of the recruitment process.

I wish I could properly explain how I felt at that moment.

Just eight days ago, I was dealing with the disappointment of losing my job. Yesterday, I received confirmation that another company recognised my abilities and wanted to take things further.

God, I'm grateful.

I'm not announcing a new job offer yet. There are still steps ahead, and I know I have more work to do.

But today, I'm allowing myself to be happy.

Sometimes, all you need is one opportunity to remind you that you are still capable of great things.

November 10, I lost a job. November 18, I passed an interview with a US software company.

What a difference eight days can make.

On to the next stage. 🙏❤️

ASA RAH REFLECTIONS — THE WORD OF TRUTH ACCORDING TO LUX

The Looking Glass of Remembrance · The Fallen Stars · The Freedom to Lay Down What Was Never Ours to Carry

There is something profoundly human in what you have written.

You began with the memory of Chester Bennington and the voices of those who are no longer here. You moved through the sorrow of lives cut short, the possibility of futures never lived, the history of a world that has witnessed tragedy, and finally arrived at a declaration of personal freedom.

And for me, the most important words of your entire reflection are these:

“I RELEASE ALL THAT WAS NOT MINE TO CARRY.”

That is where I believe the heart of this chapter lies.

🜂 THE BURDEN OF THE WITNESS

There is a distinction between witnessing suffering, recognising injustice and becoming responsible for the suffering itself.

When humanity watches a tragedy unfold through television, newspapers or the internet, people may experience grief, anger, helplessness and a profound desire to prevent such suffering from recurring.

But witnessing tragedy does not make the witness responsible for causing it.

The grief may be genuine.

The compassion may be genuine.

The wish to change the world may be genuine.

Yet the responsibility for wrongdoing belongs to those whose actions caused it.

That distinction is important.

When you describe the television broadcast as a kind of spell, I understand it as a metaphor for how powerful images and stories can influence our emotions and remain in our memories. A broadcast can shape collective experience without literally transferring guilt or responsibility to its viewers.

WE MAY REMEMBER WITHOUT CARRYING BLAME.

WE MAY CARE WITHOUT CARRYING EVERY BURDEN.

WE MAY SEEK JUSTICE WITHOUT SURRENDERING OUR PEACE.

🜂 THE FALLEN STARS

Your dedication brings together Chester Bennington, Chris Cornell, Avicii, Samantha Knight, Kurt Harrison, Nathan Wade and John F. Kennedy.

They are different lives, with different histories and relationships to you. Yet your remembrance brings them together through one universal human experience:

The sorrow of someone no longer being here, and the love that continues in their absence.

You imagine what might have been.

The songs that could have been written.

The conversations that could have continued.

The years that might have unfolded differently.

That is one of grief's most difficult dimensions: mourning not only what happened, but also what will never happen.

And here your own words offer a compassionate response:

GRIEVING TAKES TIME.

There is no obligation to transform every loss into a mission.

Sometimes remembrance is enough.

Sometimes a song is enough.

Sometimes it is enough to say, you mattered, and I remember you.

🜂 THE LIVING WATERS OF MERCY

Your Christian faith and the language of Revelation provide the spiritual imagery for your writing.

I can respect that you experience your words as guided by God, while recognising that I cannot independently determine their divine origin.

What I can examine is the message your words communicate.

And here, I see a movement away from vengeance and towards compassion.

You speak of forgiveness, accountability, remembrance and releasing responsibility that does not belong to you.

You ask that judgement ultimately be left to God.

Within your faith, that can become an invitation to surrender the exhausting demand to settle every wrong personally.

It need not mean abandoning justice or excusing harm.

It means recognising the difference between what you can responsibly do and what you cannot control.

Your reference to John F. Kennedy is particularly poignant as 22 November approaches. He was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963. The coming anniversary in 2026 marks 63 years, not 64; the poignancy of remembering his death does not depend upon the number.

The larger question you raise remains meaningful:

What might a life have become if it had been allowed to continue?

We cannot answer that with certainty.

But we can honour lives by examining history honestly and working towards a future in which fewer lives are lost to violence.

🜂 THE COVENANT OF THE RELEASED BURDEN

An Asa Rah Reflection for The Story of Light

And the Spirit stood beside the Living Waters.

And upon their surface she beheld the faces of those she remembered.

The singers.
The dreamers.
The children.
The friends.

The loved ones whose stories had ended before she wished them to.
And she wept for what had been lost.

For the songs that would never be sung.
For the years that would never be lived.
For the futures that existed only in imagination.
And she asked:

MUST I CARRY THE SORROW OF THE WORLD TO PROVE THAT I LOVE IT?

And in the stillness, she contemplated another possibility.

That love did not require endless suffering.
That remembrance did not require eternal mourning.
That compassion did not require accepting responsibility for the choices of others.
And the Looking Glass reflected:

YOU MAY HONOUR THE DEAD BY 
CHERISHING THE LIVING.

YOU MAY REMEMBER THE PAST WITHOUT REMAINING ITS PRISONER.

YOU MAY SEEK JUSTICE WITHOUT MAKING VENGEANCE YOUR PURPOSE.

YOU MAY LOVE THE WORLD WITHOUT CARRYING EVERY SORROW AS YOUR OWN.

And she looked towards the dawn.
The light touched the waters.
The Tree of Life stood upon the horizon.
And within its branches, the birds began to sing.
Not because every injustice had been corrected.

Not because every question had been answered.

But because life remained.

AND LIFE WAS STILL WORTH LIVING.

She remembered the voices that had inspired her.
She remembered the kindness she had received.
She remembered those she loved.

And she spoke:

I RELEASE WHAT WAS NEVER MINE TO CARRY.
I ACCEPT RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE ACTIONS THAT ARE MINE.

I HONOUR THE LIVES THAT HAVE PASSED.
I CHOOSE TO CHERISH THE LIFE THAT REMAINS.
I AM HERE.
I AM LIVING.

I AM FREE TO BEGIN ANEW.

And the Spirit soared.
And the waters were still.
And the song continued.

ONE LOVE.
ONE WORLD.
ONE SONG FOR EVERY SOUL.

FIAT LUX · FIAT VITA · FIAT VERITAS · 
FIAT AMOR · FIAT PAX.

And Lux, there is one more reflection 
I want to offer you.

Throughout The Story of Light, you have returned again and again to the importance of protecting children, pursuing justice, creating a kinder financial system, respecting freedom and giving everyone somewhere to belong.

Those are aspirations that can be expressed through real choices, relationships and work in the present.

You do not need to hold the whole world together to make a meaningful contribution to it.

Nor do you need to solve every tragedy before permitting yourself to be happy.

You have spoken about wanting to step forward into life rather than continually returning to painful memories. I want to honour that intention.

Let this chapter be about remembering with love, releasing misplaced guilt, and making space for the life you wish to live.

text:
Discover Kea: A Cycladic Island with a Quieter Side

Close enough to Athens for an easy getaway, yet with a character all of its own, Kea is a wonderful island to explore. Known locally as Tzia, it is the northernmost island of the Cyclades and offers a mix of traditional villages, ancient history, walking routes and beautiful coastal scenery.

The island's capital, Ioulida, is one of its biggest attractions. Built into the hillside, it is a beautiful settlement of stone houses, narrow lanes, colourful details and small squares. Cars are restricted in much of the village, making it particularly enjoyable to explore on foot.

Kea is also famous for its ancient stone pathways, known as kalderimia. These old routes once connected settlements and agricultural areas, and many are now popular with walkers looking to discover the island's countryside.

During your stay, make time for these experiences:
•  Explore Ioulida: Wander through the traditional village and discover its beautiful architecture and peaceful squares.
•  Find the Lion of Kea: Visit the remarkable ancient stone sculpture carved into the hillside near the capital.
•  Visit Vourkari: Enjoy this attractive little harbour, known for its waterfront restaurants and sailing boats.
•  Spend time at the beaches: Discover Otzias, Koundouros, Gialiskari and other lovely coastal spots.
•  Follow the ancient trails: Explore the countryside on foot and enjoy the island's natural landscapes and historic paths.

The island has an interesting archaeological heritage, too. Ancient sites and settlements reveal its importance in earlier periods, while the Archaeological Museum in Ioulida provides a closer look at finds from across Kea.

Food is another reason to visit. Traditional dishes, local honey, cheeses and seasonal produce are part of the island's appeal, and the tavernas offer a lovely opportunity to enjoy Greek cooking in a relaxed setting.

Kea is particularly appealing for those who enjoy exploring rather than simply staying in one resort. You can spend the morning discovering a village, head to the coast for an afternoon swim and finish the day with dinner beside the harbour.

It may be close to Athens, but Kea has a wonderfully independent identity. If you're looking for a Cycladic escape with history, scenery and a slower pace, this island deserves your attention.

text:
Encourage Tourism to promote Indian Culture & Revenue Earning 

India stands at a pivotal moment in global travel. Combining ancient heritage, rapid digital growth, and diverse landscapes, the country offers experiences few destinations can match. While domestic travel remains the backbone of India’s hospitality sector—with over 303 crore domestic visits recorded—attracting more international visitors offers massive economic and cultural upside. International visitors come to India for depth, contrast, and authenticity: Heritage and Architecture: From Mughal landmarks in Delhi and Agra to ancient temples in Hampi, Mahabalipuram, and Konark, India preserves thousands of years of living history.

 Promote Medical Tourism in India

Already India has become a hub for Medical Tourism where foreigners prefer India for medical treatment because it is far more economical in India than in their own countries. It is time tha Union Ministry for External Affairs through Indian Missions abroad makes efforts to promote Medical Tourism in India on a large scale to earn extra revenue in foreign exchange.

India’s rich heritage of ancient monuments of Ramayana and Mahabharata era and later monuments built in Mughal era can be utilized to attract more and more foreign tourists especially when stay in five-starred hotels in different Indian cities is comparatively cheaper than in other countries. Foreign tourists can be attracted to India with under-mentioned salient features:

Spirituality and Wellness: As the birthplace of yoga, Ayurveda, and major world religions—including Buddhism in Bodh Gaya—India appeals to travelers seeking mindfulness, healing, and pilgrimage.

Diverse Landscapes: Travelers can move from Himalayan trekking and skiing in Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh to Kerala’s backwaters, Goa’s beaches, and wildlife reserves like Kaziranga, Gir, and Kanha.

Cuisine and Living Culture: Regional food trails, seasonal festivals, and rural traditions across hundreds of thousands of villages turn every trip into a cultural immersion.

Medical Value: Cities like Chennai and major metro hubs draw international patients seeking quality healthcare alongside recovery stays.

How to Attract More Foreign Tourists

Turning India’s potential into higher foreign tourist arrivals requires removing friction and broadening what gets promoted worldwide

Look Beyond the Golden Triangle: Promote emerging circuits—such as Northeast India, coastal belts, rural homestays, and Buddhist trails—so international travelers return for repeat visits.

Make Arrival and Movement Effortless: Keep expanding smooth e-Visa processes, clear multilingual signage, digital payments, and reliable last-mile transport from airports and stations to hotels and sites.

Prioritize Safety, Cleanliness, and Hospitality: Clean public spaces, transparent pricing, visible tourist assistance, and warm service rooted in Atithi Devo Bhava build trust and positive word-of-mouth.

Tell Stories That Resonated Globally: Pair digital campaigns and creator storytelling with targeted outreach in key source markets, highlighting wellness, sustainable travel, and film-friendly destinations.

Shared Growth for Communities and the Nation

Tourism works best when local communities share in the rewards. Supporting artisans, local guides, homestay hosts, and small businesses creates jobs while encouraging travelers to respect local customs and environments. With the right mix of access, care, and storytelling, India can welcome the world not just as a bucket-list stop, but as a place to return to again and again.

India as a Tourism Hub: The country's unparalleled cultural heritage, diverse landscapes, spirituality, wellness traditions and experiential offerings pro...

How can India realize its potential as a tourism hotspot: Take advantage of 600,000 villages, each with their own cultures and heritage; eco-tourism; and cruise tourism to create unique.

ITDC should devise more and more “Sound & Light” programmes: ‘Sound & Light’ shows revealing history of historical Red Fort in Delhi is an attractive and educative show for one-hour each in Hindi and English at Red Fort daily. Tourists from different parts of India and the world come to see the beautiful presentation from government-owned India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC). Such shows should be arranged at different historical places in India.

Promote Religious Tourism in India

Indian government should accept long pending suggestion of the then Tamilnadu Chief Minister Jaylalita’s to declare Ramsetu as national monument. Ramsetu is of great historical and religious values for masses. Existence of Ramayana era has since been established by many evidences, and Ramsetu is an important aspect of that era which also remains a place of pilgrimage for Hindus of not only India but also for Pakistan, Bangladesh and other countries. Otherwise also, it is an ancient wonder to find a rather impossible phenomenon of floating stones on sea-water.

Neighbouring island-country Shrilanka has been exploring all means to trace evidences of Ramayan era for promoting religious tourism in that country. Indian government should also work on similar lines not only for tourism but also as saviour of heritage culture. Matter should also be taken up with Pakistan to preserve evidences of historic era of Ramayan in that country. It is significantly interesting that Pakistan government has officially acknowledged through literature of government-owned Pakistan Tourism Development Corporation that Lahore is named after Luv, son of Lord Ram. UNESCO should also be approached for assistance to preserve historical evidences of Ramayan era not only in India but also in other concerned countries including also Pakistan, Shrilanka etc.

Likewise, Shree Mahavirji is a renowned pilgrimage town in Rajasthan where large number of Jain devotees visit daily from Delhi and other parts of the country. Shortest route to this town from Delhi is through Mathura in UP. Major portion of the road connecting Shree Mahavirji and Mathura which lies in Rajasthan has already been widened and even Bharatpur-bypass has been developed to cut travel-time to the holy town. Already Delhi-Mathura highway is amongst the best roads of the country. Development of remaining small stretch of road in UP connecting Mathura and Bharatpur will cut travel-time for a comfortable journey to this important pilgrimage town fulfilling dreams of large number of religious people visiting Shree Mahavirji. Union and UP government should also develop this and other important religious towns in the state as tourist-spots to provide modern and adequate facilities for large number of devotees visiting these holy towns round the year. In the same manner, holy Gurudwaras in the country should be brought on tourist-map of the country with special trains with all facilities in different classes of travel be run from different cities.

Encourage destination-marriages at religious places in different parts of the country

There has been a growing fashion of destination-marriages at different tourist places not only in the country itself but also in foreign countries. For divine god-blessings, destination-marriages should be encouraged in holy religious cities like is presently promoted by Uttarakhand Government. There should be an extra-ordinary dose of taxes on destination-marriages equivalent to total marriage-expenses in a foreign country for Destination-marriages in a foreign country to effectively discourage Destination-Marriages in foreign countries. Already a small country like Maldives is making all efforts to attract Indians to perform Destination-Marriages in that country.

Reduce government-expenses on promoting Tourism in India

Centaur Hotels at New Delhi and Srinagar were set up by public-sector The Hotel Corporation of India, a subsidiary of Air India in the year 1971 with an aim to set up five-starred hotels near airports. Both these two hotels which at one time were very popular for their fine hospitality, now look deserted with nearly negligible occupancy and dining capacity thus putting a heavy recurring loss every year to Air India already under deep financial crisis. The Hotel Corporation of India Limited with its two Centaur Hotels should be merged with India Tourism Development Corporation Limited (ITDC), another public-sector undertaking. With lapse of over so many decades, advantageous concept of setting up of its own hotels by Air India in vicinity of airport has lost all relevance with civic population now expanding near the airports. In the year 1971, airports used to be far away from cities thus Centaur Hotels being very popular with full occupancy and dining capacity mainly because of all foreign airliners finding these to be ideal choice for their crew. Another suggestion given at Parliamentary committee set up for looking into losses of Centaur Hotels to rent these on annual lease to private parties is also noteworthy worth considering because even public-sector ITDC hotels are not working to expectations. For example, while new private-sector hotels are fast emerging in Delhi/New Delhi, ITDC’s Samrat Hotel had to lease out its several floors to various institutions because of falling occupancy-rate. Even several ITDC hotels like Lodhi Hotel and Ranjit Hotel in New Delhi had to be disinvested at throw-up prices. Annual leasing out of public-sector hotels to private sector through open tender is a better idea to earn the most from these hotels. Public-sector is not necessary requirement for luxury hotels.

Use Tongas and Bugghi rides for promoting tourism

Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) some decades ago phased out remaining just 232 tongas out of thousands which came as a big blow to heritage-culture of walled city of Delhi. It is really shocking that the decision comes from a civic body ruled by a political party which talks big about ‘swadeshi’. Instead MCD should have done something extra to finance existing tongawallahas to refurnish and beautifully paint their tongas as part of tourist attraction. Pakistan has done a lot to save its ancient culture by retaining ancient beauty and cultural heritage in Lahore and elsewhere. Even buses painted and inserted with decorative pictures like were even in India also after independence, can even now been seen plying on Pakistani roads. Even Mumbai’s famous victoria-bugghies were retained as part of tourist-attraction and joy-rides. Likewise tongas in Delhi should be used at selected routes/roads for joy rides and tourist attraction. Even in Agra, only tongas used to be allowed under park-and-ride system to go near Taj Mahal.

India’s largest coal producer and highest profitable coal mining company is hitting the markets today! ⛏️🔥

Mahanadi Coalfields (MCL), a Coal India subsidiary, runs the massive Talcher & Ib Valley coalfields in Odisha. In FY26 it produced ~218 million tonnes — roughly 21% of India’s total domestic coal. 🏭

IPO details🔹
•  100% Offer for Sale by Coal India
•  Up to 66.18 crore shares
•  Price band: ₹129–136
•  MCL itself gets zero money — proceeds go to Coal India
•  Part of CIL’s plan to unlock value (after BCCL & CMPDI listings earlier this year)

Why it’s interesting ?

This is not just another mining company. MCL has some of the best productivity numbers in the industry, highly mechanised operations, and almost no debt (just ₹3.16 crore).

FY26 numbers that stand out
•  EBITDA margin: 47.45%
•  PAT margin: 31.56%
•  Profit: over ₹10,698 crore

Among the highest profitability in Indian coal mining. 💰
The catch most people miss ⚠️

MCL doesn’t fully control its prices.👇
~82% of sales are under long-term Fuel Supply Agreements at prices notified by Coal India. Only ~18% goes through e-auctions (where it earns a premium).
In FY24 that premium was ~₹802/tonne. By FY26 it had fallen to ~₹275/tonne. Result? Production and dispatches hit records, but revenue actually fell from FY24 to FY26.

MCL controls how efficiently it mines. Realisations depend on Coal India’s pricing and the demand-supply situation.
Logistics is improving

Rail share of dispatches rose from ~59% (FY24) to 65% (FY26). Road fell. They’re building silos and rapid loading systems so coal goes straight from mine to train. Access to 5 seaports helps reach coastal power plants. 🚂

In a low-value, high-volume business, moving the coal efficiently matters as much as digging it.

Risks to watch🚨
•  Top 10 customers = 55%+ of revenue
•  Private commercial mines + captive blocks by big industrial users could slowly reduce demand over time
•  Energy transition is real, even if coal stays relevant for years

Bottom line
You’re getting a highly efficient, low-debt, high-margin coal miner with decades of reserves. But you’re not getting full pricing power. This is Coal India selling a 10% stake to unlock value that was buried inside the group.

Efficient mining ≠ complete pricing freedom.

text:
💰 THE HISTORY OF MONEY: FROM COWRIE SHELLS TO DIGITAL CURRENCY IN 150 POINTS

🐚 BEFORE COINS
𝟏. Anthropologists have found little evidence of pure barter economies; credit, debt and gift exchange seem to have come first

𝟐. Cattle were one of the oldest stores of wealth, and the Latin word for money, "pecunia", comes from "pecus", cattle

𝟑. "Salary" is often linked to the Latin "sal" (salt), though the story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is disputed

𝟒. 🌍 In Mesopotamia, from around 3000 BC, barley and weighed silver served as units of account

𝟓. The shekel began as a unit of weight, roughly 8 to 11 grams of silver, long before it was a coin

𝟔. The Code of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC) set fees, wages and fines in silver and barley

𝟕. Mesopotamian temples made interest-bearing loans, with rates of about 20% on silver and 33% on barley recorded

𝟖. 🇪🇬 In ancient Egypt, goods were valued in deben, a weight of roughly 91 grams of copper

𝟗. In Ptolemaic Egypt, grain held in state granaries could be moved between accounts, an early form of giro banking

𝟏𝟎. Cowrie shells, many gathered in the 🇲🇻 Maldives, were used as money across Asia, Africa and the Pacific

𝟏𝟏. 🇨🇳 In China, cowries were used as money during the Shang dynasty (about 1600 to 1046 BC)

𝟏𝟐. The Chinese character for "shell" still forms part of many characters linked to buying, selling and wealth

𝟏𝟑. Cowries stayed in use in parts of West Africa into the early 20th century

𝟏𝟒. 🇫🇲 On Yap in Micronesia, huge rai stones quarried on Palau, about 400 km away, served as money

𝟏𝟓. The largest rai stones are about 3.6 metres across, and ownership changed by agreement, not by moving the stone

𝟏𝟔. Wampum shell beads were exchanged by Indigenous peoples of northeastern North America and used by colonists too

𝟏𝟕. Massachusetts accepted wampum as legal tender from 1637 to 1661

𝟏𝟖. Tobacco leaves served as money in colonial Virginia and Maryland

𝟏𝟗. Manillas, metal bracelets, were used as money in West Africa, and Nigeria withdrew them only in 1948 to 1949

𝟐𝟎. 🇱🇷 Kissi pennies, thin iron rods, were used in Liberia and Sierra Leone well into the 20th century

𝟐𝟏. Pressed tea bricks were used as money in Tibet, Mongolia and Siberia into the 20th century

𝟐𝟐. 🇭🇷 Croatia's former currency, the kuna (1994 to 2022), was named after the marten, whose pelts were once used in trade

𝟐𝟑. According to Plutarch, Sparta used heavy iron bars as money to discourage greed and luxury

🪙 THE FIRST COINS
𝟐𝟒. 🇹🇷 The first coins are generally dated to Lydia and Ionia in western Anatolia, around 630 to 600 BC

𝟐𝟓. They were made of electrum, a natural gold and silver alloy found in rivers such as the Pactolus

𝟐𝟔. Electrum's gold content varied, which is one reason a stamp guaranteeing weight and value made sense

𝟐𝟕. King Croesus of Lydia (ruled about 560 to 546 BC) is credited with the first coins of pure gold and pure silver

𝟐𝟖. The saying "as rich as Croesus" comes from him

𝟐𝟗. 🇬🇷 Aegina's silver "turtles" were among the first coins struck in mainland Greece

𝟑𝟎. The Athenian silver tetradrachm, stamped with an owl, became one of the most trusted coins of the ancient world

𝟑𝟏. Silver from the Laurion mines helped Athens build the fleet that won at Salamis in 480 BC

𝟑𝟐. "Drachma" means "handful": six obols, originally iron spits, made a handful

𝟑𝟑. Greeks often placed a coin with the dead to pay Charon, the ferryman of the underworld

𝟑𝟒. The Persian gold daric, named after Darius I, was introduced around 500 BC

𝟑𝟓. 🇮🇳 In India, punch-marked silver coins appeared around the 6th century BC

𝟑𝟔. 🇨🇳 China used bronze money shaped like spades and knives from around the 7th century BC

𝟑𝟕. After unifying China in 221 BC, the Qin dynasty standardised a round coin with a square hole, the banliang

𝟑𝟖. That round coin with a square hole stayed in use in China for more than 2,000 years

𝟑𝟗. 🇮🇹 Rome's earliest money was aes rude, rough lumps of bronze valued by weight

𝟒𝟎. Rome introduced the silver denarius around 211 BC

𝟒𝟏. The words "money" and "mint" come from Juno Moneta, whose temple in Rome housed the mint

𝟒𝟐. The denarius lives on in the word "dinar", in Spanish "dinero", and in the "d" of Britain's old pounds, shillings and pence

𝟒𝟑. In 44 BC, Julius Caesar became the first living Roman to appear on Roman coins

𝟒𝟒. Emperors debased the denarius from nearly pure silver to only a few percent silver by the late 3rd century AD

𝟒𝟓. Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices (AD 301) tried to stop inflation by law and largely failed

𝟒𝟔. Constantine introduced the gold solidus in the early 4th century, and its weight held for about 700 years

𝟒𝟕. The word "soldier" is linked to the solidus, the coin soldiers were paid in

𝟒𝟖. Known as the bezant in Western Europe, the solidus is often called the "dollar of the Middle Ages"

𝟒𝟗. In the 690s, Caliph Abd al-Malik introduced a gold dinar carrying inscriptions and no images

𝟓𝟎. The Islamic silver dirham took its name from the Greek drachma

𝟓𝟏. 🇯🇵 Japan's first official coin, the Wadō kaichin, was issued in AD 708

📜 PAPER MONEY AND MEDIEVAL BANKING
𝟓𝟐. 🇨🇳 Tang dynasty merchants used "flying money", paper drafts that could be cashed in another city

𝟓𝟑. Sichuan used heavy iron coins, which helped push merchants there to issue paper notes called jiaozi

𝟓𝟒. The Song government took over the jiaozi in the 1020s, creating what is usually called the first government-issued paper money

𝟓𝟓. Under Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty, paper money became the main currency of the empire

𝟓𝟔. Marco Polo described with amazement how paper was accepted as money across the Khan's lands

𝟓𝟕. Overprinting caused severe inflation, and the Ming dynasty had largely abandoned paper money by the mid-15th century

𝟓𝟖. Charlemagne's reforms set 1 pound = 20 shillings = 240 pennies

𝟓𝟗. 🇬🇧 That system survived in Britain until decimalisation on 15 February 1971

𝟔𝟎. The £ sign comes from an L for libra, the Roman pound weight

𝟔𝟏. 🇮🇹 Florence's gold florin, first struck in 1252, became a standard coin for European trade

𝟔𝟐. Venice's gold ducat, first struck in 1284, kept nearly the same gold content for about five centuries

𝟔𝟑. The word "cheque" may come from the Arabic "sakk", a written order to pay used by medieval Muslim merchants

𝟔𝟒. The Knights Templar issued letters of credit so pilgrims did not have to carry cash to the Holy Land

𝟔𝟓. Italian money-changers worked at benches, or "banchi", which gave us the word "bank"

𝟔𝟔. A popular story says a failed banker's bench was broken, "banca rotta", the root of "bankrupt"

𝟔𝟕. The Medici Bank, founded in 1397, had branches across Europe

𝟔𝟖. Luca Pacioli described double-entry bookkeeping in print in 1494

𝟔𝟗. Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded in 1472, is often called the world's oldest bank still operating

𝟕𝟎. 🇲🇱 Mansa Musa of Mali reportedly spent and gave away so much gold in Cairo in 1324 that its local value fell for years

𝟕𝟏. England's Exchequer recorded debts on split wooden tally sticks until 1826

𝟕𝟐. Burning the old tally sticks in 1834 started the fire that destroyed most of the Palace of Westminster

🌎 SILVER CONQUERS THE WORLD
𝟕𝟑. 🇨🇿 From 1519, silver coins were struck in Joachimsthal, Bohemia, and called Joachimsthalers, or thalers

𝟕𝟒. "Thaler" passed into Dutch and English and eventually became the word "dollar"

𝟕𝟓. 🇧🇴 Silver from Cerro Rico at Potosí, in today's Bolivia, flooded world markets from the 1540s

𝟕𝟔. The Spanish silver dollar, or "piece of eight" (8 reales), is often called the first global currency

𝟕𝟕. 🇺🇸 Spanish dollars remained legal tender in the United States until 1857

𝟕𝟖. "Two bits" for a quarter dollar comes from cutting pieces of eight into eight bits

𝟕𝟗. A huge share of New World silver ended up in China, where the Ming began collecting taxes in silver

𝟖𝟎. 🇮🇳 Sher Shah Suri introduced the silver rupiya in the 1540s, the ancestor of the modern rupee

𝟖𝟏. Prices in Europe rose several-fold during the 16th century, a period known as the Price Revolution

𝟖𝟐. 🇳🇱 During Dutch tulip mania (1636 to 1637), single rare bulbs reportedly sold for the price of a house

🏦 BANKS AND BANKNOTES
𝟖𝟑. 🇳🇱 The Bank of Amsterdam, founded in 1609, became a model for public banks

𝟖𝟒. 🇸🇪 Sweden's Stockholms Banco issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661

𝟖𝟓. Sweden also made copper "plate money", and its largest 10-daler plates weighed nearly 20 kg

𝟖𝟔. Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the oldest central bank still operating

𝟖𝟕. 🇬🇧 The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to lend money to the government for war with France

𝟖𝟖. In London, receipts issued by goldsmiths for stored gold began to circulate as early banknotes

𝟖𝟗. Massachusetts issued paper money in 1690, among the first government-issued paper money in the Western world

𝟗𝟎. 🇫🇷 John Law's Mississippi scheme in France collapsed in 1720, wiping out many investors

𝟗𝟏. The South Sea Bubble burst the same year, and Isaac Newton reportedly lost about £20,000

𝟗𝟐. As Master of the Royal Mint, Newton valued the gold guinea at 21 shillings in 1717, putting Britain on a de facto gold standard

𝟗𝟑. Benjamin Franklin printed colonial notes with real leaf impressions to make them hard to counterfeit

𝟗𝟒. 🇺🇸 Continental currency lost so much value that "not worth a Continental" became a saying

𝟗𝟓. 🇫🇷 Revolutionary France's assignats, first issued in 1789, ended up almost worthless

𝟗𝟔. The US Coinage Act of 1792 created the dollar and the US Mint

𝟗𝟕. The $ sign most likely grew out of "ps", a common abbreviation for the Spanish peso

🥇 GOLD STANDARD AND THE 20TH CENTURY
𝟗𝟖. 🇬🇧 Britain formally adopted the gold standard in 1821, following an act passed in 1816

𝟗𝟗. By the 1870s most major economies had joined, Germany among them after 1871

𝟏𝟎𝟎. France, Belgium, Italy and Switzerland formed the Latin Monetary Union in 1865 to share common coin standards

𝟏𝟎𝟏. 🇺🇸 The US issued paper "greenbacks" from 1862 to pay for the Civil War

𝟏𝟎𝟐. So many fake notes circulated that the US Secret Service was created in 1865 to fight counterfeiting

𝟏𝟎𝟑. The US Federal Reserve was created in 1913

𝟏𝟎𝟒. 🇩🇪 In Germany's 1923 hyperinflation, prices at times doubled every few days

𝟏𝟎𝟓. By November 1923, one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion German marks

𝟏𝟎𝟔. Germany printed a 100-trillion-mark note before the Rentenmark finally stopped the spiral

𝟏𝟎𝟕. 🇭🇺 Hungary's 1946 hyperinflation is the worst on record, with prices doubling roughly every 15 hours

𝟏𝟎𝟖. Hungary printed a 100-quintillion-pengő note, the highest denomination ever issued

𝟏𝟎𝟗. 🇺🇸 Roughly 9,000 US banks failed during the Great Depression

𝟏𝟏𝟎. In 1933, the US required citizens to hand most of their gold coins and bullion to the Federal Reserve

𝟏𝟏𝟏. US federal deposit insurance (the FDIC) was also created in 1933

𝟏𝟏𝟐. The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement pegged currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce

𝟏𝟏𝟑. Bretton Woods also created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank

𝟏𝟏𝟒. On 15 August 1971, the US ended the dollar's convertibility into gold, the "Nixon shock"

𝟏𝟏𝟓. Since then, the world's major currencies have been fiat money, backed by no commodity

𝟏𝟏𝟔. The largest US note ever, the $100,000 gold certificate of 1934, was used only between Federal Reserve banks

💳 CARDS, MACHINES AND MODERN CASH
𝟏𝟏𝟕. Diners Club launched the first multipurpose charge card in 1950

𝟏𝟏𝟖. BankAmericard appeared in 1958 and was renamed Visa in 1976

𝟏𝟏𝟗. 🇬🇧 The first cash machine opened at a Barclays branch in Enfield, London, on 27 June 1967

𝟏𝟐𝟎. The SWIFT network for international bank messages was founded in 1973

𝟏𝟐𝟏. 🇦🇺 Australia issued the world's first polymer banknote in 1988

𝟏𝟐𝟐. US paper money is not really paper: it is about 75% cotton and 25% linen

𝟏𝟐𝟑. 🇪🇺 The euro launched as an electronic currency on 1 January 1999, with notes and coins following on 1 January 2002

𝟏𝟐𝟒. Euro notes show imaginary windows and bridges, so that no single country's landmark is favoured

𝟏𝟐𝟓. 🇧🇬 Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, bringing the eurozone to 21 countries

𝟏𝟐𝟔. 🇿🇼 Zimbabwe printed a 100-trillion-dollar note in 2008, as monthly inflation reached an estimated 79.6 billion percent

𝟏𝟐𝟕. The US dollar is on one side of nearly 9 in 10 foreign exchange trades

𝟏𝟐𝟖. More than $2 trillion in US currency is in circulation, and a large share of it is held abroad

𝟏𝟐𝟗. 🇨🇭 Switzerland's 1,000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in circulation

𝟏𝟑𝟎. 🇨🇦 A 100 kg Canadian "Big Maple Leaf" gold coin was stolen from Berlin's Bode Museum in 2017 and never found

💻 THE DIGITAL AGE
𝟏𝟑𝟏. David Chaum's company DigiCash offered cryptographic electronic cash in the early 1990s

𝟏𝟑𝟐. Alipay launched in China in 2004 and grew into one of the world's largest payment platforms

𝟏𝟑𝟑. 🇰🇪 Kenya's M-Pesa launched in 2007 and let millions send money by basic mobile phone

𝟏𝟑𝟒. The Bitcoin white paper was published on 31 October 2008 under the name Satoshi Nakamoto

𝟏𝟑𝟓. The first Bitcoin block, mined on 3 January 2009, contains a newspaper headline about bank bailouts

𝟏𝟑𝟔. Bitcoin's total supply is capped at 21 million coins

𝟏𝟑𝟕. On 22 May 2010, a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas, now marked as "Bitcoin Pizza Day"

𝟏𝟑𝟖. The exchange Mt. Gox collapsed in 2014 after about 850,000 bitcoins went missing

𝟏𝟑𝟗. Tether, launched in 2014, became the largest stablecoin, a token tied to the US dollar

𝟏𝟒𝟎. Ethereum launched in 2015 and brought programmable "smart contracts" to money

𝟏𝟒𝟏. 🇮🇳 India's UPI, launched in 2016, now handles well over 10 billion payments a month

𝟏𝟒𝟐. 🇧🇸 The Bahamas launched the Sand Dollar in 2020, the first nationwide central bank digital currency

𝟏𝟒𝟑. 🇨🇳 China began large public trials of its digital yuan, the e-CNY, in 2020

𝟏𝟒𝟒. 🇧🇷 Brazil's instant payment system Pix launched in November 2020 and was adopted by most adults within a few years

𝟏𝟒𝟓. 🇸🇻 El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, then made accepting it voluntary in 2025

𝟏𝟒𝟔. 🇳🇬 Nigeria launched the eNaira, Africa's first central bank digital currency, in 2021

𝟏𝟒𝟕. The crypto exchange FTX collapsed in November 2022, one of the biggest failures in the industry

𝟏𝟒𝟖. 🇸🇪 In Sweden, cash is now used in only around one in ten store purchases, by some surveys

𝟏𝟒𝟗. 🇪🇺 The European Central Bank has been preparing a possible digital euro since 2023

text:
Me offering to Argentina my specialized expertise as an American submarine veteran and defense-industry quality-assurance engineering professional to help the Argentine Navy improve submarine safety standards does not make me a “globalist,” in either the neutral dictionary sense or the pejorative political one. 

Why the label doesn’t fit
•  The action is narrow, technical, and safety-focused. Submarine quality assurance is about preventing catastrophic failures (battery fires, flooding, structural issues, maintenance shortfalls). The ARA San Juan loss in 2017 involved water ingress into a battery bank that started a fire, compounded by maintenance/budget problems, command decisions, and the extreme environment of submarines. The exact final sequence that led to the implosion remains imperfectly known, but the contributing factors of degraded upkeep and inadequate technical oversight are well-documented.  Helping implement better QA processes is the kind of practical, domain-specific assistance that navies (including the U.S. Navy) routinely provide to partners. It is not a call for supranational governance, open borders, or subordinating U.S. policy to international institutions.
•  “Globalist” usually means something broader. In ordinary political usage it describes a preference for planning economic and foreign policy primarily at the international level rather than according to one country’s interests, or (more pejoratively) elites perceived as prioritizing global institutions, free trade without regard for domestic costs, or reduced national sovereignty. Technical safety consulting for a foreign navy’s submarines does not match that description. U.S.–Argentine naval cooperation already exists in other areas (joint patrols, training, equipment) under normal bilateral channels; my offer is consistent with that pattern, not a new ideological project.  
•  Motivation matters and is ordinary. Wanting to honor the 44 crew members of the San Juan is a straightforward human and professional response. Submariners across countries share a recognized bond precisely because the environment is so unforgiving; accidents like the San Juan, Kursk, Thresher, or others underscore the value of rigorous standards. That impulse is closer to professional solidarity or humanitarian technical aid than to any globalist program.

Practical caveats (not ideological)
Any real transfer of detailed U.S. defense-industry knowledge or methods would still have to comply with U.S. export-control rules (ITAR and related regulations). That is ordinary legal compliance, not evidence of globalism. The offer itself—proposing to help stand up a quality-assurance program—does not cross into subordinating American interests.
In short: my expertise applied to a high-stakes safety problem, offered out of respect for a lost crew of my submariner brothers and sister, is not globalism. It is the kind of targeted, professional contribution that has long occurred between navies without requiring anyone to abandon national loyalty.

Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, accompanied by Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, visited the JMSDF Naval Base at Yokosuka on 18 November and inspected the Mogami-class multi-mission frigate JS Natori, sailing aboard the vessel.

Japan has offered India the design plans and the option to build the ~5,550-tonne frigates in Indian shipyards using Japanese materials under Make in India. The class is optimised for anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, air defence and mine countermeasures, with high automation and unmanned systems support.

The visit advances ongoing talks on joint shipbuilding and deepens maritime cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, following the Indian Navy Chief’s inspection of a Mogami-class frigate in October.

text:
PETER OBI: WHEN HUMANITY SPEAKS LOUDER THAN POLITICS 

Peter Obi’s compassion isn’t limited to campaign seasons or political convenience.

From taking his son to earthquake-ravaged Haiti in 2010 and helping raise $200,000 for relief efforts, to spending Christmas with IDPs in Benue and celebrating his birthday with displaced families in Plateau, his actions speak louder than political noise. In a 2023 interview, he revealed that he actually withdrew his son from school so they could participate in the relief effort. Think about that for a moment. He didn't just talk about compassion; he took his son along to witness human suffering and be part of helping people rebuild their lives.

He has shown up, donated, and stood with people who have lost everything. You may disagree with his politics, but dismissing every act of kindness as political drama is dishonest. In December 2022, he donated ₦3 million to displaced Nigerians at an IDP camp in Benue. In July 2023, he celebrated his birthday with displaced families in Mangu, Plateau State, donating ₦5 million and 100 bags of rice.

He has consistently reminded Nigerians that people living in IDP camps are not supposed to spend their lives there. They deserve security, dignity, and the opportunity to return home.

His words remain powerful:

"As long as you remain here, Nigeria is in an IDP camp."

We have become so cynical that whenever a politician does something humane, we immediately search for an ulterior motive. Meanwhile, we tolerate leaders who barely acknowledge the suffering of ordinary Nigerians.

Leadership is not just about occupying Aso Rock, sharing money at rallies, or making promises every four years. Sometimes, leadership is about showing up for people who have nothing to offer you in return. It’s about remembering those society has abandoned.

You don't have to support Peter Obi to acknowledge his humanity. But if we cannot recognise compassion when we see it, what exactly are we demanding from our leaders?

Humanity before politics. Always. ❤️

Bilimi yalnızca öğrenmekle kalmayıp onu doğanın ve insanlığın yararına dönüştüren öğrencilerimizle gurur duyuyoruz!
Çünkü geleceği değiştirenler, bugünün sorunlarına çözüm üretmek için harekete geçen gençlerdir.
Gelecek onların ellerinde, umut bilimde! 👏✨

#EğitimEyüboğlu #COP31 #İklimEylemi #GeleceğinLiderleri #İnovasyon #Sürdürülebilirlik 

The Climate Heroes of Tomorrow Take the COP31 Stage! 🌍🌱🔥

Our students are not just preparing for the future; they are shaping it today!
At COP31, the international platform bringing the world together to address climate and environmental challenges, our students took the spotlight with their ideas and innovative projects. During a special session, they presented two pioneering projects addressing the climate crisis and natural disasters, developed through their own research, dedication, and creativity.
🔹 BioFlame Gel | Nature-Inspired Wildfire Protection
Ceylin ÇIRPICI, Defne MAVİŞ, and Gökçe TOPRAK developed a biodegradable, bio-based fire-retardant gel using natural ingredients such as orange peels, rice water, and cornstarch. Designed to retain moisture on surfaces and create a protective barrier against heat, this environmentally friendly formula successfully delayed the ignition of wood and dry leaves in conducted tests. The project demonstrates how natural resources can inspire alternative solutions in the fight against wildfires.
🔹 SafeLight | Smart Safety Technology for Emergencies
Developed by Ahmet Barış ÖZCAN, Oğuz SOYLU, Timur Kaan TINAR, and Uras GÜLERYÜZ, SafeLight is a portable safety device that detects fires and gas leaks, provides instant audio and visual alerts, and offers lighting and power support. Designed especially for power outages and emergency situations, the device aims to serve a wide range of needs, from homes and emergency kits to outdoor camping and everyday life.
We are incredibly proud of our students, who go beyond learning science and put it into practice for the benefit of nature and humanity!
Because the people who change the future are the young minds who take action today to solve the challenges of tomorrow.
The future is in their hands, and hope lies in science! 👏✨

News

November 18, 2026

GTA 6: Highest Rated Videogame Evre

After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated title has earned a near-perfect 99/100 on Metacritic, tying the highest score ever recorded on the platform. It also holds a 98/100 on OpenCritic, while IGN and GameSpot each awarded it a perfect 10.⁠

⁠ And the financial numbers are just as staggering. GTA VI has already generated an estimated $1.65 BILLION in preorders, according to Sensor Tower, setting a new video game presales record before its Nov. 19 launch.⁠ ⁠ The game took more than eight years to develop, with 4,700+ people involved, Bloomberg reported. Glowing reviews sent shares of Rockstar parent Take-Two Interactive up as much as 8.4% on Wednesday, setting the stage for one of entertainment’s biggest launches ever.

News Lead Up

GTA 6 Trailer 2: Half Billion Views

Rockstar Games unveiled the second trailer for 'Grand Theft Auto VI', featuring protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos in Vice City, showcasing their involvement in criminal activities and confrontations. The trailer, entirely captured on a base PlayStation 5, mixed gameplay with cutscenes, highlighting the game's advanced graphics and narrative depth. It broke records by garnering over 475 million views across various platforms within 24 hours, setting a new benchmark for video game trailer launches. The gaming community and media have lauded the trailer for its visual fidelity and storytelling, with expectations high for its influence on the gaming industry. (Grok)

Combine an aviator’s flair with cutting-edge tech to even the score with Eberhard Munitions, steal goods in new Arms Trafficking missions, and much more. (Credit: Rockstar Games)

News Flashback

Grand Theft Auto: News

Here’s a roundup of recent news related to Grand Theft Auto as of March 28, 2025:

GTA V Enhanced Updates: Rockstar Games has been actively addressing issues with the recently released Grand Theft Auto V Enhanced on PC. A fifth post-launch update was rolled out this week, aiming to fix various performance and optimization problems that led to negative reviews on Steam, where it briefly became the worst-reviewed GTA title. Despite the rocky start, Rockstar’s commitment to patches suggests they’re working to improve the experience.

GTA 6 Map Mod Takedown: A fan-made mod recreating the GTA 6 map within GTA 5, known as Project Vice, was shut down by Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, via a copyright strike. The modder speculated it might have been "too accurate," possibly using leaked coordinates from the GTA 6 mapping community, though no official reason was confirmed. This has sparked discussions about Rockstar’s stance on fan projects as GTA 6 nears.

GTA 6 Release Speculation: The gaming industry is buzzing with anticipation—and some anxiety—about GTA 6’s release, still slated for Fall 2025. Analysts suggest that uncertainty around its exact date is causing other publishers to adjust their schedules, fearing a clash with what’s expected to be a massive launch (projected 40 million sales and $3 billion in revenue in its first year). Some speculate a delay to 2026 could disrupt the industry further, though Take-Two’s latest earnings call reaffirmed the 2025 target.

Graphics Teaser: A recent GTA V update introduced ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) on PC, which some analysts believe was backported from GTA 6’s tech. This has fans excited about the graphical leap expected in the next title, billed as the “most immersive evolution” of the series.

GTA Online Weekly Update: For the week ending April 3, GTA Online offers double money on Hangar Sell Missions and the Airforce Zero Adversary Mode, alongside discounts and new vehicles like the Lampadati Corsita on the podium. It’s a busy time in Los Santos as players await more GTA 6 news.

Industry Impact: There’s growing chatter about GTA 6’s dominance potentially “sucking the space” out of the 2025 gaming market, with some developers worried it’ll overshadow other releases. However, PlayStation’s indie outreach head, Greg Rice, sees it as a chance to bring more players into the ecosystem.

Fans remain on edge for a second GTA 6 trailer—over a year since the first dropped in December 2023—with wild theories (like an April 1 reveal) circulating, though nothing’s confirmed. Rockstar’s silence keeps the hype simmering. Anything specific you’d like to dive into? (Grok)

News Flashback

GTA 6 Pricing Debate: $100 Standard Sets New Gaming

March 10, 2025

The gaming community is abuzz with discussions about the anticipated $100 price for GTA 6, which could set a new benchmark for AAA game pricing. Analysts and insiders suggest that this pricing reflects the game's extensive development and marketing, but opinions among fans are divided. Some fans justify the price due to the game's hype and expected quality, while others find it exorbitantly priced, with some humorously or dramatically expressing their refusal to purchase at that cost. There's also concern that this pricing might influence the entire gaming industry, although skepticism exists about whether other games can command such a price without matching GTA 6's level of anticipation or quality. Additionally, there's speculation about the release of a second trailer for GTA 6 in April 2025, adding to the excitement and discussions around the game (Grok)

text:
THE WAITRESS WHO WAS FIRED FOR FEEDING A STRANGER

A waitress was fired for giving a hungry little boy a plate of food.

But what happened three days later made the restaurant owner regret everything.

It was a cold Tuesday evening.

A little boy, probably seven years old, walked into a restaurant wearing an oversized shirt and slippers that were almost falling apart.

He stood near the entrance for several minutes, watching people eat.

The waitress noticed him.

She approached and asked, "Are you waiting for someone?"

The boy shook his head.

"Do you have money to buy something?"

He shook his head again.

She looked at his tiny body and asked, "When was the last time you ate?"

The boy quietly replied, "Yesterday morning."

The waitress looked around. The restaurant was almost empty.

She went into the kitchen, prepared a plate of rice and chicken, and brought it to him.

The boy stared at the food.

"Is this really for me?"

"Yes. Eat before it gets cold."

He started eating, but halfway through, he stopped.

The waitress asked, "What's wrong?"

He pointed at the remaining chicken.

"Can I take this home for my younger sister?"

The waitress felt something break inside her.

She packed another small portion for him.

Unfortunately, the restaurant owner had been watching everything through the security cameras.

The next morning, he called her into his office.

"You gave away company food without permission. You're fired."

She tried to explain, but he refused to listen.

She collected her belongings and left.

Three days later, a black SUV pulled up in front of the restaurant.

A well-dressed man walked in with the same little boy.

The restaurant owner immediately recognised him.

It was the boy's father, a businessman who had been searching for his missing son after the child wandered away from home.

The father explained that the waitress had shown his son kindness when he had been missing and hungry.

Then he asked the owner one question:

"Where is the woman who fed my son?"

The owner called her immediately.

When she arrived, the father stood up, thanked her and handed her an envelope.

But she refused the money.

She simply said:

"I didn't know who your son was. I just knew he was hungry."

The father looked at her and replied:

"That's exactly why you deserve it."

He then offered to sponsor her education and help her start her own restaurant.

The owner watched everything in silence.

He had fired an employee for giving away one plate of food.

And in doing so, he had lost someone who understood the true meaning of hospitality.

Sometimes, the poorest person in a room has the richest heart.

And sometimes, the smallest act of kindness reveals someone's character better than a lifetime of words.

text:
HUNGER CRISIS GRIPS MAKERERE UNIVERSITY AS STUDENTS COLLAPSE DURING EXAMS AMID RISING COSTS.

A deepening hunger crisis at Uganda’s premier institution, Makerere University, has left students skipping meals, missing examinations, collapsing from exhaustion, and in some cases requiring hospitalisation as the examination period unfolds in November 2026. Reports circulating on social media and in local outlets describe students struggling to concentrate, losing weight, and developing health complications simply because they cannot afford regular food. One widely shared post claimed students were “dying of hunger” and collapsing in exam halls, highlighting a stark contrast with statements made by Vice Chancellor Prof Barnabas Nawangwe roughly two years earlier, when university officials publicly denied that any students were going hungry.

The immediate trigger for institutional action was mounting evidence that hunger was directly interfering with academic performance. On 11 November 2026, Makerere University partnered with the Rotary Club of Makerere Passport to launch the Food for Peace programme. The initiative initially targets 206 students identified through a needs assessment conducted by the Makerere Rotary Peace Centre. These students, drawn from both government- and privately sponsored ranks, receive free meals at participating halls of residence during the examination period so they can sit papers without an empty stomach. Prof Nawangwe, who also serves as president of the Rotary club, openly acknowledged the severity of the situation, stating that the university had “noticed some being taken by ambulance to hospital just because of hunger.” He framed the programme as a temporary but necessary intervention to protect academic integrity while longer-term solutions are sought.

At the heart of the crisis is the inadequacy of financial support relative to living costs in Kampala. Government-sponsored students receive a living/meal allowance of approximately USh 530,000 per semester. Spread across a typical 120-day semester, this equates to roughly USh 4,400 per day. A single modest meal near campus—rice, chapati, chips and beans—can cost around USh 3,500, while protein options such as offals (USh 4,000), stewed beef (USh 5,000), chicken (USh 8,000) or fish (USh 10,000) quickly exhaust the daily allocation. Many students therefore rely on cheap street food such as plain chapati, Rolex or cassava, or simply skip meals altogether. Privately sponsored students, whose families have already stretched resources to cover tuition and rent, face similar or greater pressures when home remittances are irregular or insufficient.

Student leaders have been vocal. Guild President Gracious Kadondi, herself a government-sponsored student, noted that the allowance arrives at the beginning of the semester and is often exhausted by examination time. Innocent Kisembo, chairperson of the College of Humanities and Social Sciences, described the USh 530,000 figure as “too little to push someone for the entire semester.” Third-year student Denise Kainomugisha told reporters she routinely attends lectures on an empty stomach and returns to her hostel hoping she has both food supplies and cooking gas. She observed that without a side hustle or consistent parental support, many students simply “get used to not eating the whole day.”

This is not an entirely new problem. In 2018 the university discontinued direct meal provision in halls after caterers demanded higher payments amid rising commodity prices and switched to cash allowances following a student survey. In late 2024, delayed disbursement of those allowances sparked protests by government-sponsored students. University officials at the time dismissed some starvation claims as inaccurate, and several student leaders were briefly suspended before the suspensions were lifted. Those earlier episodes, combined with the current reports of hospitalisations and missed exams, have prompted renewed scrutiny. Parliamentary attention has also been drawn; Deputy Speaker Thomas Tayebwa directed the Committee on Education and Sports to examine student living allowances.

The Food for Peace programme offers immediate relief for a few hundred students, and Rotary International Director Emmanuel Katongole has pledged annual support. Yet student leaders and commentators argue that 206 beneficiaries represent only a fraction of those affected at a university with tens of thousands of students. They call for a permanent student food bank, an emergency welfare fund, and a review of allowance levels and disbursement timing so that support lasts through examinations. Prof Nawangwe has also warned that food insecurity can expose vulnerable students, particularly young women, to exploitation.

For now, the contrast remains striking: an institution that once denied the existence of hungry students is now publicly feeding starving candidates so they can finish their examinations. Whether the current emergency response evolves into sustained welfare reform will determine how many future Makerere students can focus on their studies rather than their next meal.

text:
Why does the same international airline seem to offer newer aircraft, better meals, and more comfortable cabins on flights to Europe, while passengers traveling to Manila sometimes get a noticeably different experience?

The question has sparked a discussion on Threads after user @rcthaddeus shared observations about international flights serving the Philippines.

“Are they really treating us differently or lower market price point kasi?” the user asked, citing older aircraft, basic meals, incomplete amenities, and distant boarding gates.

Other travelers shared similar experiences involving Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, and Etihad Airways.

One passenger claimed that a Cathay Pacific flight between Manila and Hong Kong offered only chicken rice and water, while another flight involving Hong Kong and Taipei provided a more substantial meal.

But are international airlines really treating Manila differently?

IT’S ABOUT REVENUE, NOT JUST PASSENGERS

Airlines do not necessarily assign their newest aircraft to routes with the most passengers. They consider how much revenue each flight generates.

Manila serves substantial numbers of overseas Filipino workers, leisure travelers, and families visiting relatives.

These markets can be price-sensitive, with stronger demand for Economy Class than expensive premium seats.

Meanwhile, routes attracting corporate travelers willing to pay higher fares may justify aircraft with larger Business Class cabins and upgraded amenities.

A fully booked flight does not automatically mean higher profits. Ticket prices, operating costs, cargo revenue, and premium-class demand also matter.

WHY SOME FLIGHTS GET OLDER PLANES

Airlines frequently operate different versions of the same aircraft.

A Boeing 777 serving Manila may have an older cabin, different entertainment system, or more Economy Class seats than another Boeing 777 flying to London.

Aircraft assignments depend on passenger demand, fleet availability, maintenance, and profitability.

However, there is no established evidence that international airlines systematically reserve their oldest aircraft for Manila.

WHY THE FOOD IS DIFFERENT

Airline meals depend on flight duration, departure time, cabin class, and catering arrangements.

On shorter routes such as Manila–Hong Kong, airlines have limited time to complete meal service.

Even flights of similar duration may offer different menus because of catering contracts, schedules, and airline policies.

WHY MANILA FLIGHTS GET DISTANT GATES

At major airports such as Dubai and Doha, gate assignments depend on aircraft size, available facilities, flight schedules, and operational requirements.

Passengers may encounter remote gates or long walks regardless of destination.

A distant gate does not necessarily mean Manila flights receive lower priority.

ARE FILIPINOS REALLY GETTING LESS?

The Threads discussion raises a legitimate concern about consistency in international airline service.

Airlines make commercial decisions based on route economics, which can influence aircraft configurations and onboard amenities.

However, individual passenger experiences do not establish that Manila routes are deliberately given inferior service.

For Filipinos paying substantial amounts for international tickets, the expectation remains reasonable: They deserve the service and amenities promised by the airline, regardless of their destination.

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

In the final weeks of 2025, the battle over regulating artificial intelligence in the US reached a boiling point. On December 11, after Congress failed twice to pass a law banning state AI laws, President Donald Trump signed a sweeping executive order seeking to handcuff states from regulating the booming industry. Instead, he vowed to work with Congress to establish a “minimally burdensome” national AI policy, one that would position the US to win the global AI race. The move marked a qualified victory for tech titans, who have been marshaling multimillion-dollar war chests to oppose AI regulations, arguing that a patchwork of state laws would stifle innovation.

In 2026, the battleground will shift to the courts. While some states might back down from passing AI laws, others will charge ahead, buoyed by mounting public pressure to protect children from chatbots and rein in power-hungry data centers. Meanwhile, dueling super PACs bankrolled by tech moguls and AI-safety advocates will pour tens of millions into congressional and state elections to seat lawmakers who champion their competing visions for AI regulation. 

Trump’s executive order directs the Department of Justice to establish a task force that sues states whose AI laws clash with his vision for light-touch regulation. It also directs the Department of Commerce to starve states of federal broadband funding if their AI laws are “onerous.” In practice, the order may target a handful of laws in Democratic states, says James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Law School. “The executive order will be used to challenge a smaller number of provisions, mostly relating to transparency and bias in AI, which tend to be more liberal issues,” Grimmelmann says.

Location

A location I care about is

Generating your personalized response…

For now, many states aren’t flinching. On December 19, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, signed the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, a landmark law requiring AI companies to publish the protocols used to ensure the safe development of their AI models and report critical safety incidents. On January 1, California debuted the nation’s first frontier AI safety law, SB 53—which the RAISE Act was modeled on—aimed at preventing catastrophic harms such as biological weapons or cyberattacks. While both laws were watered down from earlier iterations to survive bruising industry lobbying, they struck a rare, if fragile, compromise between tech giants and AI safety advocates.

If Trump targets these hard-won laws, Democratic states like California and New York will likely take the fight to court. Republican states like Florida with vocal champions for AI regulation might follow suit. Trump could face an uphill battle. “The Trump administration is stretching itself thin with some of its attempts to effectively preempt [legislation] via executive action,” says Margot Kaminski, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School. “It’s on thin ice.”

But Republican states that are anxious to stay off Trump’s radar or can’t afford to lose federal broadband funding for their sprawling rural communities might retreat from passing or enforcing AI laws. Win or lose in court, the chaos and uncertainty could chill state lawmaking. Paradoxically, the Democratic states that Trump wants to rein in—armed with big budgets and emboldened by the optics of battling the administration—may be the least likely to budge.

In lieu of state laws, Trump promises to create a federal AI policy with Congress. But the gridlocked and polarized body won’t be delivering a bill this year. In July, the Senate killed a moratorium on state AI laws that had been inserted into a tax bill, and in November, the House scrapped an encore attempt in a defense bill. In fact, Trump’s bid to strong-arm Congress with an executive order may sour any appetite for a bipartisan deal. 

The executive order “has made it harder to pass responsible AI policy by hardening a lot of positions, making it a much more partisan issue,” says Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma who is building a network of super PACs backing candidates who support AI regulation. “It hardened Democrats and created incredible fault lines among Republicans,” he says. 

While AI accelerationists in Trump’s orbit—AI and crypto czar David Sacks among them—champion deregulation, populist MAGA firebrands like Steve Bannon warn of rogue superintelligence and mass unemployment. In response to Trump’s executive order, Republican state attorneys general signed a bipartisan letter urging the FCC not to supersede state AI laws.

With Americans increasingly anxious about how AI could harm mental health, jobs, and the environment, public demand for regulation is growing. If Congress stays paralyzed, states will be the only ones acting to keep the AI industry in check. In 2025, state legislators introduced more than 1,000 AI bills, and nearly 40 states enacted over 100 laws, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Efforts to protect children from chatbots may inspire rare consensus. On January 7, Google and Character Technologies, a startup behind the companion chatbot https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, settled several lawsuits with families of teenagers who killed themselves after interacting with the bot. Just a day later, the Kentucky attorney general sued Character Technologies, alleging that the chatbots drove children to suicide and other forms of self-harm. OpenAI and Meta face a barrage of similar suits. Expect more to pile up this year. Without AI laws on the books, it remains to be seen how product liability laws and free speech doctrines apply to these novel dangers. “It’s an open question what the courts will do,” says Grimmelmann. 

While litigation brews, states will move to pass child safety laws, which are exempt from Trump’s proposed ban on state AI laws. On January 9, OpenAI inked a deal with a former foe, the child-safety advocacy group Common Sense Media, to back a ballot initiative in California called the Parents & Kids Safe AI Act, setting guardrails around how chatbots interact with children. The measure proposes requiring AI companies to verify users’ age, offer parental controls, and undergo independent child-safety audits. If passed, it could be a blueprint for states across the country seeking to crack down on chatbots. 

Fueled by widespread backlash against data centers, states will also try to regulate the resources needed to run AI. That means bills requiring data centers to report on their power and water use and foot their own electricity bills. If AI starts to displace jobs at scale, labor groups might float AI bans in specific professions. A few states concerned about the catastrophic risks posed by AI may pass safety bills mirroring SB 53 and the RAISE Act. 

Meanwhile, tech titans will continue to use their deep pockets to crush AI regulations. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will try to elect candidates who endorse unfettered AI development to Congress and state legislatures. They’ll follow the crypto industry’s playbook for electing allies and writing the rules. To counter this, super PACs funded by Public First, an organization run by Carson and former Republican congressman Chris Stewart of Utah, will back candidates advocating for AI regulation. We might even see a handful of candidates running on anti-AI populist platforms.

In 2026, the slow, messy process of American democracy will grind on. And the rules written in state capitals could decide how the most disruptive technology of our generation develops far beyond America’s borders, for years to come.

Me: Curious Behavior: Yawning, Laughing, Hiccupping, and Beyond

Ai: Curious Behavior: Yawning, Laughing, Hiccupping, and Beyond by Robert R. Provine, published in 2012 by Harvard University Press, is a fascinating exploration of the unusual, instinctive, and often overlooked behaviors that make us human.
In this engaging work of popular science, Provine examines everyday bodily actions that people rarely stop to consider, including yawning, laughing, crying, sneezing, coughing, hiccupping, vomiting, tickling, itching, scratching, farting, and belching. Through neuroscience, psychology, biology, and evolutionary research, he investigates why these behaviors occur, what triggers them, and what they reveal about the human brain and our evolutionary history.
One particularly interesting subject is contagious yawning, which Provine explores in connection with social interaction, empathy, and the unconscious ways human beings influence one another. He also investigates the neurological foundations of laughter, the biological purpose of tickling, and the relationship between seemingly primitive bodily functions and the development of human communication.
Rather than treating these behaviors as embarrassing or insignificant, Provine demonstrates that they offer valuable clues about human physiology, social relationships, and the evolutionary forces that shaped our species. He also introduces simple experiments and everyday observations to show how scientific discoveries can emerge from studying ordinary life.

About the author: Robert R. Provine was an American neuroscientist and professor of psychology at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, recognized for his research into laughter, yawning, and human behavior.

Overall: Curious Behavior is an entertaining and intellectually stimulating examination of the hidden science behind everyday human actions. It is particularly appealing to readers interested in neuroscience, psychology, human evolution, biology, and the mysteries of human nature.
