text:
Request about the Rebuilding of the Elephantine Temple   (407 BCE) 

To our lord Bagavahya governor of Judah, your servants Jedaniah and his colleagues the priests who are in Elephantine the fortress.

May the God of Heaven seek after the welfare of our lord abundantly at all times, and may He grant you favor before Darius the king and the princes a thousand times more than now, and may He give you long life, and may you be happy and strong at all times.

Now, your servant Jedaniah and his colleagues say thus:

In the month of Tammuz, year fourteen of Darius the king, when Arsames had departed and gone to the king, the priests of Khnub the god who are in Elephantine the fortress, in agreement with Vidranga who was Governor here, said:

“Let them remove the Temple of YHW the God which is in Elephantine the fortress from there.”

Afterwards, that Vidranga, the wicked, sent a letter to Nafaina his son, who was Troop Commander in Syene the fortress, saying:

“Let them demolish the Temple which is in Elephantine the fortress.”

Afterwards, Nafaina led the Egyptians with the other troops. They came to the fortress of Elephantine with their implements, broke into that Temple, demolished it to the ground, and they smashed the stone pillars which were there. Moreover, they demolished the five gateways built of hewn stone, which were in that Temple.

And their standing doors, and the bronze pivots of those doors, and the cedar roof—all of these which, with the rest of the fittings (?) and other things, which were there—all of these they burned with fire. But the gold and silver basins and the other things which were in that Temple—they took all of these for themselves.

Now our fathers had built that Temple in Elephantine the fortress in the days of the kings of Egypt, and when Cambyses entered Egypt he found that Temple built. They overthrew all the temples of the gods of Egypt, but did not damage anything in that Temple.

And when this had been done to us, we, with our wives and our children, were wearing sackcloth and fasting and praying to YHW, the Lord of Heaven, who let us gloat over that Vidranga, the cur. They removed the fetter from his feet, and all goods which he had acquired were lost. And all people who sought evil for that Temple were killed, and we gazed upon them.

Moreover, before this, at the time that this evil was done to us, we sent a letter to our lord, and to Jehohanan the High Priest and his colleagues, the priests who are in Jerusalem, and to Ostanes the brother of Anani and the Jewish nobles. They did not send us a letter in reply.

Moreover, from the month of Tammuz, year 14 of Darius the king, until this day, we are wearing sackcloth and are fasting; our wives are like widows; we do not anoint ourselves with oil, and do not drink wine.

Moreover, from that time until this day, year 17 of Darius the king, meal-offering and incense and burnt-offering have not been made in that Temple.

Now, your servants Jedaniah and his colleagues and the Jews, all of them citizens of Elephantine, say thus:

If it pleases our lord, give thought to rebuilding that temple since they do not let us rebuild it. Take note of your obligees and your friends who are here in Egypt. Let a letter be sent from you to them to rebuild the Temple of YHW the God in Elephantine the fortress just as it had been built formerly.

And the meal-offering and the incense and the burnt-offering will be offered on the altar of YHW the God in your name and we shall pray for you at all times—we and our wives and our children and all the Jews who are here. If you do thus until that Temple be rebuilt, you will have more merit before YHW the God of Heaven than a person who will offer him burnt-offering and sacrifices worth a thousand talents of silver, and gold.

We have sent and informed you about this.

Moreover, we sent all these things in a letter in our name to Delaiah and Shelemiah sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria.

Moreover, Arsames did not know anything about all that was done to us.

On the 20th of Marheshvan, year 17 of Darius the king.

Jesus is our only hope - the only one who can save us and the world Jesus' entrance into Jerusalem was a gracious visitation of God's anointed Son and King to his holy city. Jerusalem's lack of faith and rejection of the Messiah, however, leads to its eventual downfall and destruction by the Romans in 70 A.D. Jesus' lamentation and prophecy echoes the lamentation of Jeremiah who prophesied the first destruction of Jerusalem and its temple. Jeremiah's prayer of lamentation offered a prophetic word of hope, deliverance, and restoration: 
"But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, his mercies are new every morning ...For the Lord will not cast off for ever, but, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love for he does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men" (Lamentations 3:21-22, 31-32). 
Jesus is the hope of the world because he is the only one who can truly reconcile us with God and with one another. Through his death and resurrection Jesus breaks down the walls of hostility and division by reconciling us with God. He gives us his Holy Spirit both to purify us and restore us as a holy people of God. Through Jesus Christ we become living temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). God has visited his people in the past and he continues to visit us through the gift and working of his Holy Spirit. Do you recognize God's gracious visitation of healing and restoration today?

text:
Let's talk facts, not abuse.

1) "Calling it Arunachalam"
Arunachalam is not a Telugu invention. It is in Tamil itself.

The Tevaram (7th-8th century) by Appar and Sambandar calls this hill Annamalai / Arunachalam — centuries before any modern state existed.
The Skanda Purana's Arunachala Mahatmyam and Arunagirinathar's Tiruppugazh also use Arunachala.
Thiruvannamalai = Thiru + Annamalai. Arunachalam is the same name in Sanskrit form. Both are Tamil heritage.

2) "Laddus as Prasadham"
Laddu is not a Telugu import. Laddu / Laddoo is mentioned in ancient Indian texts as Modaka, offered to Ganesha.
Tamil temples have offered laddu, pongal, vadai, payasam for centuries. Tirupati made it famous, but it didn't invent it. Prasadam is devotion, not a state copyright.

3) "Offering hair to God"
Tonsure / Mottai is one of the oldest Tamil traditions.
Palani, Tiruchendur, Tiruttani, Thiruvannamalai itself — devotees have offered hair for over 1,000 years as a symbol of surrendering ego — Ahamkara.
It is mentioned in Sangam literature and temple inscriptions, not brought by anyone from outside.

Thiruvannamalai belongs to no one community. Ramana Maharshi, a Tamil, made Arunachala world-famous. Devotees from Andhra, Karnataka, Kerala, North India come because the hill calls everyone.

Calling devotion a "scam" because other languages also love the same God — that is not protecting Tamil culture. That is insulting it.

text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        November 19, 1792

Revolutionary France declared war on every throne in Europe at once. It named no enemy and no border. It simply offered its help to any people, anywhere, that would rise against its king. No monarchy could hear it as anything but a threat to its very existence.

On November 19, 1792, the French National Convention decreed that France would grant fraternity and assistance to all peoples who wished to recover their liberty, and it ordered its generals to carry that help wherever it was called for. It was one of the most incendiary documents of the age, a promise of revolution for export.

A second decree on December 15 set out what liberation would mean in practice. In every land the French armies entered, the old authorities would be swept away, feudal dues abolished, and the property of the revolution's enemies seized to pay for the war. Reporting it, the deputy Cambon summed up its spirit in a phrase that became the watchword of the revolutionary armies, peace to the cottages and war on the palaces. Savoy, Nice, the left bank of the Rhine and part of Belgium were voted into France, commune by commune, beneath the banner of a war of liberation that disowned conquest even as it annexed.

Behind the crusade lay rival dreams. The foreign radicals who had flocked to Paris, exiles from Holland, Belgium and the Rhineland, men like Anacharsis Cloots, preached a single universal republic, the whole world made free in one stroke, an idea reaching back to Rousseau's design for a perpetual peace. The Girondins and Danton wanted something more solid, France enlarged to what they called its natural frontiers, the Rhine, the Alps and the Pyrenees. To the kings of Europe the two dreams sounded alike, and both sounded like the end of them.

For all their daring, the Girondins knew the conquests were fragile, and they staked their hopes less on French strength than on revolution erupting everywhere and on dividing their enemies by cunning. Their foreign minister, Lebrun, and the general Dumouriez spun a web of schemes. They would buy Prussia's neutrality with a slice of Austrian land. They would ring the frontier from the North Sea to Italy with friendly sister republics. They would set Sweden and Turkey loose on Russia to tie Catherine's hands, rouse the parliamentary opposition against Pitt in London, and tempt Britain with a trade treaty and the island of Tobago. It was statecraft built on wishful thinking, and it misjudged the depth of the quarrel with Britain, which dreaded a revolutionary France astride Belgium and Holland more than anything on earth. After the king was guillotined in January 1793, every scheme to split the coalition collapsed at once. Monarchical Europe was closing ranks.

For Britain the breaking point was the Low Countries. When the French overran Belgium and reopened the river Scheldt in defiance of old treaties, then turned toward Holland, London saw its chief rival about to seize the far shore of the Channel and set the Continent ablaze with revolution. After Louis XVI went to the scaffold, Britain expelled the French envoy. The Convention did not wait to be told its meaning. On February 1, 1793, on the report of Brissot, it declared war on Britain and the Dutch Republic. William Pitt, with no great army of his own, fell back on the oldest English method, paying others to do the fighting. He bound Prussia, Austria, Sardinia, Naples and Spain to the cause with subsidies and sealed an agreement with Russia. England's gold and England's fleet became the deadliest enemies the Revolution would face.

By March 1793 almost all of Europe stood arrayed against France in what became the First Coalition. The decree of November 19 had promised to free the peoples of Europe. Instead it had united their rulers in a war that would devour the Continent for a generation. And things grew worse before they grew better. That same March the Austrians shattered the French at Neerwinden and poured back into Belgium. The general who had saved France the autumn before, Dumouriez, went over to the enemy. The Prussians crossed to the left bank of the Rhine, foreign armies stood once more on French soil, and in the west the peasants of the Vendée rose in revolt. By summer the Republic was fighting for its life.

Now the grand promise of November was quietly buried. On April 13, 1793, the same Convention decreed that France would not interfere in the government of other powers, a flat renunciation of the armed crusade it had proclaimed just five months before. The conduct of foreign affairs now passed to Georges Danton, who still believed the Republic could be saved by negotiation. He set out to break the coalition by the Girondins' own method, luring one enemy away with the promise of another's lands.

It came to nothing. The Committee handed Danton six million livres for secret expenses, and he scattered agents across Europe, some of them little better than adventurers, to pry the powers apart. The one genuine negotiation, with Sweden, had its treaty all but drafted when France's defeats in the field led the Swedish regent to hold back his signature. No monarch would treat with a revolution that seemed to be dying, and none would recognise a republic they still meant to strangle. The Girondins fell in the rising of early June, yet Danton stayed on and kept trying until July, when the Convention dropped him from the Committee. His successors drew the opposite lesson. France would be saved not by its diplomats but by a nation thrown whole into the war, and within a year the armies the envoys could not help had hurled the coalition back across every border.

It's mind-boggling to see how many young Americans, particularly those ages 18–24, reportedly view Sharia law favorably over the American constitutional system. It makes me question what they're actually being taught.

The education system has changed dramatically since those of us now in our 40s and older went through school. Phonics and phonemic awareness were pushed aside in many schools - now kids can't read, historical education has increasingly become politicized, and difficult parts of world history are often softened, omitted, or presented primarily through the lens of how they might make students feel rather than the historical facts themselves.

How many of today's graduates actually understand the history of Islamic expansion, the centuries of Muslim rule in Spain, the Islamic slave trade, or the historical conflicts between Islamic and Christian civilizations? How many understand the distinction between religious law and a constitutional government? You cannot make informed decisions about systems of government when you haven't been taught their histories, principles, and consequences.

We've also moved increasingly toward teaching subjective interpretations of history rather than establishing the facts and allowing students to critically evaluate them. There's a difference between acknowledging historical injustices and rewriting history through a modern political lens. There's also a difference between understanding another culture and romanticizing a system of government without understanding what it entails.

And let's be clear: Sharia is not simply another version of American law. A system governed by traditional interpretations of Sharia does not operate on the same principles of individual liberty, religious freedom, equality under the law, and constitutional protections that Americans enjoy. Supporting something without understanding its implications isn't informed tolerance.

I also think we've lost sight of what made America fundamentally different. Over the last century, lawmakers have increasingly expanded government authority, regulation, and bureaucracy. The country that once offered extraordinary opportunities for individuals to acquire land, build, work, and pursue their own version of the American dream has gradually become a place where people feel increasingly governed, restricted, and dependent on government rather than empowered by their own freedoms.

The Constitution was designed to limit government power and protect individual liberty, not give government unlimited authority over our lives.

Meanwhile, our media increasingly influences which historical facts and perspectives are considered acceptable to discuss. Criticism of religious or political ideologies is too often conflated with hatred toward the people who practice them. Understanding history requires being willing to examine ALL of it, including the uncomfortable parts.

We were raised with "sticks and stones may break my bones, but words will never hurt me." Yet somehow, in 2026, we've reached a point where words are increasingly being labeled as violence, while actual physical violence is sometimes excused or justified because someone claims to have been offended by what another person said. That's completely backwards. Being offended does not give anyone the right to assault, threaten, or physically harm another person. Freedom of speech means being able to express yourself, challenge authority, criticize your government, and disagree with others, even when your words are unpopular or uncomfortable. You cannot have a free society that increasingly polices speech while simultaneously making excuses for people who commit actual violence. That's the very opposite of the individual liberties and protections a constitutional republic was designed to preserve.

You cannot protect the next generation's freedoms by keeping them uninformed about the very things those freedoms protect them from.

text:
I think we're mixing several distinct questions: how our cognitive faculties evolved, whether those faculties can reliably discover truth, and whether logical or moral truths depend on evolution.

First, I'm not arguing that evolution guarantees accurate reasoning. I'm arguing that we have positive reasons to trust our cognitive abilities, while recognizing their limitations.

Natural selection doesn't need to favor truth as an end in itself for accurate perceptions and useful reasoning to provide survival advantages. An animal that learns to navigate hazards, recognize threats, or cooperate with others benefits from understanding important aspects of its environment.

Humans have expanded those abilities through observation, trial and error, teaching, experimentation, and accumulated knowledge. We went from spears and bows to aircraft and rockets. Our ancestors didn't evolve specifically to understand quantum mechanics, but they developed capacities we eventually applied to problems far beyond their original environments.

And that knowledge isn't just useful because we believe it works. We can repeatedly test predictions against reality, identify errors, and improve our models. That provides evidence of reliability in those domains, not a guarantee of universal correctness.

Second, Hoffman's Fitness-Beats-Truth Theorem concerns evolutionary models of perception and fitness payoffs. It challenges the assumption that natural selection necessarily favors accurate representations of reality. It doesn't, by itself, demonstrate that human reasoning, mathematics, or moral reflection are generally unreliable.

Third, the laws of logic don't have to originate through evolution for evolved minds to recognize and apply them. You're conflating the origins of our reasoning abilities with the existence of the truths we investigate.

Morality raises additional philosophical questions, but we have evidence that social cooperation, caregiving, and mutual support existed long before Abrahamic religions. Neanderthals apparently cared for injured members of their communities. Humans can learn that cooperation benefits social groups, develop ethical expectations, and challenge those expectations when they produce harm.

That doesn't automatically establish objective moral truths, but neither does asserting that God intended our minds to recognize them.

And this brings me back to the distinction I've been making throughout our conversation.

I accept that naturalistic evolution and theistic evolution have different philosophical foundations. But saying God designed our minds for truth doesn't establish that every interpretation of God's intentions is correct or that our faculties are reliable in every domain.

Your position offers a possible explanation for why cognition might be trustworthy. It doesn't automatically demonstrate that trustworthiness.

Likewise, evolution explaining the origins of our cognitive abilities doesn't establish that those abilities are incapable of discovering truths beyond their original survival functions.

So the question remains: what establishes that naturalistic evolution gives us a defeater for trusting cognition, rather than producing imperfect faculties whose reliability can be evaluated through evidence, experience, and correction?

And if divine intention is your alternative explanation, how do you independently establish that your understanding of that intention is correct?

I'm not asking either worldview to guarantee infallibility. I'm asking that both be held to a consistent standard of justification.

text:
The Chronology of the Trojan War and The Odyssey in Cinema 

1. Helen of Troy (1956)
This film tells the story of how the Trojan War began, when Paris takes Helen from Sparta to Troy, triggering a massive conflict between the Greeks and the Trojans.

2. The Fury of Achilles (1962)
The story focuses on Achilles during the Trojan War, including his conflict with Agamemnon and his legendary duel with Hector. Chronologically, the events take place during the middle of the war and overlap with those depicted in *Helen of Troy*.

3. The Trojan Horse (1961)
This film explores the final stages of the Trojan War, particularly the legendary Trojan Horse strategy devised by Odysseus to conquer Troy and bring the war to an end.

4. Troy (2004)
A modern retelling that brings together much of the Trojan War's story, from Helen's abduction to the fall of Troy. Given its broad narrative scope, the film incorporates elements covered in the three movies mentioned above.

5. Ulysses (1954)
A classic adaptation of Homer's epic poem *The Odyssey*, following Odysseus on his ten-year journey home to Ithaca after the Trojan War.

6. The Return (2024)
This film focuses on the final part of *The Odyssey*, when Odysseus finally returns to Ithaca and must confront the suitors who have taken over his palace and are plotting to claim his throne.

7. The Odyssey (2026)
Directed by Christopher Nolan, this latest adaptation revisits Odysseus's epic journey on a much grander scale. It is also one of the most ambitious cinematic adaptations of Homer's legendary epic poem.

From the fall of Troy to Odysseus's long journey home, these films offer different perspectives on one of the greatest stories in ancient Greek mythology.

Which adaptation is your favorite, and which one are you planning to watch first?

text:
Grand Theft Auto VI: Baudelaire with wheels, by @stevenpoole

In GTA VI the player’s tough-guy character is not some psychopathic incel: he has a girlfriend with whom he pursues his criminal recreations. The developers have hinted this Bonnie-and-Clyde team might want to try to murder their way out of a life of murder and, I don’t know, retire to raise chickens on a ranch. But before that becomes possible, as far as we can tell from pre-release footage, there are still a lot of helicopters that will need blowing up with RPGs, a lot of cars that need stealing and a lot of nightclubs that need to be danced in.

This drama of relentless acquisition plays out in the big city (here, Miami and its environs), which for pastoral literature is always the source of corruption, the place where innocence is lost. But the attraction of GTA has always been that it restores a kind of childlike anarchy to the metropolis, recreating it as a playground in which cars can fly off cliffs and you can lead a merry conga line of pursuing cop cars while driving a tank. The tension between this fundamental silliness and the self-consciously “adult” dialogue and graphic violence means that GTA has always had a conspicuously teenaged gestalt. Like the Zelda series with its mini-games (a bowling alley that uses cute cartoony bombs is another favourite), GTA also offers endless timewasting opportunities. If you wish to progress through the structured narrative, you have to accept “missions” involving telegenic violence. But you can also play in the spirit of Herman Melville’s short story “Bartleby, the Scrivener”, preferring to refuse orders, buy cigarettes and beer and just wander around soaking up the sights.

Both, indeed, are games of virtual tourism: GTA VI presents gorgeous sunsets over the Pacific Ocean just as Ocarina of Time revels in the spectacular beauty of its meadows, clouds, lakes and mountains. And even the ultraviolent GTA can be played against the grain, serenely, as a digital dérive. Granted, the restricted types of interaction that are offered (mainly driving, shooting, punching) do tend to steer the player towards a species of psychotic flâneurie, like Baudelaire with wheels and an AR-15. But at least this time GTA VI, like Ocarina of Time, also has a fishing game as one of its side attractions. Maybe nature is finally healing.

🇮🇷|TEHRAN’S SECURITY CHIEF MOURNS A MARJA WHO STOOD ON THE FRONT LINES: REZAEI’S CONDOLENCE EXPOSES THE WESTERN LIE THAT RELIGION AND RESISTANCE ARE SEPARATE

Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, has offered his condolences on the passing of Grand Ayatollah Hossein Vahid Khorasani. The message is not a routine obituary. It is a political and spiritual statement that directly challenges the Western narrative which tries to confine Shia religious authority to quietist ritual and separate it from the struggle against oppression.

Rezaei emphasized that the reassuring presence of this esteemed Marja on the front lines of the struggle between truth and falsehood, along with his profound and enlightening remarks addressed to the fighters for the cause of Islam, served as a testament to his deep understanding of the vital importance of the presence of such combatants in the arena of defending the very essence of Islam.

This is the key sentence. It defines the Marja not as a secluded scholar issuing abstract rulings, but as a guide who understood that the defense of Islam requires bodies on the front lines and that the scholars must stand with them. The Western media will ignore this dimension because it contradicts the convenient fiction that Shia clerics are either apolitical quietists or Iranian state functionaries. Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani was neither. He was a Marja whose authority was rooted in scholarship and piety, and whose vision extended to the battlefield where truth confronts falsehood.

The condolence message itself is addressed to a wide circle of authority and devotion. Rezaei extends condolences to the Remnant of God, Imam al-Hujjah ibn al-Hasan, may God hasten his noble reappearance, to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, to the other Grand Ayatollahs, to the Islamic seminaries, to his students and followers, and in particular to his noble family, his esteemed sons, his relatives, and especially to Ayatollah Amoli Larijani.

The structure of the message matters. It begins with the Hidden Imam and moves through the Leader of the Islamic Revolution to the seminaries and the family. This is not a list of formalities. It is a map of legitimate authority in the Shia world. The Marja is not appointed by a state. He is recognized by the faithful, by the seminaries, and by his peers. Rezaei, as the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, is placing the security apparatus of the Islamic Republic in the service of that authority, not above it. He is mourning a Marja whose independence from state structures was precisely what gave his words weight on the front lines.

The Western narrative tries to present Iran as a country where religion is a tool of the state. The condolence message refutes this by showing that the state’s security chief is the one bowing to the Marja, not the other way around. Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani’s authority came from his scholarship, his piety, and his connection to the faithful. His presence on the front lines was not a state assignment. It was a decision made by a man who understood that the defense of Islam is not a metaphor.

The message also specifically mentions Ayatollah Amoli Larijani, a detail that the mainstream will overlook. This is a signal of continuity within the religious and political leadership of Iran. The Marja’s family and close associates are part of the fabric of the Islamic Republic, not separate from it. The condolence is addressed to them personally because the loss is personal, but it is also institutional. A node of knowledge and guidance has been closed, and the entire structure of Shia authority feels the break.

Rezaei’s message is therefore not just a tribute. It is a declaration that the front lines of truth and falsehood are real, that the Marja understood this, and that the security apparatus of Iran is committed to the same struggle. The Western media will not report this because it cannot fit the Marja into its framework. It cannot explain why a 105-year-old scholar would concern himself with fighters on the front lines. It cannot explain why the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council would mourn him as a comrade in arms rather than a ceremonial figure.

The answer is that Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani was not a ceremonial figure. He was a Marja who understood that Islam is defended not only in seminaries but on the ground, and that the scholars who remain silent while the faithful are attacked have abandoned their duty. His presence on the front lines was a living refutation of the quietist narrative that the West prefers. Rezaei’s condolence is a reaffirmation that the Islamic Republic and the Marja’iyya share the same understanding of what is at stake.

The loss is heavy. The message is clear. The struggle continues. And the Western narrative that tries to separate religion from resistance is exposed, once again, as a lie.

text:
Strings Attached: U.S. Arms Export Controls, Alternative Suppliers, and the Question of Indirect Responsibility

When the United States sells arms abroad, it does not simply ship weapons and walk away. U.S. law and the contracts underpinning those sales impose binding conditions: recipients must not retransfer the equipment to third parties without Washington’s written consent, and they must not use it for purposes other than those for which it was furnished without prior authorization. The Pentagon and State Department operate end-use monitoring programs—Golden Sentry for government-to-government sales and Blue Lantern for direct commercial sales—to check compliance, and violations can trigger reporting to Congress and suspension of future sales. The financial stakes are enormous: the U.S. defense industry benefits from tens of billions of dollars in foreign military sales annually, supporting hundreds of thousands of American jobs. But the United States is not the only arms exporter, and its restrictions are not unique in kind—only in scale and legal formality. Two further questions follow: Do other suppliers impose comparable restrictions? And if Washington profits from weapons that are later used in atrocities, does it bear indirect responsibility for war crimes? This report examines both.

Other Major Arms Suppliers and Their Restriction Regimes

France requires recipients to sign a final-use certificate and a non-retransfer undertaking. French law mandates that the importer and end-user commit not to transfer the equipment to any third party, in any form, without the prior agreement of the French government. The French exporting company must have the signatures authenticated by a French embassy or diplomatic mission and must retain copies of the non-retransfer clauses for ten years. French export licences also carry conditions on final use and re-export outside the European Union. France therefore operates a consent-based system for retransfer and end-use that is structurally similar to the U.S. model, though its post-shipment monitoring is generally less publicly documented than the American Golden Sentry and Blue Lantern programs.

The United Kingdom’s export licensing regime is explicitly risk-based and human-rights-sensitive. Under the Arms Trade Treaty and UK regulations, export licences should be denied where there is a clear risk that the arms might be used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian law or human rights law. The UK has suspended licences where items covered might be used in ways inconsistent with international humanitarian law. However, independent reviews have argued that the UK’s end-use monitoring remains a weak link and that parliamentary scrutiny should be strengthened. The UK therefore imposes meaningful pre-export restrictions but has been criticized for weaker post-shipment verification than the U.S. system claims to provide.

Germany has developed a formal post-shipment control system. Since 2015, Berlin has required end-use certificates in which the recipient state grants Germany the right to conduct on-the-spot checks. The purpose is to verify that weapons supplied are still present in the recipient country and in the possession of the declared end-user; random checks are used for large quantities. If non-compliance is found or inspections are refused, consequences follow under Germany’s political principles on arms exports. Germany has conducted a limited number of on-site inspections, and the system covers war weapons and specific firearms destined for state recipients. The German regime is narrower in scope than the U.S. system but explicitly includes physical verification abroad.

Russia’s arms export contracts require foreign customers to use the equipment only for the purposes declared in the end-user certificate and not to re-export or transfer it to third countries without Russia’s consent. A 2006 government resolution established a formal post-shipment verification mechanism: the exporter must follow up to confirm that the items were received and used as intended, and violators can be placed on a watch list of unreliable foreign recipients subject to restrictions or bans. Russia does not, however, publish detailed monitoring data, and it is not a party to the Arms Trade Treaty. The system is real on paper but far less transparent than the American or German frameworks.

China requires recipient governments to commit not to transfer Chinese-origin arms to any third party without prior consent of the Chinese government, and it operates a licensing system with end-user and end-use certification. China’s stated principles are that arms exports should enhance the recipient’s self-defense capacity, should not harm regional or international peace and security, and should not interfere in the recipient’s domestic affairs. However, analysts have noted that China’s regulations do not comprehensively address end-use monitoring, that enforcement capacity is underdeveloped, and that investigations often rely reactively on intelligence from the U.S. or Europe. The Chinese regime therefore contains formal non-retransfer conditions but lacks the institutionalized post-shipment verification architecture found in the U.S. or Germany.

Israel’s Defense Export Control Law of 2007 establishes a licensing system administered by the Defense Export Controls Agency within the Ministry of Defense. All defense exports require licences, and the system includes end-user and end-use verification, post-shipment verification in some cases, record-keeping for at least ten years, periodic reporting, and compliance audits. Exporters must provide certifications verifying the end-use and end-user to prevent diversion. Israel’s system is formal and legally codified, though its application to exports to entities whose conduct is contested is itself a matter of international controversy.

South Korea requires buyers to provide end-user certification legally prohibiting re-export or transfer to third parties without the prior written consent of the South Korean government. Exporters must verify the identities of purchasers, ultimate consignees, and end-users, as well as the intended end-use, before applying for an export permit. South Korea has been urged to strengthen post-export monitoring and to use a denial list for high-risk entities. Its regime is therefore consent-based on retransfer but still developing in post-shipment oversight.

In comparative terms, most major suppliers impose retransfer and end-use conditions, and several—especially Germany, the United States, and Israel—have formal post-shipment verification mechanisms. The United States is distinctive in the scale, legal codification, and congressional oversight of its system, but it is not alone in attaching strings. France, the UK, Germany, Russia, China, Israel, and South Korea all impose, in varying degrees, retransfer restrictions and end-use conditions, and several operate post-shipment verification mechanisms. What distinguishes the U.S. system is its scale, legal formalization, and congressional oversight—not the mere fact that conditions exist.

Why Countries Buy from the United States Despite the Strings

If U.S. arms come with conditions and monitoring, why do so many governments still buy them? The reasons are strategic, institutional, and financial. Defense procurement is rarely a purely commercial decision. Armament purchases are often used to reinforce a strategic or security partnership. Buying American equipment signals alignment with Washington and can be a way to secure or deepen U.S. security commitments. Analysts note that for many buyers of systems like the F-35, the purchase is understood as buying not only an aircraft but also a U.S. security guarantee. In this sense, the restrictions are part of the package: the buyer accepts conditionality because the relationship with Washington is the point.

Militaries also want to operate alongside allies. If a country’s partners already use U.S. systems, buying the same equipment creates interoperability—shared communications, logistics, tactics, and supply chains. This creates a network effect: the more militaries procure a system, the stronger the incentive for others to follow. The U.S. actively leverages this dynamic, and its reluctance to share source code and intellectual property can make integration of non-U.S. systems harder, reinforcing the pull toward American platforms.

The U.S. government’s Foreign Military Sales system offers a one-stop shop: training, maintenance, logistical support, and government-backed financing can be bundled with the equipment. Foreign Military Sales can reduce procurement timelines and administrative burdens, and it allows buyers to derogate from EU procurement rules where applicable. Foreign Military Financing provides loans or grants that make U.S. equipment more affordable for allies. For a government facing urgent security needs, the Foreign Military Sales package can be more attractive than piecing together a deal with a European or Asian supplier.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, short-term availability became a decisive factor. The United States had larger production capacity, maintained stocks, and could deliver or promise equipment at greater speed than many European suppliers after decades of downsizing. Past acquisitions also shape future ones: militaries want to replenish existing systems, buy upgraded versions of equipment they already know, and avoid the cost of retraining and rebuilding logistics for a new supplier. In some segments—such as certain drones, tactical ballistic missiles, and long-range artillery rockets—there may be no comparable non-U.S. option available on the market due to decades of underinvestment by other suppliers. Where alternatives exist, U.S. systems may offer similar performance at a competitive cost when only the purchase price is considered, because American producers benefit from economies of scale. The restrictions, in other words, are not necessarily a deal-breaker. They are one attribute of a package that also includes strategic alignment, interoperability, financing, availability, and often unrivaled capability.

Does the United States Bear Indirect Responsibility for War Crimes?

This is the hardest question, and it does not admit of a single yes-or-no answer. International law recognizes a concept of complicity in the wrongful acts of another state, but its application to arms sales is contested and fact-dependent. Under customary international law, as reflected in Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility, a state that knowingly aids or assists another state in the commission of an internationally wrongful act is responsible for that assistance if the act would be wrongful if committed by the assisting state and the assisting state does so with knowledge of the circumstances. The Arms Trade Treaty reinforces this logic: Article 6 prohibits transfers where the exporting state has knowledge that the arms would be used in the commission of genocide, crimes against humanity, or war crimes, and Article 7 requires an export risk assessment. The Arms Trade Treaty’s obligation to conduct human rights risk assessments is built on the complicity principle: states must not transfer arms where they will contribute to serious violations. The key legal questions are therefore what the supplying state knew and what it should have known. A state that sells arms with no reason to anticipate their use in atrocities is differently situated from a state that continues to supply weapons after credible evidence of systematic violations has emerged.

Two cases dominate contemporary debate. In Saudi Arabia and Yemen, the United States has provided Saudi-led coalition aircraft with refueling, targeting intelligence, and munitions used in a bombing campaign that has caused extensive civilian casualties. Critics, including U.S. legislators, have described American logistical and intelligence support as making the United States complicit in the devastation of Yemen. Investigations have documented the use of U.S.-origin guided bombs and white phosphorus in strikes affecting civilians. The United States did not directly drop the bombs, but it supplied the aircraft, the munitions, the intelligence, and the spare parts that made the campaign possible. In Israel and Gaza, since October 2023, the United States has provided Israel with military assistance and arms sales at levels described as unprecedented. Amnesty International has stated that Israeli forces have repeatedly used U.S.-origin weapons in violations of international law, and that by continuing to provide arms, the U.S. government risks complicity in genocide and other serious violations of international law. Human Rights Watch has argued that U.S. arms transfers to Israel constitute unlawful acts under international law and that U.S. military personnel risk responsibility for aiding and assisting Israeli forces. These are allegations by leading human rights organizations, not judicial findings; Israel rejects them, and the U.S. government disputes the characterization. But they illustrate the legal logic: where a supplier continues transfers after being put on notice of systematic violations, the complicity argument becomes more difficult to dismiss.

There are serious counterarguments, and a balanced assessment must state them. First, the U.S. system is consent-based and monitoring-based, not operationally directive. Washington does not select targets or authorize individual strikes. The legal responsibility for how a weapon is used rests primarily with the recipient state, which has its own obligations under international humanitarian law. Second, the United States argues that its end-use monitoring and diplomatic engagement are forms of due diligence. The existence of Golden Sentry, Blue Lantern, congressional notifications, and suspension authorities can be presented as evidence that the United States is not a passive enabler but an active regulator. Third, attribution matters. International law generally attributes conduct to the state that carries it out. Complicity requires a showing that the assisting state knowingly contributed to the specific wrongful act, not merely that its weapons were present in a conflict zone.

The counterarguments are weakened, however, by the gaps in the U.S. monitoring system itself. The Government Accountability Office has found that U.S. end-use monitoring was not designed to identify foreign partners’ violations of transfer agreements regarding use for authorized purposes. As of February 2025, the Defense Department was tracking more than 150 incidents of potential end-use violations, and the State Department’s investigations and reporting have been incomplete. A Pentagon inspector general report found that the United States had failed to properly track significant amounts of military aid to Israel, maintaining records for only 44 percent of defense articles subject to enhanced monitoring at one point. If the monitoring system does not reliably detect misuse, the claim that monitoring constitutes meaningful due diligence becomes harder to sustain. The legal consequence is not automatic. But under the complicity framework, knowledge is the pivotal variable. A state that continues to supply arms after credible, repeated, and public warnings that those arms are being used in violations cannot easily claim ignorance. The more documented the pattern, the stronger the argument that continued transfers constitute knowing assistance to wrongful acts.

Conclusion

The United States is not unique in attaching strings to arms exports. France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Russia, China, Israel, and South Korea all impose, in varying degrees, retransfer restrictions and end-use conditions, and several operate post-shipment verification mechanisms. What distinguishes the U.S. system is its scale, legal formalization, and congressional oversight—not the mere fact that conditions exist. Countries buy American weapons because the package includes strategic alignment, interoperability, financing, availability, and capability that alternatives often cannot match. The restrictions are accepted as part of a broader relationship. On the question of indirect responsibility, the honest answer is that the legal case is strongest where knowledge is clearest and monitoring is weakest. International law does not make arms suppliers automatically liable for every misuse of their weapons. But the complicity principle, codified in the Arms Trade Treaty and reflected in state responsibility doctrine, creates a real obligation of due diligence. When a supplier continues transfers after credible warnings of systematic atrocities, and when its own monitoring system is not designed to catch the relevant violations, the gap between formal conditions and effective control becomes a gap in accountability. The strings are real. The question is whether they are pulled tightly enough to matter.

Sources

This report draws on statements by Amnesty International USA and Human Rights Watch on U.S. arms transfers to Israel; reports by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on end-use monitoring and arms transfer violations; findings by the U.S. Department of Defense Inspector General as reported; French final-use and non-retransfer certificate requirements; UK export licensing and international humanitarian law risk assessment rules; the German post-shipment control framework; Russian end-use and post-shipment verification provisions; Chinese end-user certification rules and assessments of enforcement limitations; the Israeli Defense Export Control Law framework; South Korean end-user certification and retransfer consent requirements; analyses of the factors driving foreign purchases of U.S. defense equipment; Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s Articles on State Responsibility; the Arms Trade Treaty’s complicity provisions; and congressional and advocacy statements on U.S. complicity in Yemen.

Zero-Point Energy, Scalar Waves, and Toroidal Fields: Is There a Deeper Architecture Behind Energy and Consciousness?

What if the geometry of energy could help us understand the relationship between matter, the human body, and consciousness?

1. The Zero-Point Field: Energy Within Emptiness

Quantum physics tells us that even a vacuum is not entirely devoid of activity.

Quantum fields retain fluctuations even in their lowest energy states. This is known as zero-point energy.

In esoteric traditions, the zero point is often interpreted differently: as a state of absolute stillness, equilibrium, or pure potential before manifestation.

The resemblance is philosophically intriguing. 

2. Scalar Waves: The Movement of Energy and Information

In physics, scalar fields describe quantities that have magnitude but no direction. Certain scalar fields can support propagating disturbances.

Alternative theories propose another possibility: unusual scalar electromagnetic waves capable of transmitting energy or information beyond conventional electromagnetic mechanisms.

3. Toroidal Mediation: The Geometry of Circulation

A torus is a doughnut-shaped structure associated with circulation and recurring patterns.

Toroidal electromagnetic configurations are real and are studied in physics, including in advanced materials and photonics.

In alternative energy models, the torus is proposed to serve as a mediator: organizing, circulating, and stabilizing energy as it moves between an underlying field and a localized system.

The human heart produces measurable electromagnetic fields, although claims that these fields access zero-point energy through scalar waves have not been demonstrated.

4. The Proposed Connection

The speculative model follows a sequence:

Zero-Point Field → Scalar Oscillation → Toroidal Organization → Coherent Energy System

In this framework:

1. The zero point represents underlying potential.

2.Scalar oscillation represents the proposed transmission of energy or information.

3.Toroidal geometry represents circulation and organization.

Coherence represents the hypothesized emergence of an ordered system.

5. The Connection to Sacred Geometry and Consciousness

Here is where the discussion becomes especially interesting.

Across spiritual philosophies, stillness is frequently understood as the origin of movement, while circular patterns symbolize creation, return, and renewal.

The torus offers a geometric analogy for this process: energy circulating through a system rather than moving along a single linear path.

Some researchers and spiritual thinkers have proposed that consciousness, the human heart, and sacred geometry may participate in a larger organizing principle.

The deeper question may not be whether ancient traditions discovered quantum physics. It may be whether their symbolic descriptions of stillness, movement, and transformation reflect recurring ways that human beings experience and interpret the world.

Zero-point energy is real. Toroidal electromagnetic phenomena are real. Scalar fields are real.

Whether these concepts form a unified mechanism connecting consciousness and the physical universe remains an open hypothesis, not an established discovery.

Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, NI (M), HJ, Chief of Army Staff, & Chief of Defence Forces (COAS & CDF), visited Turbat, Balochistan.

Upon arrival The COAS & CDF laid a floral wreath at the Shuhada Monument and offered Fateha.

The COAS & CDF was given a comprehensive briefing on the prevailing security environment, operational preparedness and successful on-going operations against externally sponsored terrorism. He was also apprised of the progress of various ongoing socio-economic development initiatives for people of  Balochistan.

During interaction with troops, the COAS & CDF commended their high state of operational preparedness, professionalism and unwavering resolve to defend the motherland, amidst challenging operational conditions.

Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir reaffirmed Pakistan Army’s unwavering commitment to stand shoulder to shoulder with the people of Balochistan in their continued pursuit of peace, prosperity and sustainable development.

Upon arrival, COAS & CDF was received by Corps Commander Balochistan.

text:
Israel’s earlier experiences provide the necessary historical perspective. In Exodus 17, the LORD gave victory over Amalek while Joshua fought and Moses stood with the rod of God. In Joshua 6, Jericho fell according to the instructions delivered by the LORD. But Joshua 7 records defeat at Ai following Achan’s transgression concerning the devoted possessions. The contrast reveals that possessing military strength and a divinely appointed leader did not make disobedience harmless. An army may possess excellent weapons, disciplined soldiers, and impressive commanders while remaining utterly incapable of purchasing God’s blessing through military equipment. Israel’s success was connected with the LORD’s presence and commandments, not merely human organization. Deuteronomy 28:7 therefore offered extraordinary security under the conditions of national obedience. The promise should not be transformed into a declaration that every war fought by a nation claiming religious identity automatically possesses God’s approval.

Verse 8 joins military security with economic abundance: “The LORD shall command the blessing upon thee in thy storehouses.” The expression is remarkable because it presents the blessing as something the LORD Himself commands. The promise extends to what Israel sets its hand to accomplish and specifically identifies the land the LORD gives. A storehouse filled through God’s covenant blessing was not an invitation for Israel to worship the contents and forget the One who supplied them. The nation’s productive labor mattered, but divine provision remained the governing reality. This does not mean that Israel could refuse to plant, harvest, maintain its animals, or conduct ordinary agricultural responsibilities. The LORD’s blessing operated upon the work of their hands rather than replacing honest labor with magical abundance. Proverbs 10:4 condemns slothfulness, and the wider Scriptures establish the importance of diligence. God’s promise did not reward laziness; it described the prosperity accompanying faithful national obedience within the covenant.

5. A Holy People and a Feared Name — Israel’s Standing Among the Nations

Verse 9 declares that the LORD would establish Israel as a holy people unto Himself, according to what He had sworn, if the nation kept His commandments and walked in His ways. The language reaches beyond agricultural abundance and economic strength. Israel’s identity was connected with the holiness of the God who had chosen the nation. Exodus 19:5–6 had already described Israel’s peculiar standing and priestly calling, while Deuteronomy 7:6 emphasized its separation unto the LORD. God did not select Israel so that the nation could become an impressive collection of wealthy idolaters possessing better crops than their neighbors. The material blessings were connected with a covenant relationship involving obedience, worship, and national distinction. The people were to reflect the authority and holiness of the LORD through their conduct. Prosperity without obedience would not satisfy the obligations established through Moses.

text:
The Juiciest Manty

She quit her job, flew thousands of kilometers to her grandmother's kitchen in Tajikistan, and bit into one dumpling. Then she cried for ten minutes. This is the story of why. 🥟Warning: 1.7 kg of onions, 150 dumplings, one late grandfather's favorite phrase, and a recipe that changes a life. Do not read hungry.
I. The Cold Water
In the last week of October, when the first real frost had silvered the grape trellis in the courtyard and the apricot tree had let go of its final yellow leaves, Zebo Rahimova woke before the muezzin and the roosters and the milk truck, and lay for a while in the dark listening to the house.

She was seventy-four years old. Her knees spoke to her each morning in a language she had learned to ignore, and her hands, which had kneaded ten thousand loaves and rolled out a hundred thousand sheets of dough, had begun to tremble a little when they were idle. But when they were busy, they were as steady as a surgeon's. That was the secret she had discovered in her seventies: the hands only shake when they have nothing to do.

Today they would have plenty to do.

She rose, wrapped her woolen shawl around her shoulders, and shuffled to the kitchen in her felt slippers. The old house in the Sino district of Dushanbe had been built by her husband, Karim, forty-eight years ago, brick by brick, with the help of his brothers and a borrowed cement mixer. He had been gone six winters now, but his shadow still lingered in the doorframes he had planed and the shelves he had hung slightly crooked, so that every jar of preserves leaned a little to the left. Zebo had never fixed them. A crooked shelf was a kind of company.

She put the kettle on, though she did not want tea yet. She simply liked the sound of it. Then she opened the small refrigerator on the porch, where the November air did half the work for her, and took out the large steel pitcher she had filled the night before. Inside the water, small plates of ice were still floating.

Ice-cold water. Four hundred and twenty milliliters of it. Not four hundred, not four hundred and fifty. Her own mother, Nigina, had taught her that the dough for manty is a stubborn animal, and that the right amount of cold water is the bridle that makes it behave.

"Warm water makes the dough soft and lazy," her mother used to say, tapping the table with a floury finger. "Cold water makes it strong. Strong dough can be rolled thin. Thin dough is how you know a woman respects her guests."

Zebo smiled at the memory, set the pitcher on the counter, and began.

II. The Dough

She had a wide wooden bowl, darkened with decades of use, that had belonged to her grandmother and had crossed two mountain passes on the back of a donkey before it ever reached Dushanbe. Into it she poured a kilogram of wheat flour, the whole bag, shaking the last of it out with a little flick of her wrist. The flour rose in a pale cloud and settled again, smelling faintly of summer and of dust and of something warm and plain, the smell of bread before it is bread.

She made a well in the center with her fist. Into the well she poured a teaspoon of salt, then forty milliliters of sunflower oil, which gleamed in the dim kitchen light like a small pool of liquid amber. Then, slowly, she began to add the ice water, a little at a time, mixing with the fingers of her right hand while her left hand held the bowl steady.

This was the moment when it mattered. Beginners poured the water all at once and ended up with soup. Zebo had learned to feel the flour drink. She drew the dry edges into the center in circles, always in the same direction, until the mass became shaggy and rough, then a ragged lump, then something that could be gathered into a single ball.

It looked terrible. It always did, at first. Dry in some places, sticky in others, like a sulky teenager refusing to cooperate.

"Patience," she said aloud to the dough, as she did every time. "You will be beautiful. Everyone is ugly at the beginning."

She tipped the lump onto the table and began to knead, leaning into it with the heels of her hands, pushing forward, folding back, turning a quarter turn, pushing again. The first minutes were hard work. The dough fought her, tearing and clinging. Her shoulders ached and her breath grew short. But she did not stop, because she knew that somewhere around the ten-minute mark, something would change.

It always changed. The dough would stop resisting and start answering. It would grow smooth and cool beneath her palms, elastic and alive, springing back when she pressed it with a thumb. At that moment she would feel, as she had felt a hundred times, a strange tenderness toward a lump of flour and water, as if she were soothing a frightened child to sleep.

When it was done, she shaped it into a round, covered it with an overturned bowl, and set it aside to rest. Rest was not optional. The gluten needed time to loosen its grip, so that later the dough could be stretched thin without snapping back.

"Now," she said, wiping her hands on her apron, "the meat."

III. The Quiet Arithmetic of Onions

She was not alone in the house, though she had been alone for most of the morning.

Upstairs, in the small room under the roof that had once been her son's, her granddaughter Madina was asleep. Madina was twenty-six, lived in Helsinki, of all the cold, improbable places, and had arrived the previous evening with a battered suitcase, a laptop, and the shadows of exhaustion under her eyes that young people carry when they have been working too hard for too long.

She had come for her grandmother's seventy-fifth birthday, which was still three days away, but Zebo suspected there was more to it than that. Madina had always been the kind of girl who arrived at the door with her real reason hidden in the bottom of her bag.

Zebo would not ask. Asking was how you got a closed door. Feeding was how you got an open one.

So she turned to the meat.

On the counter sat a kilogram and two hundred grams of beef, bought yesterday from Rustam, the butcher at the Green Bazaar, whose father had sold meat to Zebo's father, and whose grandfather, she liked to believe, had sold meat to someone's grandfather in the days of the Silk Road. It was a good cut, deep red, lean but not too lean, with the faint blue-white marbling that promised flavor. Beside it lay three hundred and fifty grams of beef fat, creamy white and firm, the real secret of juicy manty.

Foolish cooks, she thought, were afraid of fat. They trimmed it away, they bought lean mince from supermarkets, and then they wondered why their dumplings were dry as chalk. The fat was the soul of the filling. When the manty steamed, the fat would melt slowly into the meat and into the onions, and the juice would gather inside the dough like a little secret waiting to be told.

But first, the knife.

Zebo did not believe in grinders. Grinders, she said, crushed the meat into paste. A knife respected it. She took down her old cleaver, the one with the wooden handle worn smooth as a river stone, and began to cut the beef into small, even cubes, the size of a chickpea, no larger. Her hands moved with the rhythm of a heartbeat: tap, tap, tap, tap. The fat she cut the same way, a little smaller, so it would melt evenly.

It took forty minutes. Her wrist began to ache. But the kitchen filled with the clean, iron smell of raw meat and the steady drumbeat of the blade, and she felt something she could not name, a kind of peace that lived only inside repetition.

When the meat was done, she turned to the onions.

There were one kilogram and seven hundred grams of them, a mountain of yellow-brown globes in a basket by the door. People always gasped at this number. Nearly two kilograms of onions for barely more than a kilogram of meat? Was she mad?

She was not mad. She was a Tajik grandmother, and she knew that the onion was the true heart of manty. The meat gave the dumpling its body, but the onion gave it its juice. As the manty steamed, the onion would release its sweetness and its water, and the water would mingle with the melting fat, and the result would be that legendary burst of hot broth when you bit into the dumpling.

She peeled them one by one, sitting on a low stool with a bowl between her feet. The first onion made her eyes sting. The third made them stream. By the seventh she was weeping freely, tears running down the lines of her face, and she laughed at herself, because she was not sad at all, only chemically betrayed.

"Grandmother?"

She looked up. Madina stood in the doorway in an oversized sweater, her dark hair tangled from sleep, her eyes still puffy. For a moment Zebo saw not the woman but the five-year-old who used to stand in this same doorway, demanding to know what smelled so good.

"Are you crying?" Madina asked.

"Onions," said Zebo. "Come here. You can cry too."

IV. The Granddaughter's Hands

They sat together on the kitchen floor with the basket between them, and Madina took a knife and began to dice. She was clumsy at first. Her cubes were uneven, and she chopped too fast, the way people do who learn their cooking from videos instead of from elbows.

"Slower," said Zebo gently. "The onion is not running away."

"In Helsinki I use a food processor."

"I know. I have seen the photographs." Zebo made a face of gentle horror. "Pureed onion. Like baby food."

Madina laughed, and the sound broke something open in the cold kitchen, a window of warmth. They worked side by side, the knives knocking against the boards, the pile of chopped onion growing between them like a small golden hill. Steam rose from the kettle, which Zebo had forgotten to turn off. The first light of morning began to creep gray and then pink through the frosted window.

"Babushka," Madina said, after a while, without looking up. "Did you ever want to leave? When you were young?"

Zebo's knife paused for only a moment. "Leave where?"

"Here. Dushanbe. Anywhere."

"Once," Zebo admitted. "When I was nineteen. There was a boy who wanted to take me to Moscow. He had a good suit and a terrible mustache." She chuckled. "My mother said, go if you wish, but remember that a tree can move only once, and it usually dies."

"Did you go?"

"I married your grandfather instead. He had no suit and a very good mustache." Her eyes crinkled. "I have never regretted it. But I have sometimes wondered about Moscow. A person can love the life she chose and still wonder about the one she did not. That is not a betrayal. That is only being alive."

Madina was silent. The knife in her hand had slowed. When she spoke again, her voice was small.

"I quit my job, Babushka."

There it was. The real reason, rising from the bottom of the bag like a stone from a river.

Zebo did not gasp. She did not scold. She simply reached over, took a handful of Madina's diced onions, and dropped them into the big bowl with the others, as if nothing in the world had changed.

"Tell me while we work," she said.

V. The Spices

So Madina told her. About the software company in Helsinki, with its glass offices and its free coffee and its relentless, soul-eating deadlines. About the promotions that came with more work and less meaning. About the evenings she had spent eating cold noodles in front of a screen, and the weekends she had slept through, and the morning, three weeks ago, when she had stood in the shower and realized that she could not remember the last time she had tasted anything.

"Tasted?" said Zebo.

"Really tasted. Not just eaten." Madina wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist, and this time it was not the onions. "Everything was just fuel. And then I thought about this kitchen, and your manty, and I thought, I have forgotten what it is to make something slowly. To make something that matters to someone."

Zebo nodded slowly. She did not offer advice. Advice, she had found, was usually a way of ending a conversation. Instead she stood, with a small grunt for her knees, and went to the spice shelf, the crooked one, the one Karim had hung, and took down three small jars.

"Come. Now we season."

She set the jars on the table in a row, like soldiers, and lifted the lid of the first.

"Black pepper. One tablespoon. Freshly ground, never from a packet that has been sleeping on a shelf since the last government." She measured it into the bowl with the chopped onion and meat, and the sharp, warm fragrance rose and tickled their noses.

"Cumin. One teaspoon. Zira." She said the word as if it were a name. "Rub it between your palms first." She showed her, grinding the little seeds against each other until they released their smoky, earthy perfume. "The hands wake the spice. Without this, it is only dust."

"Coriander. One teaspoon. Not more. Coriander is like a clever guest. A little makes the evening. Too much, and he takes over the conversation."

Madina laughed again, and rubbed the cumin between her palms, and breathed in. Something shifted in her face. The scent seemed to travel straight past her thoughts and into some older room inside her where she was six years old and wearing a too-big apron.

"And salt," Zebo finished. "Ten grams. I weigh it. People say a real cook never weighs, but a real cook knows when to be humble." She placed a small scale on the table and measured out exactly ten grams of coarse white salt, a tiny mountain on the little steel plate.

Last, she poured forty milliliters of oil over everything.

"Now. The hands."

VI. The Mixing

"Wash them well," said Zebo. "Warm water first, then cold. Warm hands melt the fat too soon."

Together they scrubbed their hands, and then plunged them into the bowl. The mixture was cool and wet and slippery, the onions slick against the cubes of meat and fat, the spices clinging to everything in a fine, fragrant dust.

"Squeeze," said Zebo. "Squeeze and fold. Like you are shaking hands with it."

They kneaded the filling together, pressing the onions until they wept their juice, pulling the meat through the sweetness, lifting and slapping it back down into the bowl. The juice began to gather at the bottom, pale and shining. After ten minutes the filling had changed. It was no longer a pile of ingredients but a single, glistening, fragrant mass, sticky and alive.

"Good," said Zebo, tasting nothing, for one does not taste raw meat, but judging by the smell and the feel of it under her palms. "It is ready. It will rest now, while we roll."

She covered the bowl with a plate, set it in the cool of the porch beside the pitcher, and returned to the dough, which had been waiting patiently under its bowl, its surface now silky and slack.

"Now," she said, and her voice took on a different weight, "comes the part that no one can teach you from a book."

VII. The Circles

She cut the dough into long ropes, rolling them beneath her palms until they were as thick as her thumb. Then, with a small knife, she snipped them into pieces, and she did something that made Madina stare.

She placed each piece on a small scale.

"Twenty-five grams," said Zebo. "Each one. Always."

"You weigh every piece?"

"Only the first twenty. After that, the hands remember." She winked. "My mother had no scale. She could cut twenty-five grams with her eyes closed. I am not so gifted, so I cheat a little at the start."

She took a piece of dough, flattened it with her palm, and then took up her thin rolling pin, a slender dowel, polished and nearly weightless. With quick, delicate strokes she began to roll, and here Madina saw the true skill, the one hidden in the apparent simplicity.

Zebo rolled from the center outward, always rotating the dough a quarter turn with her left hand, so the circle grew evenly. The edges she made thinner than the center, almost translucent, so that when the dumpling was folded the seams would not be thick and doughy, but the center would be strong enough to hold the juicy filling without tearing.

Within a minute, she held up a circle the size of a saucer. It was so thin that Madina could see the grain of the wooden table through it, the faint shadow of her own fingers beneath.

"Now you."

Madina's first circle was a catastrophe, thick as a pancake and lopsided as a potato. Her second tore in the middle. Her third was better but stuck stubbornly to the table.

"A little flour," said Zebo. "Not much. Dough is like people. Too much help makes it dry, too little makes it cling."

By the tenth circle something happened to Madina's hands. They stopped thinking. They began to feel. The pin glided, the dough turned, the circle spread, and for the first time in months, perhaps years, her mind went quiet. It was not the empty quiet of exhaustion. It was the full quiet of attention, the quiet of a child absorbed in a game.

"There," whispered Zebo. "You feel it?"

"Yes."

"This is what you forgot. Not the food. The feeling of making a thing with your hands until you disappear into it."

VIII. The Folding

The first guests arrived at noon, though Zebo had not invited them. This was the way of her street. When a neighbor smelled onions and spices drifting over the fence, an invitation became a formality.

First came Sitora, the widow from next door, with a bowl of pickled tomatoes and an opinion on everything. Then came Sitora's grandson, a serious boy of nine called Farrukh, who sat on a stool and stared at the dough with the intensity of a scientist. Then came old Mr. Nazarov from across the lane, with his cane, his hearing aid, and a tin of tea leaves he had been saving for an occasion.

"Is it a holiday?" he shouted.

"It is Thursday!" Zebo shouted back. "My granddaughter is visiting!"

"That's a holiday!"

And so the kitchen filled, and the work became a gathering. Sitora took charge of the filling, spooning a heaping tablespoon into the center of each circle. Mr. Nazarov, whose hands were stiff but whose pride was not, insisted on learning to fold. Farrukh was assigned to arrange the finished manty on the oiled trays.

Zebo showed them the fold. She laid a circle in her left palm, placed the filling in the middle, and then, with her right thumb and forefinger, brought the opposite edges together, pinching them closed at the top. Then she drew the two remaining edges toward the center and sealed them, creating a plump, four-cornered purse, a tiny parcel with a crown of neat pleats.

"The seal must be tight," she said. "If it opens in the steam, the juice runs out, and then you have made only a sad meatball in a bad coat."

"A sad meatball in a bad coat," repeated Farrukh solemnly, and everyone laughed.

Madina folded, and Sitora folded, and Mr. Nazarov folded, badly, but with such tenderness that nobody had the heart to correct him. The trays filled slowly, rows upon rows of little parcels, glistening faintly with oil, each one a small, round promise.

The conversation rolled like the pin. They spoke of the price of flour and the sins of the municipality. They spoke of weddings and funerals, of whose son had gone to Russia to work and whose daughter had gone to Turkey to study. Mr. Nazarov told a story about the winter of 1969 that grew more elaborate each year. Sitora disputed the details. Farrukh, who had been quiet, asked Madina what snow was like in Finland.

"It's different from here," she said. "It's quieter. It falls and falls, and sometimes in the middle of the night you wake up because the world has gone silent."

"I would like to hear that," Farrukh said wistfully.

"Maybe someday I'll take you."

"Is it lonely?" Farrukh asked, with the terrible directness of nine-year-olds.

Madina's hands paused over the dough. The kitchen seemed to hold its breath, and Zebo, without looking up, went on pleating a manty with great concentration.

"Sometimes," Madina said at last. "Sometimes very lonely. But the loneliness is not the snow's fault."

"Whose fault is it?"

"Maybe nobody's. Maybe it's just what happens when you're far from the people who know how you take your tea."

Mr. Nazarov, who had heard nothing, nodded gravely and said, "Exactly!"

IX. The Steam

By two in the afternoon there were more than a hundred and fifty manty, laid out like a small army on the oiled tiers of the steamer. Zebo had brought out the great old kazan, the heavy cast iron pot that had cooked for weddings and funerals and one memorable circumcision feast. It was filled halfway with water and set over the largest flame on the stove, and the steamer, the tiered mantyshnitsa with its perforated trays, was stacked carefully on top.

She greased each tier with oil so that nothing would stick, arranged the manty with small gaps between them, and covered everything with a tight lid.

"Now we wait," she said. "Twenty-five to thirty minutes, on the big fire. Not the small one. The big one. Manty must be cooked violently. They must feel the heat."

"Why?" asked Farrukh.

"Because strong heat sets the dough quickly, and the juice stays inside. Slow heat makes them soggy and sad." She wagged a finger. "Everything good in life requires one brief moment of fierceness."

They waited, and the waiting was its own kind of ritual. Steam hissed from beneath the lid and curled up toward the ceiling. The window fogged. The kitchen warmed until Mr. Nazarov removed his jacket and Sitora fanned herself with a dish towel. And the smell, the smell began to rise, slow at first, then thickening: the sweetness of cooked onion, the deep, rich scent of beef and melting fat, the earthy ghost of cumin and the bright whisper of coriander, all braided together with the clean warmth of steamed dough.

Madina stood by the stove with her eyes closed.

"What are you doing?" Zebo asked quietly.

"Tasting," said Madina. "With my nose. I forgot I could do this."

Zebo did not answer. She stood beside her granddaughter and for a long minute simply breathed, the two of them side by side in the fragrant fog, a seventy-four-year-old woman and a twenty-six-year-old runaway from the cold north, joined by a smell.

"Your grandfather used to stand exactly there," Zebo said eventually. "Eyes closed. Every time. He would say that he could tell by the smell whether the manty would be good. He was never wrong."

"What does it smell like when it's good?"

Zebo thought about it. "Like the moment before someone says your name with love."

X. The Table

At last she lifted the lid, and a great white cloud of steam rolled upward, and everyone leaned in.

The manty gleamed. They were plump and glossy, the dough translucent in places where the filling pressed against it, the pleated crowns still perfectly shaped. Zebo transferred them to a wide, flat platter with a slotted spoon, working fast, while they were hot, and set the platter in the middle of the low table in the guest room, where cushions had been laid on the floor in the old way.

There were small bowls of sour cream, thick and cold. There was a dish of sharp red adjika, which Sitora had brought. There were the pickled tomatoes, and flatbread still warm from the neighbor's tandoor, and a great teapot of green tea.

"Wait," said Zebo, as hands reached out. "First, a word."

She did not make speeches. But she lifted a single manty with her fingers and held it up to the light.

"Karim loved these," she said. "Every Thursday for forty-two years I made them for him, and in forty-two years he never once said they were good. He only said, 'Zebo, one more.' This is the highest praise a Tajik man knows how to give." Her voice cracked slightly, but she smiled through it. "To the ones who ask for one more."

"To one more," they echoed.

And now came the moment that every lover of manty knows, the ritual of the first bite. You must not simply bite into a manty. You must take it carefully in your fingers, lift it, and bite off a small corner of the dough, just enough to open a hole. Then you tilt your head back and drink the broth, the hot, fragrant, golden juice that has gathered inside. Only then do you eat the rest.

Madina lifted her manty, bit its corner, and tilted her head.

The broth poured over her tongue like a revelation. It was hot, almost too hot, and rich with the sweetness of onion and the savory depth of beef, laced with pepper and warmed by cumin. It tasted of fat and fire and patience. It tasted of her grandmother's hands. It tasted of every Thursday of her childhood, and of a version of herself she had thought she had lost.
