@JoshHelfgott “BREAKING🚨 An Air Force major who called for Trump's impeachment has now spent nearly 100 DAYS in solitary confinement, and he hasn't even gone to trial.

On Tuesday, military prosecutors argued at a hearing at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling that Air Force Maj. Jason Watson, a 40-year-old Air Force Academy graduate with 17 years of service, must stay in pretrial confinement to keep him from speaking out. His court-martial isn't scheduled until February 2027.

On July 1, Watson stood on the Capitol steps in uniform holding a sign that read "Impeach, Convict, Remove," protesting U.S. military action in Iran, Venezuela and Cuba. He was arrested when he refused to move. On Aug. 17, he repeated his criticism of Trump in a national TV interview. The next day he was arrested on duty and jailed.

He has been held in a county jail in Calvert County, Maryland, ever since. His lawyers say he spends 20 to 22 hours a day alone in a concrete cell with the lights on day and night. Maj. Heather Bruha, his military defense lawyer, told the judge the cell is so cold he wears thermal underwear, and a guard told him to "do more jumping jacks." 

His defense says he has been strip-searched 18 times, denied yard and shower time, and has lost weight. His calls with his lawyers have been restricted.

"He has never felt more alone there," Bruha said.

The Air Force says he is not in solitary, just kept apart from the general population under military policy. But at his preliminary hearing in September, the officer running it said Watson couldn't be held with civilians and that the law "puts him in solitary confinement."

In court, the prosecutor, Lt. Col. Chris Dunn, played Watson's interview and stopped it on the line "I believe we can defeat this government if we just take a stand." Dunn called it "serious misconduct" and warned of its "coercive nature." Bruha said there is no evidence a single service member has followed Watson. The government had nothing more to show the court after the video.

Watson is charged under Article 88, a rarely used rule that bars officers from "contemptuous" words about the president. A military defense attorney who attended his preliminary hearing said Watson offered to resign his commission to avoid a court-martial, and the request was denied within 24 hours.

The judge is expected to rule soon. His defense says one option being considered is moving him to the Naval Consolidated Brig in Chesapeake, Virginia, three months before trial.

If you appreciate my posts, it would mean the world if you followed my page. Thank you for being here.”

Yemen’s Coastal Offensive Puts Aden Under Pressure 
Protecting Aden is now an explicit priority for Yemen’s internationally recognised government. On 15 November, its armed forces publicly acknowledged a redeployment on the southern and southwestern fronts and identified protection of the temporary capital and relief of Taiz as priorities. The record supports heightened pressure on Aden. The extent of durable territorial change and the immediate threat to the city remain uncertain. القوات المسلحة تثمن دور القوات الجنوبية في حماية العاصمة المؤقتة عدن والمحافظات وفك الحصار عن تعز — Yemen News Agency (Saba) — Nov 2026 https://t.co/GCoGS0xkhL
Bab al-Mandab remained in commercial use under substantial threat. The Joint Maritime Information Center recorded approximately 22 commercial transits per day on 12–14 November, versus approximately 25 on 5–11 November, and reported no confirmed attacks or disruptions in the southern Red Sea and strait during its latest verified reporting window, ending 15 November. That window provides limited evidence about maritime effects after the redeployment. JMIC Advisory Note, Update 114 — Joint Maritime Information Center — Nov 2026 JMIC_Advisory_Update_114_FINAL
Civilian access is already impaired. UNICEF reported on 18 November that more than 330,000 people had been displaced since the escalation began, including an estimated 174,000 children. More than 800,000 people in Taiz were reportedly cut off from humanitarian assistance as of late October. The immediate decisions concern aid access and continuity at Aden’s civilian gateways. Changes to shipping posture require incident and traffic data from after the redeployment. At least 64 children killed and 64 injured in Yemen as intensified hostilities approach three-month mark — UNICEF — Nov 2026 https://t.co/gmAH75KkRQ

Yemen’s coastal war has made Aden the test of Red Sea security
On 15 November 2026, Yemen’s government acknowledged redeploying forces on the southern and southwestern fronts and made protecting Aden an explicit priority. A day later, Maersk announced that three services operated with Hapag-Lloyd would return to Suez on staggered schedules. The two decisions expose a gap in the international response. Shipping companies can restore selected routes while Yemen’s government struggles to sustain civilian access and public services. The test is whether outside partners use the commercial opening to keep essential Yemeni institutions functioning and secure verifiable commitments from the parties to the conflict. Otherwise, maritime protection can lower the cost of some voyages while the fiscal and humanitarian liabilities accumulate ashore.

Aden has to prove it can govern under pressure
The capture of Mokha, reported by UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg on 10 September 2026, changed the geography of the war. By 9 October, Grundberg was reporting a government counteroffensive and attributing claims of recovered areas around Bab al-Mandab to the government. In its assessment covering 8–12 November, the Joint Maritime Information Center found no independent confirmation of stable or complete control of the strait’s approaches or key islands. The sounder test of Aden’s position is what its institutions can still do. Presidential Decree No. 76 appointed a new head of the Yemen Gulf of Aden Ports Corporation on 2 November, and the corporation documented a completed handover on 5 November. That establishes administrative continuity at the port authority. Its value to households and businesses depends on whether cargo can move onward and essential services keep running.

The numbers show where reopening stops
The Joint Maritime Information Center counted approximately 22 commercial transits a day at Bab al-Mandab on 12–14 November 2026, compared with approximately 25 a day on 5–11 November. Its 15 November report still assessed the threat as substantial. In Taiz, more than 800,000 people were reportedly cut off from humanitarian assistance as of 23 October, and UNICEF reported in November that the city’s water production had fallen by nearly half. As of 11 November, water, sanitation and hygiene, humanitarian cash, and education accounted for US$7,171,980 of UNICEF’s US$8,557,099 published funding gap for the escalation response, or 83.8 per cent. The funding figures expose the limits of a maritime recovery. More sailings through the strait offer little immediate relief to a city whose main supply connection is cut and whose water system and hospitals depend on regular deliveries of fuel, medicines and other essential supplies.

The Cape diversion buys flexibility at a price
The 16 November Gemini advisory identifies where commercial improvement can first be measured. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd published initial load-port dates of 4 December 2026, 20 December 2026 and 14 January 2027 for the three trans-Suez service changes. If those rotations hold, the benefit comes from releasing ship-days and shortening the time cargo spends in transit. The US Energy Information Administration has documented that voyages diverted around the Cape of Good Hope can take two to three weeks longer, depending on origin and destination. Yet the availability of war-risk cover can determine whether a direct voyage is feasible before its price is compared with the cost of diversion. Gard’s August 2026 circular illustrates the constraint. It provided for reinstatement of specified cover subject to an exclusion in defined waters. A return to Suez can therefore be commercially sound for one service while another carrier continues to pay for the longer route to preserve a reliable schedule.

Enforcement at sea and fiscal support ashore have different limits
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea protects transit passage, while Security Council Resolution 2216 sets out a targeted arms embargo and conditions for inspecting Yemen-bound cargo in a member state’s territory. Resolution 2837, adopted on 12 November 2026, called for vigilance over specified dual-use items and expressed an intention to decide on further steps by 11 January 2027. Its provisions for qualifying UN and humanitarian uses matter because applying restrictions too broadly can delay legitimate supplies to a country already struggling to distribute them. The fiscal limit is equally concrete. Saudi Arabia reported providing more than SAR 224 million for Yemen’s budget and salaries on 4 October, while the IMF approved an 18-month, non-financing Staff-Monitored Program on 7 October. Saudi funding can support payments, and IMF monitoring can help improve revenue collection and expenditure decisions. Their combined value depends on whether payroll and service records show where the money went and what it kept running.

Europe’s commitments carry different obligations
Italy’s 2026 framework provides for up to 753 personnel across four missions, including EUNAVFOR ASPIDES. Germany authorised up to 350 personnel for ASPIDES through October 2027 and estimated additional expenditure of approximately €18.9 million for the mandate period. France’s defence treaty with Djibouti has a 20-year term and sets an annual contribution of €85 million for the presence of French forces under the bilateral agreement. The United Kingdom agreed on 22 September 2026 to provide an RAF Voyager aircraft in support of Saudi defensive activity and separately announced £10 million in humanitarian assistance through the UN emergency appeal. The European Commission’s October announcement brought EU humanitarian allocations for Yemen in 2026 to €110 million. These figures measure different commitments. A personnel ceiling permits a contribution, a basing agreement helps sustain a regional presence, and a humanitarian allocation finances delivery where access permits. The common diplomatic position is easier to establish than the combined effect, which depends on actual rotations and assistance delivered. NATO’s Operation Sea Guardian has its own Mediterranean remit.

Over the next 12–24 months, the bill falls where continuity fails
Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi met UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg on 8 November 2026 to discuss de-escalation and a return to the political process. Oman’s May 2025 arrangement between Washington and Sana’a showed what a limited agreement could secure: a reciprocal undertaking by identified parties to refrain from targeting one another. A wider agreement would have to produce verifiable changes in attacks, civilian access and service delivery. Over the next 12–24 months, the cost of leaving those outcomes disconnected will fall first on Yemeni households, local service providers and the government in Aden. Saudi Arabia will face pressure to provide further budget support, European contributors will have to sustain protection commitments, and carriers will continue to price in diversion and insurance uncertainty where schedules remain fragile. November’s decisions prioritised Aden’s defence and set dates for selected services to return to Suez. Their longer-term value will be measured in salaries actually paid, supplies delivered to Taiz and commercial rotations completed under sustainable cover.

The world awaited this meeting. 

In an unprecedented diplomatic move, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have concluded their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen.

This summit was perhaps less about resolving disputes and more about reopening channels of communication between the world's three biggest powers.

For Xi, it reinforces China's diplomatic stature. For Trump, it offers an opportunity to project himself as a dealmaker. For Putin, it provides direct engagement with Washington without diplomatic isolation.

No grand bargain, no dramatic breakthrough. But, simply watching Washington, Moscow and Beijing to sit together to talk at the same table is significant.

text:
MARKET UPDATE — THURSDAY, 19 NOVEMBER 2026

The S&P 500 has broken below its 200-day moving average, and one respected strategist sold every share he owned. The Fed is lining up another rate rise, and Riyadh's tallest tower was hit overnight.

Into that mood comes the biggest stock-market debut in history. Anthropic sold $81bn of shares last night at a $1.5tn valuation, and starts trading on the Nasdaq today. Futures are rallying. Wall Street now gets to see whether that demand lasts once the shares trade freely.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ANTHROPIC: THE BIGGEST IPO EVER

💠 The deal (FT, Reuters):

🔸 Priced at $83 a share, above the top of its $70–78 range.

🔸 980m shares sold, up from 825m planned, raising $81bn.

🔸 Valuation: about $1.5tn fully diluted. That puts it among the handful of US companies worth more than $1tn.

🔸 A further $26bn private sale to Nvidia, Microsoft and Google takes the total to at least $107bn, beating SpaceX's record $86bn. If underwriters use their option to sell 147m extra shares, that adds about $12bn.

💡 An IPO (initial public offering) is the first time a private company sells shares to the public. The "greenshoe" option lets the banks running the deal sell extra shares if demand is strong.

💠 Why buyers stretched:

🔸 Anthropic was valued at about $4bn in 2023 and $965bn in May. Its revenue has grown faster than any start-up in history, according to the FT.

🔸 It will hold more than $200bn of cash after the deal, earmarked for computing power. It plans to spend about $900bn on computing infrastructure by 2045, a plan it calls "bold but sane".

🔸 Investors say it hopes not to sell more shares, and is aiming for an investment-grade credit rating so it can borrow instead.

💠 Why sceptics hesitate:

🔸 Anthropic lost $1.3bn on operations in the first nine months of 2026.

🔸 Buyers were hoping for a $2tn valuation in the summer, so $1.5tn is already a reset.

🔸 Its prospectus tells investors "not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms", because profits will be balanced against "the public good".

🔸 Bearish strategist Joachim Klement (more below) cites the slowing revenue growth shown in the prospectus as one sign the AI boom is cooling.

https://t.co/M7HanNGTpv's Kyle Rodda expects a bullish listing, but warns:

"I don't think it's necessarily going to assuage all the fears about AI."

Minotaur Capital's Armina Rosenberg:

"One listing won't settle the debate."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: BELOW THE LINE

💠 Wednesday's close (Barron's):

🔸 Dow: −1.1% (−561 points) to 50,198

🔸 S&P 500: −0.2% to 7,324

🔸 Nasdaq Composite: +0.4% to 24,430

🔸 Russell 2000 (small companies): slightly higher, helped by lower bond yields

💠 Danger zones:

🔸 The Nasdaq is already in a correction. The Dow is 2.6% away from one. The S&P 500 would join it below 7,037, about 4% lower.

💡 A "correction" is a fall of 10% from a recent peak. A fall of 20% is a "bear market".

🔸 The Nasdaq 100 is 13% below its early October peak (FT).

💠 The S&P 500 has also broken below its 200-day moving average. Joachim Klement of Panmure Liberum had said that would be his signal, and he has now moved his personal portfolio out of stocks and into long-term government bonds:

"Market dynamics have turned decisively bearish, in our view."

🔸 He expects the S&P 500 to end 2027 at about 5,000, roughly a third below today's level. His reasons: falling prices for AI services, slowing revenue growth, market unease about AI spending and "circular financing", where suppliers fund the customers who buy their products.

💡 The 200-day moving average is the index's average closing price over roughly the past 200 trading days. Falling below it is a widely watched sign that the trend has turned down.

The counterargument: the signal often gives false alarms. A market that bounces around the line forces sellers back in at higher prices. Klement concedes "I may be wrong", and says he will buy back in if the index recovers above the line.

💠 This morning (about 5 am ET):

🔸 S&P 500 futures: +1.16% to 7,426

🔸 Nasdaq 100 futures: +2.07% to 27,749

🔸 Dow futures: +0.60% to 50,576

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: +0.48% to 6,192

🔸 VIX: −9.8% to 22.16

💡 The VIX measures how much investors pay to protect themselves against big swings. A near-10% drop shows nerves easing, but a reading above 20 still signals caution.

💠 Asia didn't join in. 
Taiwan's Taiex fell 4.4%, and MSCI's index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 1.7% to a seven-month low. It is heading for a weekly fall of nearly 6%, its worst since early March (Reuters). Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi edged up.

💠 Premarket movers:

🔸 Palo Alto Networks: +9% after strong results and a higher forecast, which it linked to threats from AI agents. CrowdStrike +6% (after +8% on Wednesday) and Zscaler +5% (after nearly +7%).

🔸 Alibaba: fell below $82 in early trading, its lowest since early 2025, on worries about its access to Nvidia chips. It then rose 2% to about $86 after its results.

🔸 Nvidia: +1.9% to $153.87.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 NVIDIA: THE BOUNCE THAT FADED

💠 On Wednesday morning, Nvidia was up 3% premarket after a record quarter. By the close it had fallen 2.9% to $150.96, its lowest close since June 2025. It is down 29% in a month. Trading volume was 350m shares, against a 30-day average of 200m.

🔸 The board has ruled out bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO.

💠 A $500bn plan to help Nvidia's customers finance their chip purchases has stalled, according to a report highlighted by investor Michael Burry and covered by Seeking Alpha.

🔸 Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR signed up in August. Reportedly no money has been lent yet.

🔸 Lenders want stronger protection than Nvidia's offer to guarantee up to 25% of project costs. The agreement was non-binding, and a first deal isn't expected before 2027.

💡 Lenders are happy to fund AI demand only if they are confident the data centres will earn enough to repay them. A stalled deal suggests that confidence is thinner than the headline figure suggested.

💠 Wall Street is split:

🔸 Freedom Capital Markets cut NVIDIA's target to $230 from $300 but still sees value, saying "the earnings power is intact". 

🔸 Questar Capital's Richard Reyle:

"Nvidia is the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CHIPS & CHINA: THE BACK DOOR CLOSES

💠 TSMC and Samsung have halted some chip shipments to Chinese customers while they apply for US licences, the FT reports, citing several people briefed on the matter. Neither company has confirmed it.

🔸 New US rules issued on Monday close a route Chinese designers used to have advanced chips made: going through independent packaging and testing companies that certified the designs fell outside US export limits.

🔸 The exemption for chips designed for non-AI uses such as smartphones has also gone. TSMC makes chips for Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo, so consumer electronics are affected too. Licences for phone chips are likely, an industry insider told the FT, but the delays could be significant.

🔸 Samsung's Chinese customers include Baidu's chip unit Kunlun and TikTok owner ByteDance.

💡 Why it matters: the rules have moved from paper to actual delivery stops. China already faces record memory-chip prices and limited capacity at its own chipmaker, SMIC.

The story sat alongside Taiwan's 4.4% fall and Alibaba's slide, although Reuters puts Asia's selling down to broader worries about the AI trade.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 AI'S FUNDING SQUEEZE

The question is no longer whether AI demand exists. It is who pays for the build-out, and on what terms. Three stories show the strain.

💠 Meta has suspended its plan to create a new class of non-voting shares while it fights a shareholder lawsuit in Delaware (FT).

🔸 The shares would have let Meta raise $60bn for AI without weakening Mark Zuckerberg's control. Trading was due to start in January. The trial begins in April.

🔸 Meta's filings say it will need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years for AI.

💠 Texas has resumed approving power plants for data centres, weeks ahead of schedule (Barron's).

🔸 2.9 gigawatts were approved in a few days, about as much as three large nuclear reactors. Research firm Cleanview projects another 6–10 GW before Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on halting approvals, takes office on 19 January. That is a projection, not a done deal.

🔸 SpaceX won approval for a 750-megawatt gas plant near Brownsville that isn't connected to the grid, built first with 35 small turbines and later with eight larger GE Vernova units.

💡 Permits aren't power plants. Turbines still have to be built, financed and defended against lawsuits. Data-centre stocks such as CoreWeave and Vistra have fallen sharply since Hinojosa's win.

💠 The cost of debt for data-centre developers has soared, and the Democrats' sweep of the midterms has added to doubts about the pace of the build-out (FT). That makes Anthropic's plan to borrow rather than sell more shares an important test.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE OUTAGES: CYBER STOCKS CASH IN

💠 Something has failed in America every weekday since last Thursday: a nationwide halt to flights (the longest since 9/11), a Microsoft email outage, a disruption at the National Security Agency, and problems at JPMorgan, United Airlines and Apple.

🔸 Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Congress the incidents were separate failures caused by maintenance and system changes:

"They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

🔸 Several lawmakers aren't convinced. Officials blame the flight grounding on a router installed in Arkansas.

🔸 Clayton linked the outages partly to a "substantial increase" in system upgrades, some made to fix AI-related weaknesses. Andreessen Horowitz's Anne Neuberger:

"When patching at scale, some can cause problems."

💡 Whatever the cause, investors are betting that companies will spend more on security. That is behind this week's rally in Palo Alto, CrowdStrike and Zscaler.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS, THE FED & THE DATA

💠 Minutes of the Fed's October meeting were more hawkish than the decision itself (WSJ).

🔸 Almost all officials expected rates to rise further. A few who backed the pause called it a "close call". More officials wanted a rise than the two who formally dissented.

🔸 Some accepted the pause only if markets "clearly understood" that more rises were likely.

💡 "Hawkish" means leaning towards higher interest rates to fight inflation. Higher rates make borrowing dearer for families, companies and governments.

💠 The speeches since then point the same way.

🔸 Governor Michael Barr:

"If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further."

🔸 Governor Christopher Waller wants either a half-point rise in December or a clear signal of faster rises in 2027.

🔸 St Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem expects several rises before spring 2027.

💠 Traders see a 90% chance of a quarter-point rise on 9 December, to 4.00–4.25% (CME FedWatch, via Reuters).

The counterargument (WSJ): markets are already doing some of the Fed's work. Falling AI stocks are raising borrowing costs for data-centre builders, and falling oil eases inflation. That could let the Fed slow down next year.

💠 Treasury yields are slightly higher this morning:

🔸 2-year: 4.819% (+1.5 basis points)

🔸 10-year: 5.089% (+1.9)

🔸 30-year: 5.428% (+1.6)

🔸 A solid 20-year bond auction on Wednesday had briefly pulled the 10-year yield to a one-week low.

💡 A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. When yields rise, investors are demanding more to lend to the US government, and mortgages and business loans follow.

💠 Housing sent mixed signals on Wednesday:

🔸 Housing starts: 1.309m a year, against a forecast of 1.245m. That is up 9.9% from a downwardly revised 1.191m in September.

🔸 Building permits: 1.295m, well short of the forecast of 1.377m and down 7.5% from 1.4m. September's figure was already a 3½-year low (Reuters).

🔸 Pending home sales: −4.7%, against a forecast of −2%, after −7.2% in September.

💡 Starts count homes builders began last month. Permits count approvals for the homes they plan to build next. The plunge in permits matters more: it says the pipeline is drying up, with 30-year mortgage rates around 7.11%.

💠 IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva says AI investment is making a material contribution to global growth this year, but warns that energy and AI-related demand are making inflation harder to predict.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE DOLLAR & GOLD

💠 The dollar index hit 103.97 overnight, its highest since April 2025, before easing to 103.68 as stocks rallied.

🔸 Euro: $1.0963, near its lowest since April 2025

🔸 Sterling: $1.3117, a one-month low

🔸 Yen: 159.56 per dollar, close to the 160 level where Tokyo has stepped in to support its currency before

🔸 Australian dollar: $0.6662, a 10-month low, after employment fell for a second month and unemployment hit a five-year high. UBS now expects the Reserve Bank of Australia's first cut in August 2027, not November.

💡 Higher US interest rates draw money into dollars. A strong dollar makes imports cheaper for Americans, but raises costs for other countries that pay for oil and debt in dollars.

💠 Gold is down 0.3% at $3,730 an ounce, after another sharp fall on Wednesday on the Fed signals. It was $3,772 this time yesterday.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL & ENERGY: A WORLD WITHOUT HORMUZ?

💠 Brent crude is flat at about $92 a barrel and heading for a third weekly fall. Traders expect supply to exceed demand.

💠 The International Energy Agency's annual World Energy Outlook says the world could "conceivably manage without" the Strait of Hormuz, in the words of its head Fatih Birol.

🔸 Before the war, about 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the strait.

🔸 It would cost about $240bn: $40bn for new pipelines and $200bn for oilfields elsewhere.

🔸 New pipelines in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq could move about 15m barrels a day around the strait. Flows through Hormuz could fall from 20m barrels a day before the war to 2m by 2035.

🔸 The catch: Qatar's LNG has no alternative route.

🔸 Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea saved it about $60bn in revenue in the first months of the war.

💠 The bigger warning is for the gas industry. 
Under current policies, oil demand rises from 102m barrels a day to 114m by 2050. If countries respond strongly to the crisis, it falls to 85m. Up to 260bn cubic metres of yearly LNG capacity, almost 80% of the EU's gas use, could go unwanted by 2035 if Asian buyers turn away.

Birol:

"There is a lot of LNG coming, but the question is whether there will be buyers."

💡 This is a long-term scenario, not a fix for today's shortage. But it signals where investment may flow: pipelines, nuclear, renewables and electrification. For big US and Qatari LNG export projects, the risk is that buyers are fewer than planned.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE GULF: RIYADH'S SKYLINE HIT

💠 A Houthi projectile struck the Public Investment Fund tower, Riyadh's tallest building and home to Saudi Arabia's $1.2tn sovereign wealth fund, damaging several floors, the WSJ reports, citing three people familiar with the matter.

🔸 The Saudi-led coalition acknowledged a "missile threat" and said falling debris caused material damage. The Houthis haven't claimed the attack.

🔸 The Aramco tower in the same financial district was hit on 8 November. Saudi jets struck Sanaa early on Thursday.

🔸 The strike came hours after US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh.

💡 Why it matters: the Houthis now hold coastline overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea route that Saudi Arabia's bypass pipeline depends on. The IEA's escape route from Hormuz runs past the Houthis.

💠 Iran is under growing economic strain from the US blockade of its ports (Al Jazeera).

🔸 Official data shows the economy shrank 10.1% in the spring quarter. Annual inflation is 88.7%, and 113% for food.

🔸 US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicts a 25% contraction this year. Tehran says it has $30bn in reserves to pay for essential imports.

🔸 Washington has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region. Iran struck US targets this week, including radar systems in Bahrain, after US attacks on Qeshm Island.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE WORLD: THREE LEADERS, NO DEAL (YET)

💠 Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin began their unprecedented meeting in Shenzhen.

🔸 Xi:

"Abandon Cold War mentality, not pursue decoupling and breaking chains."

🔸 He proposed a crisis communication channel and cooperation to keep energy supplies stable. He also warned that "major powers must not touch each other's bottom lines", after telling Trump to do the "right thing" on Taiwan, according to Chinese state media.

🔸 Trump said the US and China could help end the war in Ukraine, and that both he and Xi feel strongly that oil must flow through Hormuz.

🔸 Analysts expect few concrete results. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies' Craig Singleton:

"A photograph could serve all three men well."

💡 What markets are waiting for: any change to chip restrictions, rare-earth supplies or the Ukraine and Iran wars. Without those, the meeting is diplomacy, not an economic breakthrough.

💠 In Europe, Britain is resisting EU demands that it match Brussels' tariffs on Chinese goods ahead of Friday's UK–EU summit, according to a draft communiqué seen by the FT. In return, Britain is seeking access to the EU's "Made in Europe" subsidies. British carmakers have most at stake.

🟢 CRYPTO

💠 Bitcoin is up 1.3% at $63,774 and ether 1.6% at $1,803.72, rising with stock futures. Both remain under pressure from the strong dollar and expected rate rises, which weigh on assets that pay no interest.

jobless claims (forecast 197,000, previous 200,000). Continuing claims (forecast 1.71m, previous 1.697m). Philadelphia Fed survey (forecast 20, previous 20.9)

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 Anthropic's pricing proves the biggest investors still want the best AI assets. Today's trading is the real test. A strong debut supports private AI valuations and the case for borrowing to build. A weak one would show that demand at $1.5tn was thinner than the order book suggested.

🔸 The market's problem is financing, not demand. Nvidia's stalled $500bn plan, Meta's blocked share plan and rising debt costs all point the same way: the AI build-out is getting harder to pay for.

🔸 The technical picture has worsened. The S&P 500 is below its 200-day average, the Nasdaq is in correction and Asia is having its worst week since March. Until the S&P recovers the line, rallies are on probation.

🔸 The Fed is not coming to the rescue. Minutes, Barr, Waller and Musalem all lean towards more rises. The strong dollar is squeezing gold, emerging markets and the yen.

🔸 Housing is where higher rates bite hardest. The permits plunge points to less building next year.

🔸 Gulf risk is rising while oil falls. Markets are betting on ample supply and bypass pipelines, but the Houthis now threaten the Red Sea end of that bypass.

Bull case: ANT trades well, jobless claims and the Philadelphia survey show a steady economy without inflation pressure, the S&P climbs back above its 200-day average, and Shenzhen produces something concrete on chips or trade.

Bear case: ANT disappoints, the S&P confirms its break lower, Fed speakers back a half-point rise, China retaliates against the chip curbs, or a Gulf strike hits oil or shipping.

"Fire tests gold, suffering tests brave men."

Today a $1.5tn company faces its first day in the open market, and a nervous market faces a test of its own. Tests don't decide our worth; they reveal it, and often build it. Brian Hook, who served as the State Department’s special envoy for Iran during Trump’s first term and now sits as vice chairman of Cerberus Global Investments, laid out on Fox News exactly what Saudi Arabia is up against — and why Jerusalem, not Tehran, is the partner that actually helps.

“𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘰𝘮𝘪𝘤 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘪𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘺 𝘣𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘧𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘚𝘢𝘶𝘥𝘪 𝘈𝘳𝘢𝘣𝘪𝘢 𝘣𝘺 𝘤𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘐𝘴𝘳𝘢𝘦𝘭,” Hook said. Simple enough. But the reason it matters right now is what’s happening on Saudi Arabia’s own border.

Hook’s blunt read: the Saudis are 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐡𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐥𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐝𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐬 by the Houthis, who he called “𝘵𝘰𝘥𝘢𝘺 𝘐𝘳𝘢𝘯’𝘴 𝘧𝘢𝘷𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘹𝘺.” Riyadh’s response wasn’t to lean on Washington or Jerusalem — its defense minister instead flew to Tehran, with representatives from Turkey and Pakistan in tow, hunting for some kind of deal to make the attacks stop. Hook didn’t sugarcoat what that says: “𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘢 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺, 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘥𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘶𝘭𝘵 𝘴𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘚𝘢𝘶𝘥𝘪.”

That’s the contrast worth sitting with. Iran doesn’t negotiate with Saudi Arabia as an equal — it 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐢𝐭 and then lets Riyadh come begging for relief. Israel, by contrast, is the one offering Saudi Arabia actual 𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐮𝐩𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 through normalization, the same Abraham Accords framework Trump has spent years trying to widen across the Gulf.

𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐬. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐤𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭.

🗞️19 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Pre-Market

Anthropic Lit the Futures Board, Bitcoin Climbed Back From $62,000

Bitcoin tested $62,000 after the bell and spent the night climbing back toward $63,900 as Anthropic's record IPO lifted Nasdaq futures about 2%, while ETFs shed another $306 million, Hong Kong flagged Hyperliquid and court papers itemised the Binance theft.

Prepared around 5:55 AM EST on Thursday 19 November. This edition picks up from Wednesday's US Close, prepared at 4:05 PM EST, and only adds what happened since: the evening session, Anthropic's pricing, Wednesday's fund flows, Asia and the first hours of Europe. Crypto prices are live prints as of about 5:55 AM EST, and futures, oil, Treasury, dollar and gold figures are live overnight prints.

1⃣ Bitcoin defended $62,000 in the evening and climbed through the night

Bitcoin was near $62,538 at last night's edition. It kept sliding after the close and printed exactly $62,000 at 5:55 PM EST, about $50 above Saturday night's $61,950 low, before buyers stepped in. When stock futures reopened at 6:00 PM EST it jumped to about $63,200 inside the hour, then held about $62,320 to $62,350 twice, in the 8:00 PM and 10:00 PM EST hours. From there it climbed steadily: about $63,680 by 11:00 PM EST, about $63,800 in the Asia session at 2:00 AM EST and about $63,865 at 4:05 AM EST, with dips stopping at about $63,225 after midnight, $63,500 at 3:00 AM EST and $63,615 at 4:00 AM EST. It pushed to an overnight high of about $63,905 at 5:50 AM EST and trades near $63,780, about 2% above last night's edition but still about 0.7% lower over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The $61,950 to $62,000 zone held for a second time this week, and each pullback since 11:00 PM EST has stopped higher than the one before.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A clean defence of $62,000 followed by a staircase of higher lows after midnight is the best structure Bitcoin has shown since the weekend. But the whole night happened below $64,000, and that is the level that decides whether this is a recovery or just a bounce inside the range.

2⃣ Ether reclaimed $1,800, Solana and XRP lagged

Ether was near $1,754 at last night's edition. It dipped to about $1,748 at 5:50 PM EST, holding above Wednesday's $1,745 afternoon low and the $1,731 session low, then climbed through the night to about $1,812 at 5:05 AM EST, its best level since early Wednesday. It trades near $1,805, about 3% above last night's edition and slightly positive over 24 hours. Solana bottomed at about $72.20 at 5:50 PM EST, reached about $75.25 at 2:00 AM EST and is near $74.50, flat on the day. XRP fell to about $0.954 at 8:35 PM EST and is near $0.981, down about 1.4% over 24 hours. Zcash is near $950, up about 1.5%, and HYPE near $68.45, flat.

🖊️ Market significance: Ether outperformed Bitcoin overnight, while the two majors that led earlier this week, Solana and XRP, gave up the leadership.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Getting back above $1,800 matters, but $1,812 is still well below the $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped Ether since Sunday. I treat this as repair, not a breakout, until that band goes.

3⃣ The rebound was short covering, and funding flipped negative

Bitcoin perpetual open interest fell about 6% since last night's edition to about 37,560 BTC on the largest on-chain perps venue and about 3% to about 32,890 BTC on a large offshore exchange, while price rose about 2%. Funding on Bitcoin perpetuals turned slightly negative on both venues, from positive at yesterday's close. In the evening dip, six large traders on the on-chain venue were liquidated 30 times for a total of about 618 BTC, roughly $38.7 million, at prices between $62,055 and $63,364. Ether positioning is split, with open interest down about 2% on the on-chain venue and up about 4% offshore. Looking further out, a Swiss digital asset bank forecast that the Bitcoin futures carry trade will beat three-month Treasury bills by more than 2% a year in 2027 as demand for leverage returns.

🖊️ Market significance: Rising price with falling open interest and negative funding means shorts closed into the rally. Nobody added fresh long leverage to drive it.

🗨️ My viewpoint: That cuts both ways. A move built on covering can run out once the shorts are gone, but negative funding near the lows also tells me the crowd is leaning bearish, which is usually where squeezes start. I want to see open interest rise with price above $64,000 before I trust the move.

4⃣ ETFs lost another $306 million, and Binance now sells 24/7 IBIT exposure

US spot Bitcoin ETFs had net outflows of about $306 million on Wednesday, the second outflow day in a row. BlackRock's IBIT led with about $149 million out, followed by Fidelity's FBTC at about $69 million, Bitwise's BITB at about $37 million, Grayscale's GBTC at about $20 million, ARK's ARKB at about $19 million and Grayscale's mini trust at about $11 million. No fund took in money. That takes November's net outflows to about $2.9 billion. Spot Ether ETFs lost about $40 million, led by BlackRock's ETHA at about $17 million and Grayscale's mini trust at about $15 million. Separately, Binance listed on Wednesday a perpetual contract tied to IBIT, settled in USDT, with up to 20 times leverage and trading around the clock, including when Nasdaq is closed.

🖊️ Market significance: All five of the largest issuers sold on Wednesday, so this was broad de-risking, not one large holder rotating.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The custody transfers we saw on Wednesday morning pointed to exactly this print. The IBIT perpetual is a useful reminder that the ETF wrapper is now being traded offshore with leverage. I still need two or three inflow days in a row, led by IBIT, before I read the flows as turning.

5⃣ Anthropic priced at $83, and on-chain markets already trade it above $105

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share late Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range, and upsized it to 980 million shares, about 956 million from the company and about 24 million from existing holders. That raises about $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX's $75 billion in June, and values the company at about $1.5 trillion. It starts trading on Nasdaq today as ANT. The pre-IPO perpetual on the largest on-chain perps venue is near $105.50 and a similar contract offshore near $105.90, both up about 6.5% on the day and about 27% above the offer price. Kraken said Anthropic will be live on its platform from day one, and Solana's ecosystem account signalled day-one access on Solana, as tokenized equities on Solana passed $1.2 billion in circulating value, nearly double the October close. Polymarket opened a market on the size of the first-day pop.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto rails are now pricing the biggest listing in history around the clock before it opens, and the deal is setting the tone for the whole risk complex this morning.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The on-chain contracts have called the direction of most big debuts this year, so a 27% implied premium is a real signal. The risk for crypto is the other way round: a weak opening would hit the same AI trade that is lifting futures, and Bitcoin would feel it.

6⃣ Hong Kong put Hyperliquid on its suspicious platforms list

Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission added "Hyperliquid / Hyperliquid Hong Kong" to its alert list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms, naming the https://t.co/7mFtNrGwVp trading site. The regulator said the platform is not licensed in Hong Kong and is suspected of operating, or marketing, a virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public. The entry is a warning, not an enforcement action, a block or a finding of misconduct, and it sits alongside other unlicensed venues on the same list.

🖊️ Market significance: A regulator in a licensed market has now formally flagged the biggest on-chain perps venue, just as its pre-IPO markets draw global attention.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The direct impact is small, since HYPE barely moved, but it sets a precedent. On-chain venues that market to retail in licensed jurisdictions will get the same treatment as offshore exchanges, and I expect other Asian regulators to follow.

7⃣ Six senators asked Treasury not to tilt the GENIUS Act toward federal charters

A bipartisan group of six senators, including Cynthia Lummis, Kirsten Gillibrand, Angela Alsobrooks, Kevin Cramer, Pete Ricketts and Mark Warner, wrote to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning that Treasury's proposed GENIUS Act rules give a safe harbour to issuers with pending federal applications but no equivalent protection for state-supervised issuers. They said that could push firms toward a federal licence through the bank regulator, "the opposite of our intent", and asked Treasury to extend the safe harbour to issuers in states expected to have qualifying frameworks before 18 January 2028.

🖊️ Market significance: How the stablecoin law is implemented will decide whether the state path to issuance survives, which matters for every non-bank issuer.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the authors of the law correcting the regulator in public. I read it as a sign the final rules will be softened for state issuers, which keeps competition in issuance alive.

8⃣ A ratings agency kept USDT at its weakest score, and Tether hit back

S&P Global Ratings kept USDT at 5, or weak, the lowest score on its stablecoin stability scale, unchanged from a year ago. It said higher-risk assets, including gold, Bitcoin, listed equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, covered 28% of USDT in circulation at 30 September, up from 24% a year earlier, and that a sharp fall in those assets could leave the token undercollateralized. Gold holdings were about $19 billion, about 10% of circulation, and Bitcoin holdings fell to about $8.4 billion from $9.9 billion. Tether's September report showed about $191.5 billion of assets against $183.5 billion of liabilities, and the company said "the problem is S&P's framework, not our reserves", comparing the agency to its record before 2008.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest stablecoin is moving further into volatile assets just as gold fell about 3% in a day and Bitcoin trades near cycle lows.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The $8 billion cushion is real, but a 30% drop across its roughly $27 billion of gold and Bitcoin would erase about that much on paper. I do not see a peg risk today, I see a reason why the regulated dollar tokens keep winning institutional share.

9⃣ Court papers listed 192 tokens taken from Binance, and the thief moved another $248 million of Ether

An asset schedule filed with the Abu Dhabi court order shows the October attack on Binance wallets took 192 different tokens across 11 networks. USDT was the largest item at about $2.50 billion, followed by about $1.42 billion of Bitcoin and about $826 million of USDC, about 76% of the total between them. Fiat-backed stablecoins made up at least $3.46 billion, or about 55%, including nine smaller dollar and euro tokens, alongside about $58 million of tokenized gold and about $38 million of memecoins. Overnight, the hacker's wallets moved another 137,602 ETH, about $248 million, with batches of 12,000 ETH leaving between about 1:50 and 1:55 AM EST.

🖊️ Market significance: More than half the stolen value sits in tokens that issuers can freeze, which is why the court's worldwide order matters so much for recovery.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The stablecoin share is the hopeful part of this story. The Ether is the part I watch, because every batch that moves is potential supply hitting markets through laundering routes, and this is the latest in a run of large batches this week.

1⃣0⃣ Washington opened a scam-disruption centre, and BTCPay pushed an emergency patch

The Homeland Security Task Force launched a Threat Disruption Center, co-led by Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI, to bring more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners together to trace scam networks, warn victims sooner and stop payments, including crypto transfers, with a blockchain analytics firm as its main technology partner. Separately, BTCPay Server, the self-hosted Bitcoin payment software, issued an emergency update for five flaws in its Nginx web layer that the EU's cyber response team said could let attackers run code remotely without logging in. No attacks had been reported.

🖊️ Market significance: Federal enforcement is now formally wired into crypto rails for fraud, while merchant infrastructure had to patch a serious hole overnight.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Faster freezing is good for the industry's reputation and bad for the scam economy that still runs through stablecoins. Anyone running a BTCPay node should treat the patch as urgent.

1⃣1⃣ Singapore settled tokenized bills with central bank money, HSBC and PDAX brought tokens to savers

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it issued S$100 million, about $77.5 million, of four-week tokenized bills on 6 November, paid for with wholesale central bank digital currency, and five banks bid more than twice the amount on offer. It will turn the test network into a live settlement system, renamed SG Digital Ledger, and plans more tokenized bills in 2027. In Hong Kong, HSBC opened a tokenized class of its Hong Kong dollar money market fund to retail customers from HK$100, subscribed and settled only with its RedCoin stablecoin. In the Philippines, the exchange PDAX now lets users turn PYUSD, USDG and USDPT on Solana into balances that can buy government retail dollar bonds, a first for the country.

🖊️ Market significance: Central bank settlement, a global bank's retail fund and a sovereign bond sale all moved onto tokens in Asia in one night.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is where the real adoption is happening while prices struggle. Singapore turning a pilot into infrastructure is the strongest signal, because it gives tokenized assets a settlement asset with no credit risk.

1⃣2⃣ Kraken's parent is buying its co-CEO's venture firm

Payward, Kraken's parent, agreed to acquire Tribe Capital, the venture firm co-founded by Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi, with about $2.7 billion under management and stakes in private companies including SpaceX. Terms were not disclosed, and the deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: An exchange owner is buying a private-markets manager on the day the biggest private company in AI goes public.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The strategy is clear: own the pipeline of private assets that can later be tokenized and listed. The related-party angle will draw questions, and I want to see how the deal is valued before calling it a win.

1⃣3⃣ Large holders shifted coins overnight, and USDC supply kept shrinking

Two large holders unstaked about 2.31 million SOL, roughly $169 million, and deposited it with Coinbase Prime, flagged around 5:00 AM EST, often a step before selling or hedging. Four wallets withdrew about 13,408 ETH, roughly $24 million, from institutional trading desks and a large exchange late Wednesday evening, a sign of accumulation. Total stablecoin supply is near $286 billion, and USDC supply fell by about $600 million to $700 million since yesterday's close to about $68.2 billion to $68.5 billion, while USDT held near $175.1 billion.

🖊️ Market significance: Solana faces a large potential supply overhang today, and dollar balances on-chain are still draining even as prices recover.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The SOL deposit may help explain why Solana lagged the overnight bounce. The USDC decline matters more to me, because a lasting bottom usually needs stablecoin supply to stop falling first.

1⃣4⃣ The global securities watchdog warned quantum upgrades will slow blockchains

The International Organization of Securities Commissions published a report warning that moving blockchains to quantum-resistant signatures could slow transactions, raise fees and increase storage, because the new signatures are much larger. It cited a test version of Solana that ran about 90% slower with quantum-resistant signatures, said wallets that keep older keys could stay exposed after an upgrade, and urged firms to start preparing now because the transition could take years, even though no known quantum computer can break today's cryptography.

🖊️ Market significance: The quantum question has moved from developer forums into the rulebook of securities regulators, which will shape what institutions ask of the chains they use.

🗨️ My viewpoint: No near-term risk, but the trade-off is real. Chains that plan the migration early, with minimal throughput loss, will have an edge with regulated money.

Strategy's Michael Saylor and chief executive Phong Le hold an investor Q&A at 5:00 PM EST today, after STRC closed Wednesday near $96.11, about 4% below the $100 par it needs to keep selling new preferred stock. In Seoul, Parataxis Ethereum approved a KRW 1 billion share buyback of up to 632,911 shares over six months, while holding 11,729 ETH after its latest purchase of about 1,280 ETH.

🖊️ Market significance: Treasury companies are spending cash on their own paper rather than new coins, which removes a source of spot demand.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Tonight's call matters for the whole sector. I want to hear how Strategy plans to defend par without selling Bitcoin, because that answer sets the tone for every treasury firm trading below its coins.

On Wednesday the Dow lost about 1.1%, the S&P 500 slipped about 0.2% and the Nasdaq gained about 0.4%. Walmart reports before the open.

🖊️ Market significance: The bid is concentrated in tech and AI names, the same trade that sold off after Nvidia's leadership change and its post-earnings reversal.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Futures gave Bitcoin the lift overnight, so the cash open matters. If the Nasdaq holds most of this gap after 9:30 AM EST, Bitcoin has room to test $64,000; if the gap fades like Wednesday's Nvidia jump, I expect crypto to follow it down.

Brent is near $92.20 to $92.50 and WTI near $83.60 to $83.90, both modestly higher after Wednesday's inventory-led drop. Putin makes major Arctic announcement at APEC Summit
The Russian leader addressed business executives ahead of historic talks with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping
Published 18 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/o9jye5ZsV7
Russian President Vladimir Putin has pitched the country’s Arctic and Far East to Asia-Pacific investors, unveiling new incentives set to take effect in January 2027 and special rules for testing advanced technologies.
The package would offer eligible investors tax breaks on profits, property, and land, as well as reduced payroll contributions and preferential leases. Russia also plans to simplify rules for testing drones, industrial robots, and AI in both regions.
“I am confident that the business community and investors from APEC economies will fully appreciate the opportunities emerging in the Russian market – and, naturally, will take advantage of them,” Putin said in a speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in China on Wednesday.
Russia is modernizing its Trans-Siberian and Baikal-Amur railways, expanding the capacity of its Pacific ports, and developing infrastructure along its Northern Sea Route, he said.
Moscow has long promoted the Arctic as a region of international cooperation, including with Western countries.
Russia was a founding member of the Arctic Council in 1996, but joint work was largely suspended by the seven other member states following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Despite deteriorating relations, Putin has repeatedly expressed a willingness to cooperate with Washington on Arctic development. In October, he confirmed that Russia and the US were exploring joint projects in the region, including in energy and advanced technologies.
Meanwhile, the EU has increasingly shifted its focus toward militarization under its new Arctic strategy, which it adopted last month. “To defend our interests, we plan to step up investments in surveillance, infrastructure, military mobility, and capabilities,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
Britain has also moved to expand its naval presence in the Arctic and North Atlantic. Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak recently urged London to prepare for strikes against Russian military installations on the Kola Peninsula.
Moscow has repeatedly warned that NATO’s growing military activity risks turning the Arctic into another theater of confrontation.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused NATO in August of “driving the region towards militarization,” while reaffirming Moscow’s commitment to “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation.”
Russia’s economic initiatives have centered on developing the Northern Sea Route, an Arctic shipping corridor that has gained increased importance amid disruptions to Middle Eastern shipping routes caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Chinese and South Korean shipping companies have already sent container ships through the route in recent months. China’s Sea Legend launched a scheduled service in August, while South Korea’s PanStar completed its first trial voyage to Europe in September. India also plans to send its first pilot cargo vessel along the route in 2027.

text:
A warning to Europe: do not follow the Trump administration's line on appeasing Putin. A Trumpian peace is the worst option on offer, because it would settle Europe's security over Europe's head and on Russia's terms.
Washington has made a marked shift toward a European arrangement that appeases Putin, Trump's "friend". 

None of this is new. Trump deals with great powers personally and treats institutions and values as obstacles. In that view Ukraine is one item in a concert of major powers. It is not a defence of territorial integrity or of alliance norms.

Tying Ukraine to Europe's security architecture changes the frame, and the change serves Moscow. Russia has wanted a say over Europe's security order for decades. Europe wants a ceasefire first and now finds its own security on the table.

The clock matters. Democrats take both chambers in January, so the administration has weeks to show progress and shape a legacy. Congress will not run foreign policy. The president keeps that, and his veto holds. But a new Congress brings harder realities for this White House: hearings, investigations, and a fight over every dollar.

text:
@implausibleblog THE EMPEROR, TWO DICTATORS AND THE KEYS TO FORT KNOX
Imagine showing Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping around Fort Knox, the Pentagon, Silicon Valley… handing them the keys, and assuring them that anything they fancy is negotiable provided they say A FEW BIG NICE WORDS about the proprietor.
That is the nightmare we find ourselves, at the heart of Trump's brand of diplomacy.
Far from stupid themselves, both Putin and Xi shrewdly command immense authoritarian states with formidable intelligence services, military establishments and well known long-term strategic ambitions. Their objectives extend decades into the Post Trumpian future. Unlike the Don, but equally ruthless, both men understand the value of precise thinking, playing games at which they excel, patience, leverage, exploiting divisions and the comical current weaknesses of their adversaries.
And right now the American presidency offers them the spectacle of a leader who repeatedly personalises international relations, prizes public displays of fawning and treats alliances and security guarantees as negotiable transactions. He would sell his own grandmother for a lease on a prime golf course.
What must Russia and China make of it? We cannot read their minds. But neither needs to be a genius strategist to recognise the golden opportunities offered by Trump’s dying presidency to reset the international world order in their favour.
Ukraine's sovereignty, Taiwan's security, Europe's shaky defences, the stability of international law: these should not be properties in a Trump hotel portfolio. They cannot legitimately be traded for a handshake, a flattering photograph or the promise of some magnificent commercial arrangement.
B UT where are the guardians of the American Constitution? The bastions of Western Democracy?
The Founders constructed a republic expressly to prevent the concentration of arbitrary power in one dangerous man's hands. Yet Congress has repeatedly struggled to exercise effective restraint over the presidency. The machinery of constitutional accountability has too often appeared paralysed by personal interest, partisan calculation, individual ambition and fear of political retaliation. By a failure of moral backbone.
What a grotesque historical irony! A republic founded in rebellion against swaggering monarchy finds itself struggling to control the personal diplomacy of its elected showman.
The danger extends far beyond Washington. When the world's most powerful democracy makes its commitments unpredictable, brutal authoritarian governments gain opportunities to test boundaries, smaller nations become vulnerable, and the institutions painstakingly constructed to prevent another catastrophic international conflict are weakened.
Nor can the climate crisis be treated as an optional extra in a world already confronting the consequences of global warming. The planet cannot afford great-power politics conducted without sustained international cooperation.
Western leaders must recognise the difference between respecting the American presidency and spinelessly acquiescing in every decision of its eccentric occupant.
The presidency is not a throne. The American Constitution is not a decorative antique. NATO is not a protection racket. Ukraine and Taiwan are not bargaining chips. And the future of democratic civilisation is not Donald Trump's personal property.
The question is no longer whether Trump can produce another spectacular diplomatic performance.
It is whether democratic institutions can ensure that the decisions emerging from such performances remain subject to law, scrutiny and accountability.
The keys to Fort Knox belong to the republic. Not to the man child who happens to have filched them.

While the press is concentrating on Trump's nap during APEC - "Next Draft" reveals a more disturbing truth:

"We’ve been hacked. I’m not talking about the Microsoft downtime, the air travel grounding, the bank inaccessibility, the Apple outage, or the fact that, for about 45 minutes this morning, my NextDraft pun generator wasn’t working. The more we learn, the more it looks like those software snafus were likely due to attempted upgrades, ill-advised patches, and endeavors aimed at AI-enabling communication systems that were originally built with two cans and a long string. But while it looks like our computers weren’t hacked, the last week made it plainly clear that we have been. We didn’t know what was going on during these tech failures, and when we were given a series of explanations by the hack jobs in the administration, we didn’t believe them. And why would we? They lie as a matter of policy. They lie every time they speak. The truth has systematically been twisted into a pile of misinformation more tangled than the box of old plugs, cables, and cords you never got around to throwing out. As George W Bush famously explained: “Fool me once, shame on — shame on you. Fool me — you can’t get fooled again.” In an age defined by isolation and loneliness, Billy Joel may have prophesied the loneliest thing of all when he sang: Honesty is such a lonely word. So, when you hear the administration-offered statements like Marco Rubio’s proclamation that “there’s ‘zero’ information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor,” you’re right to have zero certainty they’re telling the truth. You’re getting that explanation from a malign actor. You don’t trust them because they’ve spent years intentionally hacking your trust to smithereens. We have been trust-falled into the deepest bowels of hell. At this point, even Charlie Brown wouldn’t try to kick a football held by anyone in this administration. And that’s why I’m trying to explain that the biggest hack of this era is that we’re all worried our government is lying to us about the causes of the outages. Trust is glitching. Trust has been hijacked. Our democracy’s terms of service have been rewritten, and our citizenry is no longer willing to blindly click to agree. I’d suggest that when it comes to matters of IT, you’d be better off getting explanations from tech companies than from the administration, but we don’t trust tech companies either."

text:
As long as there has been AI, there have been people sounding alarms about what it might do to us: rogue superintelligence, mass unemployment, or environmental ruin from data center sprawl. But this week showed that another threat entirely—that of kids forming unhealthy bonds with AI—is the one pulling AI safety out of the academic fringe and into regulators’ crosshairs.

This has been bubbling for a while. Two high-profile lawsuits filed in the last year, against https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq and OpenAI, allege that companion-like behavior in their models contributed to the suicides of two teenagers. A study by US nonprofit Common Sense Media, published in July, found that 72% of teenagers have used AI for companionship. Stories in reputable outlets about “AI psychosis” have highlighted how endless conversations with chatbots can lead people down delusional spirals.

It’s hard to overstate the impact of these stories. To the public, they are proof that AI is not merely imperfect, but a technology that’s more harmful than helpful. If you doubted that this outrage would be taken seriously by regulators and companies, three things happened this week that might change your mind.

A California law passes the legislature

On Thursday, the California state legislature passed a first-of-its-kind bill. It would require AI companies to include reminders for users they know to be minors that responses are AI generated. Companies would also need to have a protocol for addressing suicide and self-harm and provide annual reports on instances of suicidal ideation in users’ conversations with their chatbots. It was led by Democratic state senator Steve Padilla, passed with heavy bipartisan support, and now awaits Governor Gavin Newsom’s signature. 

There are reasons to be skeptical of the bill’s impact. It doesn’t specify efforts companies should take to identify which users are minors, and lots of AI companies already include referrals to crisis providers when someone is talking about suicide. (In the case of Adam Raine, one of the teenagers whose survivors are suing, his conversations with ChatGPT before his death included this type of information, but the chatbot allegedly went on to give advice related to suicide anyway.)

Still, it is undoubtedly the most significant of the efforts to rein in companion-like behaviors in AI models, which are in the works in other states too. If the bill becomes law, it would strike a blow to the position OpenAI has taken, which is that “America leads best with clear, nationwide rules, not a patchwork of state or local regulations,” as the company’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote on LinkedIn last week.

The Federal Trade Commission takes aim

The very same day, the Federal Trade Commission announced an inquiry into seven companies, seeking information about how they develop companion-like characters, monetize engagement, measure and test the impact of their chatbots, and more. The companies are Google, Instagram, Meta, OpenAI, Snap, X, and Character Technologies, the maker of https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq.

The White House now wields immense, and potentially illegal, political influence over the agency. In March, President Trump fired its lone Democratic commissioner, Rebecca Slaughter. In July, a federal judge ruled that firing illegal, but last week the US Supreme Court temporarily permitted the firing.

“Protecting kids online is a top priority for the Trump-Vance FTC, and so is fostering innovation in critical sectors of our economy,” said FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson in a press release about the inquiry. 

Right now, it’s just that—an inquiry—but the process might (depending on how public the FTC makes its findings) reveal the inner workings of how the companies build their AI companions to keep users coming back again and again. 

Sam Altman on suicide cases

Also on the same day (a busy day for AI news), Tucker Carlson published an hour-long interview with OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman. It covers a lot of ground—Altman’s battle with Elon Musk, OpenAI’s military customers, conspiracy theories about the death of a former employee—but it also includes the most candid comments Altman’s made so far about the cases of suicide following conversations with AI. 

Altman talked about “the tension between user freedom and privacy and protecting vulnerable users” in cases like these. But then he offered up something I hadn’t heard before.

“I think it’d be very reasonable for us to say that in cases of young people talking about suicide seriously, where we cannot get in touch with parents, we do call the authorities,” he said. “That would be a change.”

So where does all this go next? For now, it’s clear that—at least in the case of children harmed by AI companionship—companies’ familiar playbook won’t hold. They can no longer deflect responsibility by leaning on privacy, personalization, or “user choice.” Pressure to take a harder line is mounting from state laws, regulators, and an outraged public.

But what will that look like? Politically, the left and right are now paying attention to AI’s harm to children, but their solutions differ. On the right, the proposed solution aligns with the wave of internet age-verification laws that have now been passed in over 20 states. These are meant to shield kids from adult content while defending “family values.” On the left, it’s the revival of stalled ambitions to hold Big Tech accountable through antitrust and consumer-protection powers. 

Consensus on the problem is easier than agreement on the cure. As it stands, it looks likely we’ll end up with exactly the patchwork of state and local regulations that OpenAI (and plenty of others) have lobbied against. 

For now, it’s down to companies to decide where to draw the lines. They’re having to decide things like: Should chatbots cut off conversations when users spiral toward self-harm, or would that leave some people worse off? Should they be licensed and regulated like therapists, or treated as entertainment products with warnings? The uncertainty stems from a basic contradiction: Companies have built chatbots to act like caring humans, but they’ve postponed developing the standards and accountability we demand of real caregivers. The clock is now running out.

text:
WHY HAS BITCOIN BEEN WEAK? 

I want to outline five factors that are contributing to $BTC’s weakness and, above all, why we cannot yet consider a low to be confirmed.

The market never necessarily falls for a single reason. It is often a combination of liquidity, macroeconomic conditions and investor behaviour.

1. CHAIN REACTION LIQUIDATIONS AND LEVERAGE

Let’s start with what I consider fundamental in the short term: liquidity.

When BTC breaks below key levels, thousands of over-leveraged long positions are at risk of being liquidated.

Forced liquidations generate further selling pressure, driving the price down and triggering further liquidations.

It’s a domino effect.

This explains why we often see sudden, violent price movements, even in the absence of any specific news.

2. OUTFLOWS FROM SPOT BITCOIN ETFs

Over the last two weeks under review, US spot ETFs have recorded net outflows of approximately $2.35 billion.

This means that redemptions have exceeded new investments.

When institutional demand via ETFs declines, an important component of price support is lost.

And if redemptions require the sale of BTC, downward pressure may increase.

However, it is important to note that these flows are not permanent. They can change rapidly and return to supporting the market.

3. GLOBAL LIQUIDITY, REAL INTEREST RATES AND THE DOLLAR

This is a factor that many underestimate.

When US real interest rates remain high, investors can achieve attractive returns even through less risky instruments.

Consequently, the incentive to take on exposure to volatile assets diminishes.

Furthermore, a strong dollar tends to make global financial conditions more restrictive.

Bitcoin is extremely sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk appetite.

It is therefore not enough to simply look at the BTC chart to understand the broader context.

4. WEAKNESS IN THE TECH SECTOR AND STABLECOINS

Bitcoin continues to behave, in many respects, as a risk-sensitive asset.

When investors reduce their exposure to the technology sector, interest in the crypto market often wanes as well.

But we must also look at stablecoins.

Stablecoins represent a key part of the liquidity available on exchanges.

If capital is withdrawn from the system or remains idle, the effective demand capable of absorbing sell-offs decreases.

And without sufficient buyers, even relatively modest selling pressure can trigger significant price movements.

5. STRATEGY AND PRESSURE ON THE INSTITUTIONAL MARKET

Strategy is one of the listed companies with the greatest exposure to Bitcoin.

When BTC falls, the value of its reserves decreases and investors’ concerns about its financial exposure increase.

Added to this is the uncertainty surrounding the company’s possible exclusion from certain MSCI indices.

Such an exclusion could force certain index funds to sell their Strategy shares.

This does not mean that the company would automatically have to sell its Bitcoin, but it could increase financial pressure and negative sentiment surrounding the sector.

But explaining a downtrend does not mean knowing when it will end.

A slowdown in outflows, a reduction in liquidations and an improvement in liquidity could help bring about stabilisation.

But the price must confirm this.

As I have been saying for days, a bottom may take time, a long accumulation phase or a final capitulation before a recovery.

As for my trading, I’m continuing to monitor the 60–62K area on the H4 chart, looking exclusively for liquidity dips, level retracements and triggers with clear invalidations.

For spot investments, the reasoning is different: sharp corrections can offer opportunities for gradual accumulation, whilst accepting the possibility of further declines.

I hope you find this useful

text:
@POTUS in Shenzhen today: "As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth." President Xi answered that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. @KremlinRussia_E @MFA_China

Nobody at that table speaks for the one dyad where two nuclear-armed neighbours actually fought last year.

Big-three arms control has a basement. South Asia lives in it, and Pakistan's security dilemma is shaped there too.

The numbers: @SIPRIorg Yearbook 2026 puts China at ~620 warheads (the Pentagon expects 1,000+ by 2030, per @BelferCenter), Bharat ~190, Pakistan ~170. And SIPRI's read of Bharat: its longer-range systems "appear to be focused on China, but its planning still remains heavily influenced by its long-standing rivalry with Pakistan."

Translation: every Chinese warhead Washington counts becomes a Bharati alibi, and the alibi's weapons sit on Pakistan's border.

Three tests for whatever comes out of Shenzhen:

1st: Equality. Beijing wants "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity." Belfer's Hui Zhang goes further: "No agreement should legalize any party's strategic inferiority." Good principles. Pakistan has heard "equality" before, from regimes that then carved out exceptions for Bharat. A rule that protects Beijing must hold one floor down.

2nd: Declaratory honesty. China's no-first-use is unconditional. Bharat says it has "strictly adhered" to NFU, yet its 2003 doctrine keeps a nuclear option against "biological or chemical weapons", and its Defence Minister added: "What happens in future depends on the circumstances." Pair that with dual-capable or deliberately ambiguous BrahMos and Pralay, and NFU becomes a posture with an expiry clause, riding on missiles whose payload no one across the border can know in flight. Pakistan's Army Rocket Force is conventional. That asymmetry is the stability problem.

3rd: The paradox. @CarnegieEndow's Tong Zhao warns in @WarOnTheRocks that greater stability among the big three "could embolden aggression at lower levels of violence". South Asia does not need the warning. May 2025 was the experiment, and the belief that war can be started low, kept low and stopped on command is the real danger.

Stability bought at the top and exported downward as risk is not arms control. It is outsourcing. Restraint, like deterrence, has to be mutual. Pakistan's Strategic Restraint Regime offer is still on the table. New Delhi has yet to come to it.

text:
@lizziecundy THE EMPEROR, TWO DICTATORS AND THE KEYS TO FORT KNOX
Imagine showing Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping around Fort Knox, the Pentagon, Silicon Valley… handing them the keys, and assuring them that anything they fancy is negotiable provided they say A FEW BIG NICE WORDS about the proprietor.
That is the nightmare we find ourselves, at the heart of Trump's brand of diplomacy.
Far from stupid themselves, both Putin and Xi shrewdly command immense authoritarian states with formidable intelligence services, military establishments and well known long-term strategic ambitions. Their objectives extend decades into the Post Trumpian future. Unlike the Don, but equally ruthless, both men understand the value of precise thinking, playing games at which they excel, patience, leverage, exploiting divisions and the comical current weaknesses of their adversaries.
And right now the American presidency offers them the spectacle of a leader who repeatedly personalises international relations, prizes public displays of fawning and treats alliances and security guarantees as negotiable transactions. He would sell his own grandmother for a lease on a prime golf course.
What must Russia and China make of it? We cannot read their minds. But neither needs to be a genius strategist to recognise the golden opportunities offered by Trump’s dying presidency to reset the international world order in their favour.
Ukraine's sovereignty, Taiwan's security, Europe's shaky defences, the stability of international law: these should not be properties in a Trump hotel portfolio. They cannot legitimately be traded for a handshake, a flattering photograph or the promise of some magnificent commercial arrangement.
B UT where are the guardians of the American Constitution? The bastions of Western Democracy?
The Founders constructed a republic expressly to prevent the concentration of arbitrary power in one dangerous man's hands. Yet Congress has repeatedly struggled to exercise effective restraint over the presidency. The machinery of constitutional accountability has too often appeared paralysed by personal interest, partisan calculation, individual ambition and fear of political retaliation. By a failure of moral backbone.
What a grotesque historical irony! A republic founded in rebellion against swaggering monarchy finds itself struggling to control the personal diplomacy of its elected showman.
The danger extends far beyond Washington. When the world's most powerful democracy makes its commitments unpredictable, brutal authoritarian governments gain opportunities to test boundaries, smaller nations become vulnerable, and the institutions painstakingly constructed to prevent another catastrophic international conflict are weakened.
Nor can the climate crisis be treated as an optional extra in a world already confronting the consequences of global warming. The planet cannot afford great-power politics conducted without sustained international cooperation.
Western leaders must recognise the difference between respecting the American presidency and spinelessly acquiescing in every decision of its eccentric occupant.
The presidency is not a throne. The American Constitution is not a decorative antique. NATO is not a protection racket. Ukraine and Taiwan are not bargaining chips. And the future of democratic civilisation is not Donald Trump's personal property.
The question is no longer whether Trump can produce another spectacular diplomatic performance.
It is whether democratic institutions can ensure that the decisions emerging from such performances remain subject to law, scrutiny and accountability.
The keys to Fort Knox belong to the republic. Not to the man child who happens to have filched them.
