text:
On 18 May 2010 a Florida programmer named Laszlo Hanyecz posted an offer on a bitcoin forum: 10,000 bitcoin to anyone who would get two pizzas delivered to his house.

For four days nobody took it. One forum member pointed out that he could sell the coins for $41 in cash, which tells you how seriously people took the money back then.

On 22 May a 19 year old named Jeremy Sturdivant accepted, ordered two pies from Papa John’s and collected the coins. It is remembered as the first time bitcoin bought a real thing.

People retell this as the most expensive meal in history, and they miss what happened that afternoon. Somebody had to spend bitcoin before it could be called money, and he volunteered.

He also never stopped. In 2018 he bought pizza again, this time over the Lightning Network, and it cost him 0.00649 BTC.

Holding made bitcoin valuable, and it took a man spending it to make it money.

There was a time German Television was allowed to speak and think. 
Here is the transcript by Grok: “English transcript of the Monitor report from 21 August 2014:
No, this is not just a war within Ukraine.
It is a conflict between East and West, a struggle for supremacy in Eastern Europe, with NATO support.
What does the Western alliance hope to achieve with this?
What strategy is it pursuing?
A report from the NATO Defense College from the previous month already makes clear where things are headed.
It proposes stronger airspace surveillance, intensified military exercises, the build-up of military infrastructure in Central Europe,
and the stationing of a US combat brigade.
It is the old game of the great powers; NATO now sees itself as the one to move.
Example: expansion.
Since the end of the Soviet Union, NATO has continued to expand further east.
Twelve former Eastern Bloc states have now joined the Western alliance.
And now even five more countries are under discussion for NATO membership:
Sweden, Finland, Montenegro, Macedonia, and Georgia.
This would bring NATO even closer to Russia’s borders.
Robert Legvold is one of America’s most renowned political analysts.
George Bush thanked him for his advice, as did the later US President Bill Clinton.
Legvold believes it is wrong to keep pushing Russia further into a corner.
Russian rearmament?
According to SIPRI, Russia spent $88 billion on the military last year; France, Germany, and England spent $168 billion, and the USA even $640 billion.
These four NATO countries alone had nine times the military expenditure of Russia last year.
From the perspective of NATO leadership, that is still not enough.
But what role does Ukraine play in the West’s strategic planning?
Already in the 1990s, this man defined how the West should deal with Russia and Ukraine: Zbigniew Brzezinski, former advisor to Jimmy Carter
and later to Ronald Reagan, the éminence grise of US security policy.
In 1997 he wrote:
“Ukraine, a new and important space on the Eurasian chessboard, is a geopolitical pivot point.”
“However, if Moscow were to regain control over Ukraine, Russia would automatically acquire the means to become a powerful empire spanning Europe and Asia.”
Old strategic plans, now in a new guise.
The July report from the NATO Defense College is about a stability partnership with Ukraine, to enable Kyiv to move toward the West,
even if that would provoke a strong Russian response.
Rearmament, expansion, confrontation.
For Maria Huber, Eastern Europe expert, a clear sign that the hardliners in the NATO alliance, the so-called hawks, have prevailed.
NATO continues to train for a ground war in Europe.
The enemy once again seems to stand where some in NATO have always seen him.
NATO is an institution that has been searching for a new enemy image for over 25 years.
Now Russia practically offers itself automatically, and of course for someone who thinks from the philosophy and from the interest of the institution, this is a virtually ideal opportunity
to push through all the things that cannot be implemented in more normal, quieter times.
Once one has started to view each other as enemies, once this thinking becomes entrenched and determines foreign policy, then it also means
that this will come back to haunt all sides—the West and Russia—in the coming months and years regarding the crisis in Central Europe.”

text:
UPDATE:  Six Flags Over Georgia Roller Coaster Tragedy: Medical Examiner Reveals Cause of Death.

Key takeaways.
• Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old educator, was ejected from a roller coaster and died at Six Flags in Austell, Ga., on Oct. 12
• The Cobb County Medical Examiner’s Office determined that he died from blunt force injuries he sustained to numerous parts of his body after he was ejected
• His death, which is still under investigation by police, has been ruled an accident.

Hassan Kariem, 42, died from blunt force injuries after he was ejected from Goliath and fell onto a roof. The medical examiner ruled his death an accident.

AUSTELL, Ga. — The Cobb County medical examiner released an autopsy report Wednesday afternoon on thedeadly roller coaster fall at Six Flags Over Georgia.

The report says 42-year-old Hassan Kariem died from blunt force injuries after he was ejected from the Goliath roller coasteron Oct. 12 and landed on a roof of a building inside the park. 

The medical examiner ruled his death an accident.

Dr. Natasha Grandhi performed the autopsy the day after the fall and documented extensive injuries to Kariem’s head, neck, torso, arms and legs. 

How he came out of his seat remains an open question.

More than a month after the Oct. 12 fall, Cobb County Police and state safety officials are still investigating how Kariem was ejected from Goliath. 

One question is whether the ride’s restraint was fully locked. 
The autopsy report lists Kariem’s height at 5'9" and his weight at 301 pounds and offers no findings about the restraint. Engineers from the Georgia Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire went to the park as part of the state’s investigation. 

Goliath remains closed, and Six Flags plans to add seat belts to the ride.

Kariem lived in Atlanta and had a 10-year-old daughter. He survived cancer twice and spent more than a decade at Wesley International Academy, where he managed the school’s technology, taught students and coached robotics.

May his memory be a blessing.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Senator Bernie Sanders: Iran Wasn't Trump's Idea. Someone Else Pushed Him Into It!

Overview
Bernie Sanders frames the coming midterms as a referendum on whether the United States remains a democracy or yields to an authoritarian president he describes as a pathological liar, corrupt, and a narcissist. The deeper argument is structural: a legal system of unlimited money lets wealthy donors shape both parties, so working people lose faith in democracy while the far right offers scapegoats. His remedy is a grassroots political revolution built on universal benefits, Medicare for All, a wealth tax on billionaires, a higher minimum wage, and guardrails on advanced AI, paired with an honest admission that democracy must visibly improve daily life or it will keep losing legitimacy.

Key Themes
- The midterms are a democracy-or-authoritarianism choice, not a normal partisan contest, given Sanders' assessment of Trump's character and the Republican Party's transformation.
- Campaign finance is the root corruption: unlimited contributions and lobbying are legal while direct bribery is illegal, so wealthy donors and industry interests shape both parties.
- Economic hardship persists in the richest country in history, and younger generations may end up with a lower standard of living than their parents despite technological progress.
- Restoring faith in democracy requires delivering tangible universal benefits, especially guaranteed healthcare, rather than incremental tinkering around the edges.
- A 5% annual wealth tax on roughly 2,000 billionaires, raising about $400 billion a year, is the centerpiece of a transfer from the top to working families.
- AI and robotics are the most transformative technologies in history, carrying serious risks to jobs, privacy, relationships, and warfare, and warrant a pause and binding international rules.
- Media and political bias is structural: wealthy owners and advertisers shape which issues get discussed, which is why podcasts and the internet open space corporate media avoids.
- Sanders roots his politics in family history, including relatives killed by Hitler, and in a working-class upbringing where money stress was constant.

Detailed Summary
Sanders treats the midterms as a referendum on democracy itself. He calls Trump a pathological liar, corrupt, and a narcissist, and says he does not hate Trump but detests the racism and divisiveness. He cites Trump's rhetoric against Abdullah Sayed in Michigan, including calling a medical doctor a terrorist, as an example of the climate he condemns. He describes the Republican Party as once center-right and big-money-dominated, now a right-wing extremist party with elements of white nationalism and a cult of loyalty to Trump.

The core problem, in his telling, is a corrupt campaign finance system on both sides. Unlimited money is legal while direct bribery is illegal, so wealthy donors control both parties. He points to super PAC contributions of $100 million or $400 million, including Elon Musk putting over $400 million into a campaign, as legal but outrageous. Industry lobbyists sometimes offer to help with re-election and even write legislative provisions for members of Congress. He notes drug companies reportedly have over 1,500 lobbyists in Washington for 535 members of Congress, roughly three per member.

Despite the U.S. being the richest country in history, he cites widespread hardship: 60 percent of Americans live paycheck to paycheck, 60,000 people die a year because they cannot afford a doctor, the highest childhood poverty rate, higher than the UK, and 20 percent of seniors living on $15,000 a year or less. He warns younger generations may face a lower standard of living than their parents. His father was a paint salesman and sole earner in a rent-controlled Brooklyn apartment, yet today two earners are often needed where one once sufficed, despite computers and AI.

His answer is Medicare for All. He describes a four-year transition: the first year lowers the Medicare age from 65 to 55, includes all children, and expands coverage to dental, hearing, and vision, then lowers to 45, then 35, then everyone. He says the U.S. spends twice as much per capita on healthcare as any other nation yet has 90 million uninsured or underinsured and about half a million people going bankrupt annually. He describes the plan as closer to the Canadian model than the British NHS and says polls show Americans want it. His mother received good, free care during a serious heart problem and died a few days after the operation, an experience he ties to his view that healthcare is a human right.

He proposes a 5% annual tax on the wealth of roughly 2,000 billionaires, raising about $400 billion a year, or $4 trillion over 10 years. He says many billionaires pay an effective real tax rate lower than a truck driver or a nurse, and cites Bezos reportedly having a salary of $80,000 a year. The interviewer raises a startup founder whose company was valued at $10 billion and who holds most value in equity, meaning a 5% wealth tax could mean $500 million a year despite a modest salary, and describes wealthy people taking tax-free loans against equity and paying no tax. Sanders acknowledges details matter but argues the wealthy are not paying their fair share. He criticizes billionaires who threatened to leave California over a proposed one-time wealth tax, calling it arrogance from a ruling class, and says billionaires spent over $300 million to defeat a California measure.

He lists uses for the revenue: wiping out childhood poverty, universal free child care, a $3,000 stipend in the first year to working-class individuals under $150,000, tuition-free public colleges and universities, and 7 million units of low-income and affordable housing. He cites a RAND Corporation estimate of an $80 million transfer of wealth from the bottom 90 percent to the top 1 percent over 50 years, captured as stated, and says inequality is worse today than in the Gilded Age of Rockefeller and J.P. Morgan. He also proposes raising the minimum wage to at least $20 an hour from $7.25, and shifting federal priorities away from military spending, which he says exceeds $1 trillion a year, toward social needs. He calls for ending military aid to Israel and the war in Iran.

He explains Trump's support partly as a global phenomenon: working people have not benefited from technological progress and are anxious about the future, including AI's impact on their children's jobs and home ownership. The far-right narrative blaming undocumented people gains traction across the Western world because mainstream governments and parties failed to deliver, eroding faith in democracy. He distinguishes most Trump voters from racists and haters: most are struggling, cannot make ends meet, and worry about their kids and AI. He says the Democratic Party failed to speak to these people, who looked at Democrats, felt failed, and went to Trump. Within the Democratic Party, he frames the struggle as status-quo incremental politics versus confronting big-money interests, noting European social democratic and Labor parties are in bad shape.

He distinguishes his grassroots political revolution, a bottom-up party of ordinary people running and winning, from a Democratic establishment he says only wants to tinker around the edges. He had virtually zero support from establishment mayors or governors and only one senator, Jeff Merkley, when he ran. He says he does not think reporters are liars; the problem is ownership and advertisers, since a reporter writing about billionaires paying fair taxes while the boss is a billionaire, or criticizing drug and insurance companies that advertise, faces pressure. He asks how often major networks run programs on why the healthcare system is broken, and cites a CBS segment on Musk owning more wealth than the bottom 53 percent of Americans.

On AI, he frames it as the most transformative technology in history, with risks to jobs, privacy, human relationships, warfare, and control over humanity. He cites Anthropic CEOs warning about many millions of jobs disappearing, Bezos assembling a $100 billion fund to automate factories, 18-wheelers driving without drivers in Texas, and 67 million transportation jobs. He wants a ban on developing superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI until sufficient guardrails exist, arguing it should not be treated as a partisan or China-related issue. He cites Geoffrey Hinton's warning that AI may become smarter than humans and humans may not be able to control it. He argues every call, text, email, and website visit could be known, and worries about children spending significant time with bot companions and young people struggling to talk on the telephone.

He proposes government ownership of 50 percent of big AI companies so public representatives sit on half of boards of trustees, preventing Musk, Bezos, and others from unilaterally making decisions affecting millions. He acknowledges slowing AI is hard because China, Russia, North Korea, the UK, and Europe may not slow down, and compares falling behind to missing out on the internet. His answer is a binding international agreement with an enforcement mechanism, comparing it to Reagan and Gorbachev negotiating a nuclear agreement despite ideological differences. He challenges the motivations of tech leaders, naming Musk, Bezos, Ellison, and Sam Walton, and argues their goal is more wealth and power rather than primarily benefiting humanity. He distinguishes respect for Musk as a hardworking, smart, demanding businessman from opposition to his political role: Musk owns X, is enormously influential in robotics and AI, pours huge amounts into American elections and right-wing parties around the world, and some of what he puts out is absolutely racist and unacceptable. He says Musk once seemed concerned about climate change and a leading voice in electric vehicles, and is not sure what happened.

He points to Scandinavian countries as the best-performing models for eliminating poverty, providing free education and healthcare, reducing inequality, and being more democratic with a small D. He frames a trade-off with the US model's higher median disposable income, lower taxes, higher GDP, higher ceilings for top earners, and fewer regulatory hurdles, and argues most ordinary people care more about quality of life and social safety nets. He challenges GDP growth as a measure, saying a person working 50 hours a week to feed a family is not worried about GDP. He wants the country to focus on issues rather than beauty contests, pressing candidates on healthcare and AI so leadership emerges from substance, and resists making politics about personality.

On governing, he says Democrats could pass Medicare for All, raise the minimum wage to $20 an hour, impose strong AI guardrails, and transform the energy system, but explains constitutional limits: presidential veto power and the need for two-thirds of both chambers to override. He argues Trump is not stupid and is a good politician with no ideology who cares about his own well-being and popularity, so a veto of enormously popular healthcare legislation could be politically costly. He is not certain Trump would reject strong popular legislation and suggests he might negotiate or sign something.

He says he probably will not run for president again, citing the prospect of taking office at 87 and finishing a first term at 91. He would support a candidate who stands with the working class, has courage to take on oligarchs, and fights for working families rather than tinkering around the edges; the socialist label does not matter to him. He praises Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as smart and thoughtful and notes she writes her own speeches, while stressing she is not the only strong candidate and resisting a beauty contest. He names Ro Khanna, Abdul El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Greg Casar, and Pramila Jayapal among other possible leaders.

On foreign policy, he claims the Vietnam War, Iraq War, and war in Iran were based on lies. He says the Iranian government was not prepared to attack the United States, argues Netanyahu has for 40 years tried to get U.S. presidents to go to war against or destabilize Iran, and that Israel pushed the war on Trump. He describes Iran as an authoritarian society that has committed terrorist acts while still rejecting the premise of the war. He says the American people want an end to the war and that he wants an end to it.

His politics are rooted in two experiences: being Jewish and learning that his father's family was wiped out by Hitler, with six million killed for being Jewish, and growing up working class seeing the stress of lack of money. He visited Poland about 15 years ago with his brother, saw the house where family lived before the Jews of the town were killed by Nazis, and was shown a site where hundreds were killed and dumped into a mound. He recalls a middle-of-the-night phone call from Europe revealing one of his father's cousins had survived in a displaced persons camp. He cites Rosa Luxembourg's idea of socialism or barbarism as framing the struggle to bring out the better parts of humanity and says he wants to be remembered as a decent, honest human being who tried to make the world a little better. He also recounts being arrested by police and spending a night in jail as a University of Chicago student, and says his generation experienced the Vietnam War, which he says was based on a lie.

text:
“I am losing precious days. I am degenerating into a machine for making money. I am learning nothing in this trivial world of men. I must break away and get out into the mountains to learn the news.”

- John Muir

During the 1880s, John Muir reportedly struggled with the demands of managing a commercial fruit ranch in California, feeling increasingly trapped by the repetitive responsibilities of business and everyday life. He worried that pursuing financial success at the expense of personal fulfillment would gradually diminish his curiosity, creativity, and connection to the natural world.

Muir believed that nature offered something society often could not: clarity, wisdom, and spiritual renewal. By contrasting the distractions of modern life with the peace and beauty of the wilderness, he emphasized that spending time outdoors was not merely an escape, but an essential part of intellectual growth, inner freedom, and a meaningful existence.

Sports Promoters: Brands

Sports promoters are critical in bridging brands like Nike, Adidas, Red Bull, and emerging players like YouTube with sports ecosystems. They craft partnerships that resonate with fans, leveraging events, athletes, and digital platforms to drive engagement and revenue. For brands seeking to enter or expand in sports, working with agencies like Octagon, SPORTFIVE, or rEvolution ensures strategic alignment and impactful campaigns.

Sports promoters are key players in connecting brands with sports events, athletes, and fans to create mutually beneficial partnerships. They facilitate sponsorships, endorsements, and marketing campaigns that amplify brand visibility while enhancing the sports experience. Below is an overview of notable brands involved in sports promotion, based on their prominence in the industry and partnerships, as well as the role of sports promoters in these collaborations.

Key Brands in Sports Promotion

Sports promoters often work with global brands across various industries, leveraging the emotional and cultural appeal of sports to drive engagement. Some prominent brands include:

Nike: A leader in sports marketing, Nike partners with athletes and teams worldwide, using campaigns like #BetterForIt to promote inclusivity and fitness through influencer and athlete endorsements.

Example: Nike’s campaigns often feature athletes as brand ambassadors, such as their work with social media influencers and everyday athletes to motivate active lifestyles. Adidas: Known for high-profile collaborations with teams, athletes, and designers, adidas merges sports and lifestyle through partnerships like those with Ivy Park, Bad Bunny, and Gucci.

Promoters facilitate these deals, ensuring alignment with events like soccer tournaments or fashion-driven campaigns. Red Bull: Specializes in extreme sports and high-energy branding, Red Bull works with promoters to create visually stunning campaigns, such as those featuring snowboarder Travis Rice, aligning with their adventurous brand image.

Promoters manage event sponsorships and athlete endorsements to maximize Red Bull’s reach. Gatorade: A staple in sports hydration, Gatorade signs college athletes like Cooper Flagg, Paige Bueckers, and JuJu Watkins for endorsement deals, expanding its influence in youth markets.

Promoters negotiate these contracts to ensure brand alignment with emerging talent. Reebok: Recently extended a multiyear endorsement with Chicago Sky’s Angel Reese, including a signature shoe release planned for 2026.

Promoters handle such deals to integrate Reebok’s branding into WNBA events and fan engagement. Under Armour, Puma, and New Balance: These brands compete in the athleisure and performance markets, often collaborating with promoters to secure sponsorships for events like marathons or partnerships with rising stars.

Example: New Balance’s revival through collaborations with designers and athletes highlights promoter-driven strategies. Non-Traditional Brands: Companies like YouTube (partnering with Mr. Beast for NBA jersey patches) and luxury brands like Hugo Boss and Gucci (F1 and tennis sponsorships) are increasingly entering sports through innovative partnerships.

Promoters bridge these brands with sports audiences, crafting campaigns that appeal to diverse demographics.

Role of Sports Promoters

Sports promoters act as intermediaries, orchestrating partnerships that benefit brands, athletes, and events.

Their roles include:

Event Promotion: Organizing and marketing events like tournaments, matches, or festivals, ensuring brands gain visibility through sponsorships (e.g., Sports Marketing Australia’s work with AusTriathlon).

Athlete Endorsements: Negotiating deals between brands and athletes, such as Jannik Sinner’s partnerships with Gucci, Nike, and Rolex. Sponsorship Activation: Creating campaigns that integrate brands into sports culture, like Starbucks and Seattle Seahawks’ co-branded merchandise.

Digital and Social Media Campaigns: Leveraging platforms for influencer-driven marketing, as seen with Nike’s #BetterForIt or Red Bull’s extreme sports content.

Global Reach: Connecting brands with international markets, such as Allsport Promotion’s campaigns for global brands across Europe and beyond.

text:
Starlink lost 1000 customers after Forcing Pilots Onto Expensive New Plans
SpaceX reveals the subscriber impact in response to a class-action lawsuit over a March restriction and price hike affecting small plane owners.
Starlink’s decision to increase prices on small plane owners in March caused about 1,000 of them in the US to cancel the satellite internet service, according to a class-action lawsuit.
The figure was revealed in a court document SpaceX filed while moving the lawsuit from California Superior Court to US District Court. The class action was filed in September by a California customer, Thomas Daniel, who alleged that Starlink engaged in a “bait-and-switch” scheme by promoting its service to plane owners, only to suddenly change the plans.
SpaceX imposed a 100mph limit on the more affordable Starlink Roam plans, effectively blocking planes from accessing it. Instead, the company pushed affected customers to new, but pricier aviation plans that permitted speeds of 300mph and 450mph, but could cost as much as $1,000 per month, and required extra payment to exceed the data caps.
In a 10-page court filing, Cory Clark, a senior partnership manager for Starlink’s aviation business, disclosed the subscriber impact. “Approximately two weeks after the aviation plans were offered, more than 1,500 customers in the United States switched from a non-aviation plan to an aviation plan. This data excludes customers who initiated an aviation plan without any prior history with Starlink,” he said. 
But on cancellations, Clark noted: “There were more than 1,000 customers in the United States who received the March 1, 2026, email advising that they exceeded the speed threshold and thereafter cancelled their service within 35 days (the next billing cycle).”
That said, it’s possible some of those customers returned. In late April, Starlink slightly improved some of the pricing and perks for the aviation plans. However, Clark’s filing doesn’t address this.
In a separate court filing, SpaceX said it intends to oppose the class-action lawsuit. However, the company also noted “in the aggregate, there are at least 100 putative class members” and "if [Daniel] were to prevail on all claims asserted in his Complaint, the requested monetary recovery would exceed $5 million."
Daniel is demanding Starlink pay restitution, noting he spent $2,311.11 to buy a Starlink Mini dish and to install it on his plane. "[He] would not have purchased Starlink hardware or subscribed to the Roam plan, or would have paid substantially less for them, had he known that [SpaceX] would unilaterally withdraw aviation functionality without notice and require substantially higher payments to restore materially reduced service," his complaint says.
(PCmag Australia, Michael Kan principal reporter)

text:
New York State and California are limiting an employer's right to claw back a bonus.

New York State, from 19 December: agreements that require an employee to repay money for leaving before a set date become unenforceable. A signing bonus or relocation money can still be reclaimed if the person left of their own accord or was dismissed for misconduct, and if the job was described honestly. If the role is made redundant, nothing is repaid. Only agreements entered into on or after 19 December are covered.

California, from 1 January: a similar ban, with conditions: a separate agreement, five working days to consult a lawyer, repayment without interest and pro rata, and a retention period of no more than two years.

If you are discussing an offer in either state, go through its bonus repayment terms with a lawyer.
